e01.abstract.existence.TorusEuler.theorem11: The odd shear $u(x,y,z)=(\sin(2\pi y),0,0)$ is zero at the origin, where its curl is $(0,0,-2\pi)$. Oddness fixes a particle at the origin and leaves room for a velocity gradient there. Theorem 1.1 constructs an unforced flow for which the curl at that fixed particle tends to infinity at a finite time.

e01.abstract.bounded-velocity.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: The periodic shears $u_n(x,y,z)=(n^{-1}\sin(2\pi n^2y),0,0)$ have speeds at most $n^{-1}$ and curl magnitudes as large as $2\pi n$. The estimates here use the same distinction between amplitude and frequency along a single evolving flow. At order zero, the new wave and the rest of the stage increment each contribute at most $\lambda_j^{-1}$ to the velocity increment. The sum of these bounds is finite, giving one speed bound for every $t<T_*$. Forming the curl differentiates the waves, so the same estimate cannot be applied to the curl.

e01.abstract.central-vorticity.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: Take a wave varying in the first coordinate whose velocity points along the second. Its curl points along the third, so measuring the first component ignores the wave’s curl. This is the projection used at each handoff. The lower bound has to hold between every pair of sufficiently late launches. Projecting the central curl onto the newest wave vector kills that wave’s own leading contribution $k\times a$. The preceding wave supplies a positive component in this direction that dominates the older flow and the errors. The intervals cover a full left neighborhood of $T_*$, so the lower bound holds at all sufficiently late times.

e01.abstract.off-origin.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: On a compact set away from the origin, the late oscillations disappear from the local velocity estimates because their supports shrink. For $\partial_tu$, the pressure still feels the flow near the origin. Its kernel is smooth across the positive distance to the compact set, so uniform convergence of the velocity on the torus suffices for the distant contribution.
e01.abstract.off-origin.TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits: Fix a compact $K$ away from the origin and an order $m$. A single local $C^m$ function $g$ must give the limits through order $m$. The limit of each spatial derivative of order $j\le m$ on $K$ is the corresponding derivative of $g$. In the periodic lift, the compact set must avoid every integer translate of the origin.

e01.intro.goal.TorusEuler.theorem11: The datum is the limit of the stage data $U_j(0)$. At time zero the late oscillations have yet to start, so the tail in $U_j(0)$ is made of the summable corrections, with bounds at every fixed derivative order. The resulting smooth datum is the one whose solution reaches the accumulation time and develops the singularity.

e01.torus.cell.TorusEuler.centeredCell: A periodic field may be integrated over the closed cube $[-1/2,1/2]^3$ to integrate it over one torus period. Taking the closed cube duplicates representatives only on its faces, which have zero volume, so neither the integral nor the essential supremum needs a boundary correction.

e01.torus.periodicity.TorusEuler.SpatiallyPeriodic: The face identifications become the identity $f(x+n)=f(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. For a smooth lift, differentiating that identity shows that the spatial derivatives agree across the faces as well. Thus the gradient and curl computed on $\mathbb R^3$ descend to the torus.

e01.euler-equations.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: Read the `momentum` field as the first equation of (1.1). The expression `fderiv ℝ (u t) x (u t x)` takes the spatial derivative at $x$ and applies it to the local velocity $u(t,x)$, giving $(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The `timeDerivative` term uses the derivative within $[0,T_*)$, so it is right-sided at $0$. The `incompressible` field gives the second equation. The `mean_zero_pressure` field fixes the freedom to add a function of time to $p$.

r5-root-introduction-scope.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1: Identifying opposite faces gives a torus with no physical boundary. Oddness fixes the particle at the origin. The proof bounds the speed throughout that domain while making the curl at one fixed particle diverge. On a compact set at positive distance from that particle, the same construction gives convergence of all spatial derivatives of the velocity and its first time derivative.

r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_1_1: The theorem chooses one smooth odd, divergence-free datum and one flow whose speed stays bounded while the magnitude of its curl at the origin tends to infinity at a finite time. The first conjunct, `EulerSingularityWitness u₀ T u p`, includes the two divergent time integrals and the spatial limits of both $u$ and $\partial_tu$ away from the origin. In the last conjunct, `v 0 = u₀` selects any other maximal solution from that datum. The conclusion gives it the same lifespan $T$ and equates the velocities on $[0,T)$.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1: The proof applies Proposition 8.1 to the constructed stage sequence at its accumulation time $T_\infty$. This gives the datum $u(0)$ and the Euler flow on $[0,T_\infty)$. Proposition 8.2 gives (1.3), Corollary 8.3 identifies $T_*=T_\infty$ and proves (1.2), and Proposition 8.4 supplies the two compact-set limits. Each step uses the same $u$.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsMaximalEulerSolution: A continuation is a smooth Euler velocity on $[0,S)$ with $S>T_*$ that agrees with $u$ for all $t<T_*$. Its curl at the origin would be continuous on the compact interval $[0,T_*]$ and therefore bounded there. The divergence in (1.3) rules out every such continuation.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution.velocity_eq_o: For two velocities with the same datum, set $w=u-v$ and work on a closed interval inside both lifespans. In the derivative of $\int_{\mathbb T^3}|w|^2$, periodic integration by parts kills the transport term and the pressure term, using $\operatorname{div}v=\operatorname{div}w=0$. The remaining term is bounded by $2\|\nabla u\|_\infty\int|w|^2$, so Grönwall and $w(0)=0$ give equality throughout the common interval.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: The witness asks both for pointwise curl divergence at the origin and for divergence of the time integral of its spatial supremum. The paper obtains the integral conclusion from the continuation criterion. The Lean proof obtains it directly by multiplying a lower bound on the curl between launches by a lower bound on each late interval’s duration. The gradient integral then follows from $\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_\infty\le C\|\nabla u\|_\infty$.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: The construction first passes to the limit in the equation after projecting onto divergence-free fields. For a smooth periodic limit the removed gradient is recovered as the gradient of a smooth pressure, with its spatial mean fixed to zero. The Lean predicate requires this velocity–pressure equation on $[0,T_*)$, with the derivative taken from the right at the initial time.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits: The distance of $K$ from the origin determines when the shrinking wave supports miss a neighborhood of $K$. The derivative order $m$ determines when the stage estimates control the required derivatives. Once both conditions hold, the remaining velocity increments are summable on $K$ through order $m$. Proposition 8.4 applies a separate pressure estimate to obtain the corresponding limit for $\partial_tu$.

e01.remark.smooth-extension.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.remark_1_2: The extension has to be smooth jointly in time and space near the terminal slice, so its mixed derivatives of every fixed order must reach $T_*$. The result in Theorem 1.1 supplies spatial limits for $u$ and $\partial_tu$. The stronger choice in the remark adds time-derivative estimates before extending the field across the slice.
e01.remark.smooth-extension.TorusEuler.Paper.remark_1_2: The additional estimates are built into the choice of the frequency schedule. On that schedule, the same limit has all the conclusions of Theorem 1.1 and summable increments in each fixed mixed space-time norm away from the origin. Those mixed bounds give the smooth extension for that particular solution.

r2a1.intro.smooth-extension-proof-route.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.remark_1_2: In the auxiliary note, the threshold $\mathcal B$ is chosen to absorb constants in the estimates for time derivatives as well as spatial ones. The mixed-derivative tails then converge up to $T_*$ on compact sets away from the origin, where the late waves vanish. The checked proof obtains those bounds for a particular scheduled construction and uses its smooth extension to prove the existential remark.

e01.intro.approximate-sequence.TorusEuler.paperTheorem71: The construction chooses the threshold function before choosing the starting frequency $N$. For each sufficiently large $N$, the recursion fixes a sequence of orders and frequencies, and the construction supplies the corresponding stages on a common time slab. The orders tend to infinity, so any fixed derivative order can eventually be controlled along that sequence.
e01.intro.approximate-sequence.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: At each stage $U_j$ is already smooth, periodic and divergence-free. Its Euler momentum residual is bounded by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$ on the whole stage slab $[0,S_j]$. Since the terminal time lies before every $S_j$, the residual tends to zero on one domain shared by the stages.

e01.intro.spatial-convergence.TorusEuler.PaperLimitAgreement: In Proposition 8.1 the velocities converge uniformly even on the closed slab through $T_\infty$. That is the `closed_velocity_limit` field. For any higher spatial order $m$, first fix $S<T_\infty$. Beyond some stage, the waves have yet to activate on $[0,S]$, leaving a summable tail of corrections in $C^{m,1/2}$. Lean records this in `prefix_convergence` using `spatialHolderHalfNorm`. The `initial_convergence` field records the same convergence of the stage data at time zero.
e01.intro.spatial-convergence.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.paper_pr: Integrate the projected momentum equation in time before taking the limit. On a fixed interval $[0,S]$ below $T_\infty$, the residual integral is bounded by $S\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$. Convergence in $C^{1,1/2}$ controls the quadratic term after projection. The resulting integral identity gives the Euler equation for the limit, which agrees with the classical solution from $u_0$ by uniqueness.

e01.intro.localized-small-waves.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: Two successive frequencies control different parts of the new oscillation $O_j$. The old frequency $\lambda_{j-1}$ gives the support radius $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$, while the new frequency gives the velocity bound $\lambda_j^{-1}$. At the origin, the central gradient includes a rank-one term $a_j\otimes\kappa_j$ once the wave is fully active, so that small velocity can still supply a large shear.

e01.intro.finite-growth-time.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: Write $\tau_j$ for the upper bound on $t_{j+1}-t_j$. The schedule gives $\tau_{j+1}\le \tau_j/4$, so the total time remaining at the $j$th launch is at most $4\tau_j/3$. This is shorter than the stage’s remaining slab length $2\tau_j$, which puts the accumulation time inside every stage slab.

r2a1.intro.wave.background.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: For the background alone, the material acceleration is $(D'+D^2)x$, since differentiating $Dx$ along a trajectory adds $D\dot x=D^2x$. A linear vector field is a gradient exactly when its matrix is symmetric, which gives the quadratic pressure. The trace condition handles divergence separately. The linked theorem carries both conditions into the superposition and uses a time derivative of $D$ within the interval.

r2a1.intro.wave.velocity.TorusEuler.affineWaveVelocity: In the paper $w=\mathbf a(t)F(k(t)\cdot x)$ is the added wave on $\mathbb R^3$. The Lean function returns the full velocity. The term `D t x` is the affine background and `F ⟪k t, x⟫_ℝ • a t` multiplies $\mathbf a(t)$ by the scalar profile at the phase $k(t)\cdot x$. If $F$ is odd, both terms vanish at $x=0$, so the particle there stays fixed even with a large wave gradient. The wave equations impose the perpendicularity of $\mathbf a$ and $k$ separately.
r2a1.intro.wave.velocity.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The wave derivative sends $v$ to $F'(k\cdot x)(k\cdot v)\mathbf a$. Taking its trace gives $F'(k\cdot x)(k\cdot\mathbf a)$, and feeding in $w$ gives $F'(k\cdot x)F(k\cdot x)(k\cdot\mathbf a)\mathbf a$. Thus one perpendicularity condition removes both the wave divergence and its quadratic self-interaction. The exact-wave theorem uses the two ODEs in (1.4) for the remaining terms.

intro.affine-euler.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: After the phase terms cancel, the acceleration is $(D'+D^2)x+p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$. Its two summands are canceled by the gradients of the background pressure and the wave primitive term. The trace condition and transversality give zero divergence. These identities verify Euler on $\mathbb R^3$ for differentiable $F$ with $P'=F$. A nonzero $D$ makes $Dx$ unbounded along some lattice direction, so a bounded periodic profile alone cannot put the superposition on the torus.

intro.affine-equations.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn: The first equation evolves $k$ as a covector. If $M'=DM$ is the background deformation with $M(t_0)=I$, then $(M^Tk)'=0$, so $k=M^{-T}k(t_0)$. The second equation evolves the velocity amplitude with its normal pressure term. The Lean predicate packages the two relative derivatives on the time interval, including the one-sided derivatives at included endpoints.
intro.affine-equations.TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff: For $k\ne0$, write $\Pi_k v=(k\cdot v)k/|k|^2$ for projection onto the wave normal. Since $p_{\rm w}k=2\Pi_k(D\mathbf a)$, the amplitude equation applies the reflection $2\Pi_k-I$ to $D\mathbf a$. The normal component of $D\mathbf a$ is preserved and the tangential component is reversed. Lean's coefficient definition supplies precisely the scalar for this reflection.

intro.affine-pressure.TorusEuler.affineWavePressure: The pressure adds the quadratic potential for the background to a primitive term for the wave. The minus sign before $p_{\rm w}P$ makes $-\nabla p$ contribute $+p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$. Oddness gives the periodic profile $F$ zero phase mean, so $P$ can be periodic. Subtracting the mean of $P$ then changes the pressure by a function of time alone.

intro.self-advection.TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection: At fixed time, the map $x\mapsto x+h w(x)$ stays in the same phase plane for all $h$, since $k\cdot w(x)=0$. Differentiate $w(x+h w(x))=w(x)$ at $h=0$ to obtain the self-advection identity as soon as $F$ is differentiable at that phase. The mixed term $(w\cdot\nabla)Dx=F(k\cdot x)D\mathbf a$ still enters the momentum equation.

r2a1.intro.phase-and-pressure-cancellati.TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAccelerati: The $F'$ term from $\partial_t w$ contains $k'\cdot x$, and the one from advection by $Dx$ contains $k\cdot Dx$. Their sum is $(k'+D^Tk)\cdot x=0$. With self-advection also gone, the wave contributes exactly $F(k\cdot x)(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)$. This acceleration lemma keeps $\mathbf a'$ general, so the pressure balance can be imposed on the remaining coefficient.
r2a1.intro.phase-and-pressure-cancellati.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_affineWavePress: In `hasGradientAt_affineWavePressure`, the linear map $S$ is $D'+D^2$ in the paper. The hypothesis `hS` makes $S$ self-adjoint, so the derivative of $-x\cdot Sx/2$ in direction $v$ is $-\tfrac12(v\cdot Sx+x\cdot Sv)=-v\cdot Sx$. The hypothesis `hP` supplies $P'=F$ at the phase $k\cdot x$. The chain rule gives the second gradient term, $-p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$. It cancels the remaining wave acceleration when $\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a=p_{\rm w}k$.

intro.pressure-transversality.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePa: The two derivatives each contribute $-k\cdot D\mathbf a$ to $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'$. The pressure contributes $p_{\rm w}|k|^2$, which cancels their sum. Lean proves this as a derivative identity at each time with $k\ne0$. On an interval the pairing is therefore constant, so transverse data at one time give transverse data throughout.

intro.origin-gradient.TorusEuler.hasFDerivAt_planeWave: At $x=0$, every time slice samples the same phase, so $F'(0)=1$ gives the linear map $v\mapsto(k\cdot v)\mathbf a$. Its operator norm is $|k||\mathbf a|$, attained in the normal direction, and its curl contribution is $k\times\mathbf a$ of the same length under perpendicularity. The wave can therefore have small speed and still supply a large central gradient by increasing its frequency.

intro.preceding-frame.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame: The shear acts on a vector $v$ as $\sigma(E_1\cdot v)E_2$. Its vorticity is $\sigma E_3$. Thus the choice $k=\lambda E_3$ both aligns the new normal with the preceding vorticity and leaves the new transverse plane spanned by $E_1,E_2$, the two directions between which amplification takes place.
intro.preceding-frame.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The strength $\sigma$ is the magnitude of both the rank-one gradient (in operator norm) and the vorticity of the preceding wave at the origin. Here it is a function of time; in §2.2.1 it is denoted by $\sigma_p(t)$, and $\sigma=\sigma_p(t_0)$ is frozen at launch. The latter is `initialStrength` in Lean.

intro.preceding-shear.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r: In the model, $k_2(t_0)=0$, so the preceding shear initially makes no contribution to $\dot k_1$. The rotating-frame equations give $\dot k_2(t_0)=-2\eta\lambda$ and $\ddot k_1(t_0)=2(\sigma+\nu)\eta\lambda$. Thus the tilt towards $E_1$ begins quadratically, even though the displacement towards $-E_2$ begins linearly. The two derivatives account for the factor $(\sigma+\nu)\eta$ in the introductory turning law.

intro.two-coupling-frame.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.movingFrameDeriva:
Differentiating a unit vector discards the component of its derivative along itself. In the $E_1$ equation, projecting $-B^TE_1$ leaves $-
u E_2-B_{13}E_3$. In the $E_2$ equation, the pressure adds $2
u E_1$ to the projected $-BE_2$, giving $+
u E_1-\eta E_3$. The introductory model sets $B_{13}=0$, and its two off-diagonal entries also make $B_{33}=0$, so the preceding strength is constant in that model.

intro-amplification-polarization.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteComparison:
At launch $a_3=0$ and pressure acts only along $E_3$. The frozen two-component system has growing rate $g=\sqrt{2
u(\sigma-
u)}$ and ratio $a_1/a_2=-2
u/g=-S^{-1}(1-1/(2S^2))^{-1/2}$, where $S=\sqrt{\sigma/(2
u)}$. Taking just $-S^{-1}$ makes the scaled initial data exactly $(-1,1)$ in (2.3); the discarded relative correction is $O(S^{-2})$.

r2a1.intro.strong-shear-factor.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: Put $x=\tan\varphi$. In the first scaled amplitude equation the pressure contributes $x(x+\varepsilon)/(1+x^2)$ times $\alpha_2$, which adds to the direct term $-\alpha_2$. Since $-1+x(x+\varepsilon)/(1+x^2)=-(1-\varepsilon x)/(1+x^2)$, the net driving term in the equation for $a_1$ in physical time is $-2\nu\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)a_2$ in the strong-shear approximation. The pressure also contributes a term proportional to $a_1$; the stated factor describes only the coefficient of $a_2$.
r2a1.intro.strong-shear-factor.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3: The vanishing of the driving coefficient is not the vanishing of the growth rate. Put $s=\cos\varphi$. Eliminating $\alpha_1$ in (2.5) gives $(s^{-2}a_{\rm ref}')'=(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)a_{\rm ref}$. Since $a_{\rm ref}>0$ and $a_{\rm ref}'(0)=1$, the weighted derivative is still positive when $\varepsilon\tan\varphi=1$. Only afterwards does it decrease to zero, at the maximum located by Lemma 2.5.

intro-amplification-gain.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteReturn: The gain permits us to prescribe a small maximum for the new velocity without prescribing an appreciable velocity at launch. More is needed for the periodic construction: while the time cutoff changes, the amplitude must remain small throughout an interval. Proposition 2.8 bounds it by $e^{3-\varepsilon^{-1/2}}$ times its maximum during the first unit of the growth clock $\tau$.

intro-amplification-new-frame.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame: The new normal for the following launch will be chosen along $E_{3,+}$, the vorticity direction of the present wave. The direction is unchanged by positive rescaling of either $k$ or $\mathbf a$. The size of their product, in contrast, fixes the shear $\sigma_+$ and hence helps set the next growth rate $\sqrt{2\sigma_+\nu_+}$.

intro-amplification-new-couplings.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry: The older gradient here is the one seen by the present wave (called $M$ in §2.2). Its coupling entries in the new frame are unchanged by adding $\mathbf a\otimes k$, since $(\mathbf a\otimes k)E_{2,+}=0$. In the periodic construction the actual next parent also has a central correction error; that error must be estimated separately, rather than included in the prescribed ratio.

intro-amplification-cancellation.TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators: The cancellation in the third coupling is a consequence of the amplitude direction as well as the normal. In the notation of (2.13), put $s=\cos\varphi$ and $u=\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi/2$, so the logarithmic amplitude rate satisfies $Y/s=1+e-u$. The second expression for the reference couplings, divided by $s$, is $\varepsilon\tan\varphi-1+2(Y/s+u)^2-2u^2$. Since $2u^2=\varepsilon\tan\varphi\sin^2\varphi$, this reduces to $1+4e+2e^2+\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$. The remaining coefficient is close to one; estimating the original terms separately would lose the small factor $s$.

intro-amplification-late-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_7:
The old ratio $\varepsilon$ governs the present wave; the new ratio starts at $1/\varepsilon$ in the reference calculation and will govern its successor. Near the desired crossing, $
u_+/
u$ is close to one while $\eta_+/
u_+$ is comparable to $\cos\varphi$. Thus it is the third coupling that becomes small, not both couplings at once.
intro-amplification-late-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7:
The two conclusions have different precision requirements. A fixed multiplicative estimate for $\eta_+/
u_+$ suffices to bracket a crossing. For the first coupling, the bound $|
u_+/
u-1|\le\varepsilon$ is stronger: the logarithmic changes at successive crossings are then summable as the ratios decrease. A fixed comparison of $
u_+$ with $
u$ would not ensure that the inherited growth rate stays uniformly controlled.

intro-amplification-crossing.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteReturn: After the reference peak, the two factors of the new shear have different time scales. With $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$, the proof of Proposition 2.8 gives $|\mathbf a|/A\asymp1/(\varepsilon\tau)$ and $|k|/\lambda\asymp\varepsilon\tau^2$. Their product divided by $\lambda A$ is comparable to $\tau$. At a late crossing, $\tau\asymp(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$, so waiting for a smaller successor ratio is compatible with retaining a large shear. These are estimates of values on the comparison interval, not monotonicity of the perturbed wave.

e01.initial-shear.formula.TorusEuler.stationaryShear: The base flow is a single sine in the second coordinate, with velocity in the fixed direction $e_1+\rho e_3$. Its frequencies are therefore $\pm e_2$, and differentiation at the origin gives $2\pi(e_1+\rho e_3)\otimes e_2$. In the initial frame this gives the two entries $2\pi$ and $2\pi\rho$ that set the coupling ratio for the next wave.

e01.initial-shear.euler.TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_stationaryShe: Every particle moves within a plane of fixed $x_2$, on which $U_0$ is constant. Hence $U_0\cdot\nabla U_0=0$, while the only potentially nonzero column of $\nabla U_0$ is column two, with zero diagonal entry. The stationary momentum equation and incompressibility then hold with $p=0$. Lean verifies this for any real $\rho$ on any positive time slab.

e01.initial-shear.couplings.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_origi: Here the derivative is a matrix with just one nonzero column: $B_\rho v=2\pi v_2(e_1+\rho e_3)$. The two couplings are entries of that column, rather than two components of the shear velocity (which vanishes at the origin).
e01.initial-shear.couplings.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_coupl: Take the first wave with normal $e_1$ and amplitude along $e_2$, so that the third frame vector is $e_3$. Then $B_{12}=2\pi$ and $B_{32}=2\pi\rho$. The tilt $\rho$ can therefore be used to prescribe the gain of the second wave without changing the first coupling.

e01.initial-shear.flow.TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow: The label $a_2$ is constant on a seed trajectory, so $X_0(t,a)=a+tU_0(a)$ and the inverse map is $X_0(-t,\cdot)$. Composing the initial phase $\lambda a_1$ with this inverse gives $\lambda(x_1-t\sin(2\pi x_2))$. Its gradient at the fixed origin is $\lambda(e_1-2\pi t e_2)$, the changing covector that enters the first-wave amplitude equation.

localized.intro.periodic-localization.TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile: At $x=X(t,a)$ the leading wave is $g(a)F_h(k_*\cdot a)\mathbf a(t,a)$. Both scalar factors are constant along the parent trajectory, so the material derivative differentiates only the seed. In particular the moving edge of the support produces no term $U\cdot\nabla g$ in the amplitude equation.

localized.intro.real-wave-vector.TorusEuler.localizedCompletedWave_proper: The condition $k_*\cdot n\in\mathbb Z$ for every lattice vector $n$ would be necessary for the phase modulo one to be well defined everywhere on the torus. Here we periodically extend the evaluated, supported potential instead. Its zero collar removes the need to match phases on opposite faces, leaving the direction of the wave vector free; its curl is then a smooth periodic solenoidal velocity.

c8-endpoint-choice-introduction.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: In the scalar analogue $y''-m^2y=f$ of (1.7), a constant force and zero initial position and velocity give $y=f(\cosh(mt)-1)/m^2$. If instead we choose $y'(0)=-(f/m)\tanh(mT/2)$, the solution has $y(0)=y(T)=0$ and $|y(t)|\le |f|/m^2$ on the entire interval. The choice of the initial velocity removes the large response; the problem below is to make such a choice with the incompressibility constraint.

e01.endpoint.flow-equation.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn: At fixed $a$, $\partial_t(h\circ X)=(\partial_t h+u\cdot\nabla h)\circ X$. This converts material differentiation into ordinary time differentiation. The flow in Lean has a further argument for the starting time: the paper uses $X(0,t,a)$ in that notation, and its inverse is $X(t,0,\cdot)$.

e01.endpoint.first-variation-equation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_endpointDisp: Let $F=D_aX$ and $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$. Differentiating the flow with respect to its initial position gives $F_t=MF$. Thus $(F^{-1}\xi)_t=F^{-1}(b\circ X)$, and the terminal condition is precisely $\int_0^T F^{-1}(b\circ X)\,dt=0$ at each label. The linked product rule is the forward identity for $\xi=Fz$; it assumes the equations for $F$ and $z$, rather than differentiating the perturbed flow itself.
e01.endpoint.first-variation-equation.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The displacement variable of §4 has a direct interpretation. The relative map $X(t,\cdot)^{-1}\circ X_\delta(t,\cdot)$ is the identity at $\delta=0$, and its derivative in $\delta$ is $z=(D_aX)^{-1}\xi$. Its time derivative is $v=(D_aX)^{-1}(b\circ X)$ by (1.5). Both maps preserve volume, so $z$ is divergence free in labels. These are the displacement and velocity stored in the smooth mean solution.

r2a1.intro.initial-displacement.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The endpoint condition is on the position of each particle. Since $X_\delta(0,a)=a$ for every $\delta$, the initial displacement is zero independently of the choice of $b$. At either end, (1.5) now gives $\xi_t=b\circ X$; the slopes at the two ends need not vanish. In particular $b(0)$ is available to enforce the terminal condition.

e01.endpoint.selected-initial-value.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: For two choices of initial velocity with the same force and zero terminal displacement, the difference solves (1.7) with $f=0$ and both traces zero. The quadratic form in (1.8)–(1.9) rules out a nonzero difference. This is injectivity of the linearized endpoint map; existence of the required initial value is the additional content of the inverse in §4.3.

e01.endpoint.linearized-euler.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: At fixed label put $B=b\circ X$ and $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$. The linearized momentum equation becomes $B_t+MB+(\nabla q)\circ X=f\circ X$, with $B=\xi_t-M\xi$ from (1.5). Substitution cancels the two terms containing $M\xi_t$ and leaves the Jacobi equation with coefficient $-(M_t+M^2)$. This is why a first-order equation for $b$ leads to a two-endpoint problem for $\xi$.

e01.endpoint.pressure-cancellation.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.det_labelDeriva: Let $F=D_aX$. Since $F_t=MF$ and $\operatorname{tr} M=0$, Jacobi’s formula gives $(\det F)_t=0$ and $\det F=1$. This removes the change-of-variables factor in (1.8). Vanishing of the pressure integral also uses the first-order constraint on $\xi\circ X^{-1}$.
e01.endpoint.pressure-cancellation.TorusEuler.integral_inner_gradient_cente: Volume preservation of the relative map $X^{-1}\circ X_\delta$ gives $\operatorname{div}_a((D_aX)^{-1}\xi)=0$. Equivalently, the physical vector $w=\xi\circ X^{-1}$ is divergence free by Piola. The linked cancellation is the last step: $\int_{\mathbb T^3}\nabla q\cdot w=-\int_{\mathbb T^3}q\operatorname{div}w=0$, with no boundary term on the torus.

e01.endpoint.poincare-local.TorusEuler.terminal_poincare_pointwise: Only the terminal condition is used here: $\xi(t,a)=-\int_t^T\xi_s(s,a)\,ds$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the factor $T-t$, and its integral from $0$ to $T$ is $T^2/2$. The zero initial trace enters separately when testing the Jacobi equation by $-\xi$, to remove the other boundary term.

e01.endpoint.coercivity.TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementEnergy_co: If $H\le hI$ with $h\ge0$, (1.8) gives the lower bound $(1-hT^2/2)\|\xi_t\|_2^2$. Thus it is the product of the upper curvature bound with the square of the interval length that matters for this estimate. With $h=1$ and $T\le1$ the loss is at most one half, regardless of the magnitude of negative eigenvalues.
e01.endpoint.coercivity.TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_coercive: The form in (1.9) is written in the physical displacement. Appendix A solves instead for the label velocity $v=(D_aX)^{-1}(b\circ X)$, with $z=\int_0^t v$ and $\xi=D_aXz$. The identity (4.7) is what transfers the lower bound to the quadratic form of that operator. The linked lemma is this transfer for continuously differentiable paths; the $L^2$ version used in the inverse is obtained by density.

r2a1.intro.hessian-upper.TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementEnergy_co: The sign in the energy is $-\xi\cdot H\xi$. A negative eigenvalue therefore improves the lower bound, even if its magnitude is large. Later the wave pressure Hessian has leading term $-p_{\rm w}F_h'(s)k\otimes k$; for $p_{\rm w}>0$ only the shallow negative part of $F_h'$ produces positive curvature. This explains the asymmetric profile in (1.10).

r2a1.intro.zero-source-uniqueness.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: The kernel statement concerns initial velocities whose induced displacement returns to zero. If $f=0$, the energy identity and coercivity first give $\xi_t=0$, then $\xi=0$ by the initial trace. Equation (1.5) then gives $b=0$ throughout the interval. The same proof, applied to a difference, works for any prescribed force.

e01.endpoint.approximate-hessian.TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHe: Write $B=b\circ X$. Combining $\xi_t=M\xi+B$ with $B_t=-MB-(\nabla q)\circ X+f\circ X$ gives $\xi_{tt}=(M_t+M^2)\xi-(\nabla q)\circ X+f\circ X$. Thus the coefficient of $\xi$ on the left of (1.7) is $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$ even without an exact Euler equation. Differentiating the parent's residual identity then gives (4.3); a pressure Hessian alone would omit the residual gradient.

e01.endpoint.quantitative-inverse.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse: For a solution satisfying the two end conditions, (1.8)–(1.9) and volume preservation give $\tfrac12\|\xi_t\|_2^2\le \|f\|_2\|\xi\|_2\le (T/\sqrt2)\|f\|_2\|\xi_t\|_2$. Hence $\|\xi_t\|_2\le\sqrt2T\|f\|_2$. This estimate cannot control a value of $\xi_t$ at an individual time, in particular $b(0)$. That is why the existence proof in §4.3 must recover a time-continuous velocity with the stronger spatial Hölder estimate.

localized.intro.affine-pressure-hessian.TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian: At fixed time the affine coefficient and normal are constant in space. Along a unit direction $e$, the second derivative of $-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$ is $-p_{\rm w}F'(k\cdot x)(k\cdot e)^2$. All directions tangent to the phase planes therefore have zero curvature; only the normal curvature needs a sign estimate.

localized.intro.profile-slopes.TorusEuler.hasDerivAt_waveProfile_zero: For a fixed normal $k$ and amplitude $\mathbf a$, the gradient at phase zero is $\mathbf a\otimes k$ for every $h$. The region in which the bump makes the slope large has thickness $O(h/|k|)$ in the normal direction. The height of the whole profile is $O(h)$, so the velocity can be small while its central shear is unchanged.
localized.intro.profile-slopes.TorusEuler.deriv_waveProfile_bounds: Periodicity forces $\int_0^1F_h'=0$. We therefore cannot choose a nonnegative slope throughout the period. The narrow bump in $F_h'$ permits its compensating negative slope to be $O(h)$, rather than order one as for a sine normalized to have unit central slope. The explicit Lean family satisfies $-h/2\le F_h'\le1$.

localized.intro.central-plane-gradient.TorusEuler.hasFDerivAt_planeWave: At phase zero the derivative sends the unit normal $k/|k|$ to $|k|\mathbf a$ and kills the plane perpendicular to $k$. It is a shear because $\mathbf a\perp k$. Its size is $|\mathbf a||k|$, not $|\mathbf a|\|F_h\|_\infty$.

localized.intro.positive-curvature.TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u: For any $v$, the pressure term in the displacement energy is determined by $v\cdot D^2p_{\rm wave}v=-p_{\rm w}F_h'(k\cdot x)(k\cdot v)^2$. If $p_{\rm w}\ge0$, this is at most $(h/2)p_{\rm w}|k|^2|v|^2$. The estimate is one-sided: the large negative value at the center contributes with the favorable sign to the energy in (4.7).

localized.intro.small-velocity.TorusEuler.norm_waveProfile_le: Over a period the positive and negative variations of $F_h$ are equal, since $\int_0^1F_h'=0$. The negative variation is at most $Ch$, by the lower slope bound. Both variations are therefore small, and $F_h(0)=0$ gives $\|F_h\|_\infty\le Ch$ although $F_h'(0)=1$.

localized.intro.bump-construction.TorusEuler.waveSlope: A narrow positive bump alone cannot be the derivative of a periodic function. Its mean $c_h$ is subtracted to make the integral zero, and the result is divided by $1-c_h$ to restore slope one at zero. Outside the bump the resulting slope is the constant $-c_h/(1-c_h)=O(h)$ in magnitude.

e01.correction.frequency-truncation.TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalC: The cutoff puts $u=S_\Lambda V$ in the band $2\Lambda$, but its residual $R_u=\partial_tu+\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)$ lies in the band $4\Lambda$: the time derivative preserves the fixed band, while multiplication adds frequencies. Bernstein therefore estimates derivatives of the small defect $R_u$ itself, without estimating the much larger summands of its momentum separately. In particular $\|\nabla R_u\|_\infty\le C\Lambda\|R_u\|_\infty$, which is used to preserve the endpoint coercivity in the next step.

e01.correction.parent-residual.TorusEuler.momentumResidual: Frequency truncation leaves an error $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$. In the new expansion $R_U\circ X$ has no dependence on the independent phase $s$, so it is the first mean, $B_2$, that cancels it: $\bar f_2=-\langle H_2\rangle-R_U\circ X$. In the momentum of the completed approximation the old defect cancels exactly; the remaining terms come from the finite depth and the time cutoff.

localized.intro.phase-trajectory.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject: Along the parent, $(\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla)\theta=0$. Adding the leading velocity does not change this identity, since $A_1\cdot\kappa=0$. The completed wave need not be tangent to the phase surfaces: its normal component is determined by (3.6), and the full phase drift is controlled in Lemma 5.10.

localized.intro.phase-gradient.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_transportedPhas: The identity $\theta\circ X=k_*\cdot a$ implies $(D_aX)^T\nabla_x\theta=k_*$. The inverse transpose therefore transports the normal, whereas $D_aX$ transports particle separations. This calculation takes place in the lifted cell and does not require $\theta$ to be a single-valued real phase on the torus.
localized.intro.phase-gradient.TorusEuler.labelWaveVector: The formal normal uses the derivative of the reverse flow, evaluated at the current particle: $(D_xX^{-1})^Tk_*$. Differentiating $X^{-1}\circ X=\operatorname{Id}$ identifies it with $(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$. In particular the normal cannot vanish as long as the flow is invertible and $k_*\ne0$.

localized.intro.slow-fast-derivatives.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule: At fixed physical $x$ the spatial derivative of a profile has two terms, $D_xA_1$ at fixed $s$ and $(\partial_sA_1)\kappa^T$. The latter differentiates the oscillation and can be much larger. Along the parent, however, $(\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla)\theta=0$, so there is no corresponding fast term in the material derivative.

localized.intro.time-cutoff.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff: For $t_0>0$ the cutoff is flat at the activation time, so the seed need only be constructed on $[t_0,T]$. The cutoff does not determine the later initial data of the *mean* correction, which are selected by the two-endpoint problem. In particular, switching off the oscillation is not the same as switching off the whole velocity increment.
localized.intro.time-cutoff.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first: For the first wave take $t_0=0$ and $\widetilde\chi=1$ throughout the slab. No activation derivative appears in its residual, unlike the later waves for which $\widetilde\chi'$ must be estimated.

localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Zd: At level $p\ge2$ the correction $C_p=C[V_{p-1}]$ is known before we form the error to be canceled. It is grouped with the new fields $B_p,V_p$ because of its size, rather than with $V_{p-1}$, the oscillation from which it was computed. This grouping is used to collect the quadratic terms in (5.26).
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Cd: In the stored family the correction has the index of the oscillation from which it is computed: `u.C p` is $C_{p+1}$, not $C_p$. The definition `Cd` shifts the index back to the paper’s convention; the zero entry of the stored family represents $C_1=0$.
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.expansion: For divergence it is preferable to group the same sum as $W=\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$. Each pair $V_p+C_{p+1}$ is a curl and each $B_p$ is solenoidal. The last pair uses $C_{P+1}$ even though there is no level-$P+1$ mean or transverse solve.
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity_eq: The sum of the $Z_p$ contains $C_1,\ldots,C_P$, whereas the sum of completed oscillations contains $C_2,\ldots,C_{P+1}$. Their difference is $C_{P+1}$ since $C_1=0$. In particular the finite expansion is a sum of curls and solenoidal means even though the individual $Z_p$ need not be solenoidal.

localized.intro.leading-level.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: The first level is prescribed, not obtained by solving a forced inverse problem. In `IsExpansion` the activated seed wave and its pressure are given at level one, with $B_1=C_1=0$. Its own curl completion is $C_2$, and the first unknown mean and oscillation are $B_2,V_2$.
localized.intro.leading-level.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr: The first oscillation and its pressure enter the recursion as data, with $B_1=\bar q_1=0$. The theorem retains this supplied pair; the identification with $\widetilde\chi A_1$ and $\widetilde\chi\mathsf p[A_1]$ is made using (3.7), not by applying the zero-start inverse to the seed.
There are no stored profiles at index zero or above $P$. This does not set the paper's $C_{P+1}$ to zero: it is stored at index $P$, alongside the oscillation that generates it.

localized.intro.level-scaling.TorusEuler.hierarchyOscExponent: At its normalization the seed amplitude is $\lambda^{-3/4}$, while the phase profile $F_h$ has size $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. Their product gives $\lambda^{-5/4}$. Each increase of level is assigned a gain $\lambda^{-2/3}$; the estimates in Theorem 5.6 show that the actual errors gain at least this much.

localized.intro.phase-split.TorusEuler.phaseMean: A phase average is taken before evaluating the phase at its physical value. For example, the profile $b(t,x)F_h(s)$ has zero phase mean at every $x$, but the value $b(t,x)F_h(\theta(t,x))$ need not vanish or have zero spatial integral for general $b$. The operation retains the spatial dependence of the force that is to enter the mean equation.
localized.intro.phase-split.TorusEuler.phaseOscillation: Write $H_2=\langle H_2\rangle_s+(H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s)$. The second summand has zero phase integral at each $(t,x)$, as required by (1.12): the phase pressure derivative also has zero integral. The mean equation absorbs the first summand, for which this transverse equation alone cannot provide a centered response.

e01.correction.mean-source.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_: The part of the wave error seen by the mean equation at level two is $\mathbf d\cdot\langle V_1\otimes V_1\rangle_s$ (row divergence in labels), not the full stress of $V_1+C_2$. The fast product of $C_2$ with $V_1$ supplies the term $\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V_1)V_1\rangle_s$ needed to obtain this divergence. Since $V_1=\widetilde\chi g\mathbf a F_h$, the tensor is $\widetilde\chi^2 g^2\langle F_h^2\rangle_s\mathbf a\otimes\mathbf a$. Its negative divergence and $-R_U$ force the mean. The linked algebraic identity assumes the fast-product cancellation proved in (5.25).
e01.correction.mean-source.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.meanSource: The residual belongs entirely to the phase-independent part: it is the same at every $s$. Even where the localized wave vanishes, the mean equation still has the inherited force $-R_U$ (or $-R_U\circ X$ in labels). It is therefore a torus-wide solve, not a correction supported only where the wave lives.

e01.correction.mean-equation.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: We average in the independent phase $s$ while keeping $(t,x)$ fixed. Averaging the profile equation therefore gives the Eulerian source $-\langle H_2\rangle_s-R_U$ for $B_2$, including the truncation residual of the parent. The inverse takes this full spatial field as its force; it is not a projection of the physical wave onto the zero spatial Fourier mode.
e01.correction.mean-equation.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_: The first mean error is a slow divergence of a stress. Indeed $\kappa\cdot\partial_s C_2=-\mathbf d\cdot V_1$, so periodic integration by parts replaces $\langle(C_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1\rangle_s$ by $\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V_1)V_1\rangle_s$. Together with $\langle(V_1\cdot\mathbf d)V_1\rangle_s$ this is $\mathbf d\cdot\langle V_1\otimes V_1\rangle_s$. Thus the source contains two velocity factors and a slow derivative rather than a fast derivative of the wave; the parent residual is added separately. The linked assembly lemma takes the phase integration by parts as a hypothesis.

e01.correction.mean-endpoints.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: To see the terminal condition, solve (1.5) by variation of constants: $\xi(T,a)=D_aX(T,a)\int_0^T(D_aX(t,a))^{-1}B_2(t,X(t,a))\,dt$. The integral must vanish at each label. The factor $(D_aX(t,a))^{-1}$ converts velocities at different times into the same particle coordinates before they are added.
e01.correction.mean-endpoints.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: With the parent at rest and solenoidal $f$ supported on $[t_0,T]$, the correction satisfies $b(t)=b(0)$ on $[0,t_0]$. Requiring zero displacement at both ends forces $\int_0^T b(t)\,dt=0$, giving $b(0)=-T^{-1}\int_{t_0}^T(T-s)f(s)\,ds$. A force that starts later can therefore change the initial datum. In Lean, the two `PaperSmoothMeanSolution p force` arguments share a parent and source, and the conclusion `EqOn a.mean b.mean J(T)` makes their mean velocities equal at every time in $[0,T]$.

localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr: The new term to cancel is the fast transport of $V_1$ by $B_2$. It is linear in the newly determined mean and in the known leading oscillation, so it can be added to the force for $V_2$. Although $B_2$ is phase independent, its advection of $V_1$ need not be small compared with the centered part of $H_2$: the derivative through the phase costs up to a parent power times $\lambda^{3/2}$. The recursion in Lean takes the two inverses as separate inputs.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryPhaseSolve_: Along a parent particle $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. Enforcing $\partial_t(\kappa\cdot V)=0$ determines the phase pressure derivative, leaving a linear ODE for $V$ at each fixed phase. The existence theorem here is at a fixed label, for continuous periodic centered forcing; smooth dependence on the labels is established separately.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.TransverseSolution: The pressure here has a different role from the pressure of the mean equation: its phase derivative enforces $\kappa\cdot V_2=0$ in the moving transverse plane. The mean-zero condition fixes the constant of its periodic primitive separately at each time and label. These conditions specify the desired pair; the projected ODE gives it.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: At level two, $Y_1=V_1$ because $C_1=0$. Consequently (5.28) has precisely one term, $-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$. The expansion specification requires the transverse solution for this force plus $-(H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s)$, rather than for the centered error alone.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.suppSource: The transported phase is kept fixed by the parent: $D_t\theta=0$. In the flow with the mean added its material derivative would be $B_2\cdot\kappa$, since $\nabla_x\theta=\kappa$. Equation (1.12) compensates this change in the amplitude equation instead of rebuilding the phase for the perturbed flow.

localized.intro.mean-fast-zero-average.TorusEuler.hierarchy_phaseMean_supplemen: Since $B_2\cdot\kappa$ is independent of $s$, the phase average of its product with $\partial_sV_1$ is zero. Thus adding $B_2$ to remove the mean error does not change that mean error at level two. It changes only the force used in the subsequent transverse solve; the mean equation need not be solved again.

localized.intro.zero-start-correction.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryPhaseSolve_: The correction is launched from zero, in contrast to the leading seed and the endpoint-selected mean. The fixed-label existence theorem works for a continuous centered forcing; after solving the velocity ODE it recovers a periodic pressure with zero mean. It does not impose any condition on the terminal displacement of the oscillation.

localized.intro.exact-divergence-correct.TorusEuler.divergence_completedWaveOn: The identity $\kappa\cdot V_2=0$ removes the fast divergence but leaves $\mathbf d\cdot V_2$. Taking $C_3=\mathbf d\times Q[V_2]$ gives $V_2+C_3=\widetilde{\mathbf d}\times Q[V_2]$. On evaluation at the physical phase the right-hand side is an ordinary curl, which is the divergence-free field asserted by the local theorem.
localized.intro.exact-divergence-correct.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: The curl completion is not an additional solution of Euler: it is computed directly from the newly determined $V_2$. The condition $C_3=C[V_2]$ in `IsExpansion` enforces that choice; (3.6) gives the exact divergence identity for the pair.

localized.intro.next-level-completion.TorusEuler.hierarchy_completion_previous: In (3.5), $\kappa/|\kappa|^2$ contributes $\lambda^{-1}$ up to parent powers. The phase primitive and the slow curl introduce no positive power of $\lambda$. Consequently a completion is smaller than its generating oscillation by $\lambda^{-1}$, although passing from one level to the next requires only $\lambda^{-2/3}$. The extra $\lambda^{-1/3}$ is kept for the estimates of the fast interactions.

e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.expansion: Truncating the sum by size alone would omit $C_{P+1}$, leaving the slow divergence of $V_P$ uncompensated. In the actual expansion all $P$ oscillations retain their own curl corrections, so divergence vanishes exactly at every finite depth.
e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: The condition $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ is imposed for $1\le p\le P$, whereas the new mean and transverse equations are solved only for $2\le p\le P$. Thus the last operation is a curl completion, not another inverse problem.
e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity: Each $V_p+C[V_p]$ is evaluated at $s=k_*\cdot a$, $x=X(t,a)$. On the lifted label space the compatible extension has $V(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=V(t,a,s)$ for $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, and the same holds for its completion. Evaluation on the graph is therefore periodic in $a$ even for nonintegral $k_*$. Vanishing near the cell faces gives a smooth extension, while the means are already periodic.

e01.correction.depth-remainder.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trunc: At depth $P$ the uncanceled terms start at level $P+1$, of size $\lambda^{-5/4-2P/3}$ in profile norms. Increasing $P$ reduces this part of the error, but not $R_{\widetilde\chi}$, which comes from switching on the seed. The later frequency choice makes the former small relative to the frequency of the next wave; the amplification gain controls the latter.
e01.correction.depth-remainder.TorusEuler.hierarchyOscExponent: The exponent of a profile at the first omitted level is $-5/4-2P/3$, obtained by substituting $p=P+1$ in the level scale. The factor $\lambda^{-2P/3}$ measures the depth gain relative to the leading wave. This exponent identity does not bound the evaluated physical remainder.

e01.correction.approximate-velocity.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Physi: The construction removes the old momentum defect at the same time as it adds the wave. The mean equation at level two includes $-R_U\circ X$; evaluation at the inverse parent label changes this term back into $-R_U$. The parent equation and the profile equations then give (5.46), with a new residual consisting of the finite hierarchy tail and the time-cutoff term.

The finite correction consists of the completed primary wave, the higher oscillatory terms and the mean. In the later steps the oscillatory terms are supported near the central particle and vanish through the activation time. The mean, whose initial data are selected by the endpoint problem, may be nonzero even when the oscillation is zero; it needs a separate smallness estimate in every prescribed spatial order.

e01.correction.cutoff-error.TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalC: Let $u=S_\Lambda V$ and $v_\Lambda=u-V$. In the projected momentum equation the new quadratic error is the divergence of $u\otimes u-S_\Lambda(V\otimes V)=v_\Lambda\otimes u+V\otimes v_\Lambda+(I-S_\Lambda)(V\otimes V)$. The first two terms contain the velocity tail; the last is the tail of the product. To estimate the new residual in $C^{1,1/2}$, all three tensors are estimated in $C^{2,1/2}$. This gives $C_P\Lambda^{2-P}\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}^2$, explaining the power and the square in (5.55). The inherited contribution $\mathbb P S_\Lambda R_V$ is estimated separately.

e01.correction.next-coercivity.TorusEuler.inductionPressure_endpointHes: The differentiated momentum equation gives $H^\#=(D^2p_U-\nabla R_U)\circ X$. The sum of the pressure allowances is at most $2/N$, so $H^\#\le I$ if $N\ge4$ and $\|\nabla R_U\|_\infty\le1/2$. In the displacement variable $\xi$, the mean equation has energy $\int_0^T(|\xi_t|^2-H^\#\xi\cdot\xi)\,dt$. The endpoint conditions give $\int|\xi|^2\le(T^2/2)\int|\xi_t|^2$; thus this energy controls $\frac12\int|\xi_t|^2$. Returning to label displacements $z=(D_aX)^{-1}\xi$ loses only the factor $D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2$ of §4. This is why an upper pressure bound, rather than a bound on the full Hessian, suffices.

e01.correction.transported-support.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Physi: Outside the transported closed support, all oscillatory corrections vanish, including products of a mean with an oscillation. The mean correction itself is global, as is the Fourier truncation. Thus the support argument used at the terminal time must be applied to the untruncated oscillatory part, with the other two parts estimated by their small norms.

intro.pressure-not-control.TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff: An extra scalar $\delta$ added to $p_{\rm w}$ would add $\delta|k|^2$ to $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'$. For a wave with $k\ne0$, the transverse constraint fixes that scalar freedom as soon as the background and wave data are given. The coefficient in Lean is evaluated from those instantaneous data.
intro.pressure-not-control.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePa: The wave normal evolves by $k'=-D^Tk$. The pressure force in the amplitude equation lies along that normal and has zero dot product with a transverse amplitude, so $\tfrac12(|\mathbf a|^2)'=-\mathbf a\cdot D\mathbf a$. The pairing identity keeps $\mathbf a$ in the moving transverse plane. Its instantaneous change in length comes from the strain in $D$.

r5-root-central-gradient-setting.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: Oddness keeps the origin a fixed particle in every stage, so the covector and amplitude there solve ordinary differential equations with the central velocity gradient as coefficient. The rank-one part of that gradient must be recovered accurately; the field need not agree with a linear flow on any open neighborhood of zero.

e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_sub_rea: For a nonzero torus frequency $k$ and velocity coefficient $a$, the discarded coefficient is $k(k\cdot a)/|k|^2$. This is the longitudinal component, so the retained coefficient is perpendicular to $k$. At $k=0$ the discarded coefficient is zero. Lean checks this mode by mode for real $L^2$ fields by relating the real weak projection to its complex Fourier coefficients.
e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode: The scalar potential solves $\Delta q=\operatorname{div}v$ with zero mean. At $k\ne0$, divide the divergence coefficient $2\pi i\,k\cdot a$ by the Laplacian eigenvalue $-4\pi^2|k|^2$ to obtain the coefficient of $q$. Multiplying that scalar by $2\pi i k$ gives the gradient coefficient subtracted by the projection, with the two factors of $i$ accounting for the positive longitudinal multiplier.
e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero: The zero Fourier mode of the scalar potential is its spatial mean. Choosing it to be zero fixes the constant left undetermined by the Poisson equation. The gradient has zero constant mode for any such choice, so the Leray projection keeps the mean of a general velocity. The constructed velocities have zero mean by oddness.

e01.conventions.pressure-normalization.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: For a given Euler velocity, the momentum equation determines the spatial gradient of $p$. Subtracting $\int_{\mathbb T^3}p(t,y)\,dy$ selects the representative with zero integral over the centered unit cell. Lean imposes this condition on each time slice of the exact solution, including $t=0$.

e01.conventions.periodic-flow-displaceme.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVect: For $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, the curve $X(s,t,x)+n$ starts at $x+n$ and obeys the same lifted ODE, because the velocity is periodic. Uniform spatial Lipschitz control gives uniqueness on the time slab, so this curve is $X(s,t,x+n)$. Subtracting its own starting point shows why $X(s,t,x)-x$ is periodic and descends as a vector field on the torus.

r2a1.intro.derivative-conventions.TorusEuler.divergence: Column $j$ of $\nabla U$ is the derivative in direction $e_j$. Lean takes the $j$th component of each such derivative and sums over $j$, giving the trace. Applying the vector formula to row $i$ of a matrix gives $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_j A_{ij}$. In particular, the product rule gives $\operatorname{div}(U\otimes U)=(U\cdot\nabla)U$ for a divergence-free field.

r5-root-schedule-purpose.TorusEuler.paperTheorem71: There are two small quantities to arrange at each step: the correction in every retained derivative norm, and the new residual at the frequency of the following wave. The order $q_j$ controls the former; the expansion depth and early gain control the latter. The schedule is chosen once, with $q_j\to\infty$, so the resulting velocity sequence works at every fixed order.
r5-root-schedule-purpose.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: The two estimates on an increment serve different purposes. The oscillation is summable in velocity, and can have a large gradient; the remaining increment is summable through order $q_j$. At time zero all oscillations except the first are absent, so the second estimate gives convergence of the initial data in every fixed derivative norm.

e01.parameters.exponent.TorusEuler.frequencyExponent: At step $j$, $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q_j+1)}$ with $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$. Thus $\mu^{10b(m+2)}=\lambda^{(m+2)/(32(q_j+1))}$. For $m\le q_j$ the exponent is at most $1/16$. The same identity with $m=P$ explains why high-order norms may grow with the expansion depth: they will be used with the Fourier tail, not summed in the limit.

e01.parameters.monotone-threshold.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold: The fixed-order constants need not increase with either order or depth. For each $s$ sum their absolute values over the finite family of estimates and the square $0\le m,p\le7K(s)$, then take the maximum of this sum and $\exp(4K(s+1)^3)$. Enlarging $s$ enlarges the square, so the resulting majorant is nondecreasing. This is the explicit choice made by `fixedOrderThreshold`.
e01.parameters.monotone-threshold.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_mono: The square of indices $0\le m,p\le7K(s)$ expands with $s$. Its sum of absolute costs can only increase, even if the costs themselves are not monotone. The other term in the maximum, the exponential floor, is also increasing.
e01.parameters.monotone-threshold.TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold: The analytic estimates first specify a lower majorant $F(s)$ for the costs. The schedule can then use any nondecreasing $\mathcal B\ge F$ satisfying the logarithmic floor. This permits further fixed-order estimates, for example those of the terminal regularity argument, to be included before the initial frequency is chosen.

e01.parameters.cost-domination.TorusEuler.abs_fixedOrderCost_le_thresho: The costs of step $j$ are bounded by testing the order $q_{j+1}$, since the depth is $P=6K(q_{j+1})$. The extra order $P+1$ is included: a $C^{P,1/2}$ bound follows from control through $P+1$ ordinary derivatives. Both indices of the fixed-order cost table therefore lie within $7K(q_{j+1})$.
e01.parameters.cost-domination.TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold: At depth $6K(s)$ one must also bound derivatives at order $6K(s)+1$. The range through $7K(s)$ contains both and all the lower orders. The majorant is a finite-order bound at each $s$, not a bound uniform in the differentiation order.

e01.parameters.log-floor.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_log_floor: The future gain $L_{j+1}$ contains $\log\lambda_{j+2}=K_{j+2}K_{j+1}K_j\log\lambda_{j-1}$. We know the threshold test at $s=q_{j+1}$, not at $q_{j+2}$. The floor with $K(s+1)^3$ bounds all three exponents, even if the order increases once more.
e01.parameters.log-floor.TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold: The lower bound on $\mathcal B$ is imposed independently of the analytic costs. It gives $4K_{j+2}K_{j+1}K_j\le\log\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\log\lambda_{j-1}$. Thus the next gain is bounded by the square of a logarithm at the present parent scale.

e01.parameters.initial-frequency.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters: The assumption $N\ge\mathcal B(1)$ makes order one available at the first maximum. Thereafter the frequency in the test never decreases, so an order already admitted cannot become inadmissible. In particular the recurrence defines an order at every step.

e01.parameters.initial-order.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters: Although $q_1=1$, the first wave already requires the constants at depth $6K(q_2)$. For this reason the maximum defining $q_2$ is tested against $N=\lambda_0$, which bounds the cost of constructing $U_1$ over the stationary shear.

e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_exists: Given $q_j$ and $\lambda_{j-1}$, the first recurrence determines $\lambda_j$ and the maximum rule determines $q_{j+1}$. Iterating these two operations gives the whole frequency and order sequence; $\Lambda_j$, $L_j$ and $\varepsilon_j$ can then be read from it. In particular prescribing the target coupling ratio for each crossing requires no information about when the crossing will occur.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters: The exponent of $\lambda_{j-1}$ uses $q_j$, but the expansion depth uses $q_{j+1}$. Thus the test for $q_{j+1}$ must use the same parent scale $\lambda_{j-1}$. In `InductiveEulerParameters` the corresponding index is $i=j-1$, and the tested order is $q_{i+2}$.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.L: The gain parameter is the inverse square root of the ratio inherited from wave $j-1$. With the peak of wave $j$ fixed, the relative amplitude during its switch is bounded by $e^{3-L_j}$. Taking $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ makes this $e^3\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$, which is the scale of the expansion remainder chosen in §7.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.ε: A small ratio reached by wave $j$ is an input to the growth problem for wave $j+1$, not a measure of the amplitude of wave $j$ at that time. The choice $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$ fixes the exponential factor $e^{-L_{j+1}}=\lambda_{j+2}^{-4}$ needed when wave $j+1$ is switched on.

e01.parameters.arbitrary-threshold-growt.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_order_tends: Suppose that $q_j=s$ from some stage onward. Then $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(s)}$ grows without bound, whereas $\mathcal B(s+1)$ is a fixed finite number. Eventually $s+1$ is among the admissible orders and the maximum rule takes it. Thus no rate of growth of the fixed-order constants has to be assumed: even very large constants can only postpone an increase by finitely many stages.

e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders: At any stage the only possible increase is from $q_j$ to $q_j+1$. If the latter is still too costly, the order stays fixed while the frequency continues to grow. The order cannot remain fixed forever, because the cost of that one additional order is a fixed finite number.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_1_3: The maximum condition has two uses: membership gives $q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$, while maximality applied to the still affordable $q_j$ gives $q_j\le q_{j+1}$. There is no lower bound on how often the order must increase.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3: The restriction on a single increase is used immediately in bounding $K_{j+2}$ in terms of $q_{j+1}$. The divergence of the orders has a later use: for each fixed $m$ the estimates of §8 apply from some stage onward with $q_j\ge m$.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_1_3: If $q_j=s$, there are only two possibilities for $q_{j+1}$: $s$ and $s+1$. The latter is taken as soon as $\lambda_{j-1}\ge\mathcal B(s+1)$. The proof uses this recurrence with frequency index $i=j-1$, so that the order tested against $\lambda_i$ is $q_{i+2}$.

e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders: At the stage with parent frequency $\lambda_{j-1}$, three frequency powers intervene before $L_{j+1}$. Their product satisfies $4K_jK_{j+1}K_{j+2}\le4K(q_{j+1}+1)^3\le\log\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\log\lambda_{j-1}$. Multiplication by $\log\lambda_{j-1}$ proves (1.15). This is the bound used when estimating powers of the normalized comparison interval.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_1_3: The last exponent in $L_{j+1}=4K_jK_{j+1}K_{j+2}\log\lambda_{j-1}$ is $K_{j+2}$. Although this order has not yet been tested against $\lambda_{j-1}$, the increase by at most one gives $q_{j+2}\le q_{j+1}+1$. This is why the floor is written with $K(s+1)$ rather than $K(s)$.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3: For each fixed $A$ and $c>0$, (1.15) gives $\mu^{-c}L_{j+1}^A\le\mu^{-c}(\log\mu)^{2A}$, with $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$. The right side tends to zero uniformly for $\mu\ge N$ as $N\to\infty$. This allows a single initial-frequency threshold in all the comparison estimates at a fixed $C_0$.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_1_3: It is important that the estimate bounds $L_{j+1}$, not just $L_j$, by $(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$: the comparison and the endpoint length for wave $j$ both involve $L_{j+1}$. In the numerical theorem this is the three-step logarithmic bound $4\log\lambda_{i+3}\le(\log\lambda_i)^2$ with $i=j-1$.

affine.background-hypotheses.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The background acceleration is $(D'+D^2)x$. A quadratic pressure differentiates to the symmetric part of its matrix applied to $x$, so symmetry is what lets the pressure cancel the entire acceleration. The trace condition acts separately on $\operatorname{div}(Dx)$. These are conditions on the linear flow on $\mathbb R^3$, before localization and passage to periodic data.
affine.background-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_1: The symmetry condition applies to $D'+D^2$, so $D$ can be a nonsymmetric shear. For instance, a constant shear with $D^2=0$ and trace zero already gives a stationary linear Euler flow with constant pressure. The Lean statement takes the derivative of $D$ within the time interval, which suffices for the momentum calculation.

affine.wave-equations.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn: The structure of (2.1) lets us evolve $k$ first and use its path as a coefficient in the equation for $\mathbf a$. Lean packages these two evolution equations together. Transversality enters separately. The Euler calculation uses it at each time, and the propagation argument obtains it by keeping the initial pairing constant.
affine.wave-equations.TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff: The $D$-terms in the derivatives of $k$ and $\mathbf a$ each contribute $-k\cdot D\mathbf a$ to the pairing. A correction along $k$ contributes $p_{\rm w}|k|^2$, so the coefficient is fixed by setting the sum to zero. The nonzero wave vector makes this division possible.
affine.wave-equations.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The Euler identity uses $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ at each time to cancel the wave's self-advection. The propagation conclusion supplies that hypothesis throughout the interval from one time at which both vectors are nonzero and perpendicular. It also gives the nonvanishing of $k$ needed to use the pressure formula.
affine.wave-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.WaveOn: If $k$ is replaced by $ck$ for a nonzero constant $c$, the pressure coefficient is divided by $c$. The correction $p_{\rm w}k$ in the amplitude equation is therefore unchanged. The same amplitude can serve a rescaled normal, even though the phase $k\cdot x$ in the physical wave changes.

affine.euler-and-pressure.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The wave part of the material acceleration is $(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F$. The amplitude equation makes it parallel to $k$, and $P'=F$ then writes it as the gradient of $p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$. This fixes the minus sign in the wave pressure, since Euler adds the pressure gradient to the acceleration.
affine.euler-and-pressure.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_1: The local calculation only uses differentiability of $F$ and the identity $P'=F$ for the profile and its primitive. The paper's normalization $F'(0)=1$ gives the wave's gradient at the origin directly, and an additive constant in $P$ only changes the pressure by a function of time. The formal statement keeps differentiability of the velocity and pressure explicit alongside momentum and divergence.
affine.euler-and-pressure.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_1: Momentum and incompressibility use different parts of the calculation. The phase and self-advection cancellations leave an acceleration that the two pressure terms cancel. Incompressibility follows directly from the spatial derivative, whose background part has trace $\operatorname{tr}D=0$ and whose rank-one part has trace $(k\cdot\mathbf a)F'=0$.

affine.nonzero-perpendicular.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: First use the linear equation for $k$ to keep the normal nonzero. Only then does $1/|k|^2$ give a continuous coefficient for the amplitude equation everywhere on the interval, and the pressure choice can keep the pairing constant there.
affine.nonzero-perpendicular.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_1: Uniqueness of the linear equations is based at any point of the interval. A hypothetical zero there forces the same solution as the zero datum at that point, including at $t_0$. The formal assertion consequently covers earlier times in the same interval as well as the forward times stated in the text.

r2a1.wave.phase-transport.TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAccelerati: First solve the particle equation for the affine strain $U(x)=(x_1,-x_2,0)$. Along a particle, $x_2(t)=e^{-t}x_2(0)$, so $k(t)=e^t e_2$ keeps $k(t)\cdot x(t)$ constant. Choose amplitude $e_3$ and check that the wave velocity dotted with the phase gradient is zero. These are the two cancellations that let the paper study a single wave by ordinary differential equations before localizing it. Along $x'=Dx$, the phase has two contributions to its derivative, $k'\cdot x$ from the moving normal and $k\cdot Dx$ from the moving point. The transpose in $k'=-D^Tk$ cancels them. Thus the background carries each level of the phase along unchanged, leaving only the time derivative of the amplitude in the transported wave.

r2a1.wave.self-advection.TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection: At fixed time $\nabla w$ sends a direction $v$ to $\mathbf a F'(k\cdot x)(k\cdot v)$. For self-advection, set $v=w=F(k\cdot x)\mathbf a$. The factor $k\cdot\mathbf a$ vanishes because the velocity perturbation is tangent to the phase planes.

r2a1.wave.acceleration.TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAccelerati: The wave affects the background through $(w\cdot\nabla)(Dx)=D\mathbf aF$. Meanwhile the derivative of $w$ along the background supplies $\mathbf a'F$, and its derivative along $w$ vanishes. The two surviving wave terms have the same profile factor, so the amplitude equation determines their sum.

r2a1.wave.pressure-gradient.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_affineWavePress: At fixed time the spatial derivative of $P(k\cdot x)$ is $F(k\cdot x)k$. In the quadratic term both factors of $x$ differentiate, and symmetry of $D'+D^2$ makes the two contributions equal. This accounts for the factor $1/2$ in the background pressure.

r2a1.wave.divergence.TorusEuler.divergence_affineWaveVelocity: The wave's spatial derivative has matrix $F'(k\cdot x)\,\mathbf a\otimes k$. Taking its trace contracts the output direction $\mathbf a$ against the input covector $k$. The resulting scalar $k\cdot\mathbf a$ makes the wave contribution vanish, independently of the background trace condition.

affine.pairing-cancellation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePa: Treat the pressure coefficient as free when applying the product rule. The adjoint identity turns $(-D^Tk)\cdot\mathbf a$ into $-k\cdot D\mathbf a$. It adds to the identical term from $k\cdot(-D\mathbf a)$, leaving one scalar equation for the coefficient of $k$.

Substitution cancels the factor $|k|^2$ because $k$ stays nonzero. The derivative vanishes for any initial pairing, so the equations preserve its initial value. Choosing that value to be zero makes the wave transverse for the Euler calculation.

affine.wave-vector-nonvanishing.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: The equation for $k$ is homogeneous with continuous coefficient $-D^T$. If the normal reached zero, uniqueness based at that time would identify it with the zero solution also at $t_0$. This is the same nonvanishing mechanism as invertibility of the fundamental matrix, and it secures the pressure denominator before the amplitude equation is used.

affine.linear-amplitude-equation.TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator: The map $kk^T/|k|^2$ projects onto the normal line. Consequently $\operatorname{Id}-2kk^T/|k|^2$ reflects $D\mathbf a$ across the plane perpendicular to $k$ before the leading minus sign is applied. Once $k(t)$ is prescribed and nonzero, this is a continuous linear coefficient acting on $\mathbf a(t)$.

affine.amplitude-nonvanishing.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: Once the normal is known to stay nonzero, the amplitude satisfies a homogeneous linear equation with a continuous coefficient. If the full vector $\mathbf a$ vanished at any time, the zero datum there would force $\mathbf a(t_0)=0$. Individual components can still pass through zero while the vector changes direction.

c8-frame-trace-scope.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_2: For nonzero transverse wave data, the derivatives of the axes come from the two wave ODEs evaluated at a single time. Trace zero enters only when the two logarithmic length rates are added and $-B_{11}-B_{22}$ is rewritten as $B_{33}$. Thus the prescribed gradient $B(t)$ and the wave data at $t$ suffice for the frame calculation used in the prescribed-matrix system of §2.2.

frame.normalized-axes.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame: With $F'(0)=1$, the wave adds $k\times\mathbf a=|k|\,|\mathbf a|E_3$ to the curl at the origin. The order of the cross product therefore gives the direction of the wave's vorticity. When the successor normal is launched along $E_3$, its transverse amplitudes lie in the plane spanned by $E_1$ and $E_2$.

frame.matrix-entries.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry: To read $B_{ij}$, apply $B$ to the input direction $E_j$ and take the output component along $E_i$. For example, the added shear $\sigma E_2\otimes E_1$ has its only nonzero entry at $(2,1)$ because it sends $E_1$ to $\sigma E_2$. This fixes which entry changes when the preceding wave is added to the older gradient in §2.2.1.

frame.strength-couplings.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: Dividing the pressure term $p_{\rm w}k$ in (2.1) by $|\mathbf a|$ gives $2\nu E_1$. Thus $B_{12}$ contributes both through $-B\mathbf a$ and through pressure, while the $E_3$ component of $-B\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ is $-\eta$. These two components turn the amplitude direction in the frame identities below.

frame.derivative-identities.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.movingFrameDeriva: For distinct $i,j$, the coefficient of $E_j$ in $E_i'$ is the negative of the coefficient of $E_i$ in $E_j'$, as differentiating $E_i\cdot E_j=0$ requires. Equivalently, the axes obey $E_i'=\Omega\times E_i$ with $\Omega=-\eta E_1+B_{13}E_2-\nu E_3$. Thus each axis turns at a rate bounded by $|\Omega|$.
frame.derivative-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_2: In the formal statement, `WaveOn` supplies the two differential equations and the pressure coefficient. Nonvanishing and $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ are supplied separately at every time in the set, where the three axes and their derivatives are evaluated. The propagation argument for (2.1) supplies these pointwise hypotheses when the data are nonzero and transverse at launch and $B$ is smooth on the interval.
frame.derivative-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_2: At launch of the successor, put $k_+=\lambda E_3$ and take $E_c=0$. The added shear $\sigma_p E_2\otimes E_1$ annihilates $E_2$, so the wave equation gives $k_+'\cdot E_2=-\lambda B_{32}$. The moving frame contributes another $k_+\cdot E_2'=-\lambda B_{32}$. Multiplying the sum by $S/(\lambda r)$ gives $\zeta_2'=-2Sb_{32}$ at launch, the value of the term $-2Sb_{32}\zeta_3$ when $\zeta_3=1$.

r2a1.wave.normalized-vector.TorusEuler.normalizeDerivOfScaled: Differentiate $v/|v|$ by writing it as $|v|^{-1}v$. The derivative of $v$ contributes $v'/|v|$ and that of the inverse norm subtracts $\widehat v(\widehat v\cdot v'/|v|)$. Only the component tangent to the unit sphere remains, as is needed for the derivatives of both unit axes.
r2a1.wave.normalized-vector.TorusEuler.logNormDerivOfScaled: The scalar $\widehat v\cdot v'$ is the rate of change of $|v|$. Dividing by $|v|$ gives the fractional rate of change, whose integral along a smooth nonzero path is $\log(|v(t)|/|v(t_0)|)$. The same radial component that is subtracted in the unit-vector equation enters the change of length here.

r2a1.wave.first-axis.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The wave-vector equation gives $k'/|k|=-B^TE_1$. The equality $E_j\cdot B^TE_1=E_1\cdot BE_j$ makes the transverse components $-B_{12}$ and $-B_{13}$, with the row index fixed at $1$. Normalizing removes the remaining $-B_{11}E_1$ component.
r2a1.wave.first-axis.TorusEuler.logNormDerivOfScaled: For the logarithmic norm rule, take $v=k$ and $v'/|v|=-B^TE_1$. Its component along $E_1$ is $-E_1\cdot BE_1=-B_{11}$. Thus a positive $B_{11}$ makes the wave number decrease. The distance $|k|^{-1}$ corresponding to one unit of phase increases.

r2a1.wave.second-axis.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The $E_1$ component of $-BE_2$ is $-B_{12}$, so adding the pressure contribution $2B_{12}E_1$ leaves $+B_{12}E_1$ in $E_2'$. It cancels the contribution $E_1'\cdot E_2=-B_{12}$ to the derivative of $E_1\cdot E_2$. The longitudinal component along $E_2$ is removed by normalization.
r2a1.wave.second-axis.TorusEuler.logNormDerivOfScaled: The pressure term is parallel to $k$. Its dot product with $\mathbf a$ is zero, so taking the dot product of the amplitude equation with $2\mathbf a$ gives $(|\mathbf a|^2)'=-2\mathbf a\cdot B\mathbf a$. Dividing by $2|\mathbf a|^2$ leaves the logarithmic rate $-B_{22}$.

r2a1.wave.cross-axis.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The $\nu$ terms make contributions proportional to $E_2\times E_2$ and $E_1\times E_1$, so they vanish separately. The other terms give $-B_{13}(E_3\times E_2)=B_{13}E_1$ and $-\eta(E_1\times E_3)=\eta E_2$. When $B_{13}=\eta=0$, the first two axes may turn within their plane while the vorticity direction stays fixed.

frame.log-strength-calculation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The strength at time $t$ is its launch value multiplied by $\exp(\int_{t_0}^t B_{33}(s)\,ds)$. This freezes the strength in the model with $B_{33}=0$ even while the axes turn. In Lemma 2.4, the same formula in normalized time gives the relative bound $|\sigma_p/\sigma-1|\le 2T\delta$ from $|b_{33}|\le\delta$ and $T\delta\le1$.
