r5-reference-small-ratio-gain.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: The reference normal reaches $\varphi=\pi/4$ at $\tau=\sqrt{2/\varepsilon}$. Up to that time, $\cos\varphi\ge1/\sqrt2$, so the integral in (2.14) already contributes at least $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ to the logarithm of the amplitude. The factor $\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$ costs only $\tfrac14\log2$ at that time. The peak occurs later, on the scale $\varepsilon^{-1}$.
r5-reference-small-ratio-gain.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: In the parameter schedule a wave of index $j\ge2$ inherits $\varepsilon=L_j^{-2}$, with $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$. The first-unit bound becomes $e^3\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. The time cutoff costs a derivative of size $Cr$, but the induction has $Ce^3r\le\lambda_{j-1}$; thus the activation error is already small on the scale of the following frequency, not just the frequency of the wave being added.

r5-reference-reference-system-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: The order of the calculation matters. The normal solves a closed linear equation, so we first obtain $\zeta_0$ by integrating three successive equations and then insert it in the pressure coefficient. The resulting two-dimensional amplitude system depends only on $\varepsilon$ and $\tau$. Its solution can be multiplied by any launch amplitude, without changing its direction or the normal.
r5-reference-reference-system-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3: The strong-shear limit must be taken in the scaled equations. For instance, the preceding shear contributes $\sigma_p(k\cdot E_2)(\mathbf a\cdot E_1)$ to the pressure numerator. In units of $\nu\lambda$ this is $2(\sigma_p/\sigma)\zeta_2\alpha_1$. It remains an order-one coefficient even though the corresponding two physical projections carry factors $S^{-1}$. At reference inputs it produces the damping term in (2.5).

r5-reference-additive-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: The normal is independent of the amplitude, and the amplitude equation is linear on the plane perpendicular to that normal. The same operator $(2P_k-\mathrm{Id})M$, with $P_k$ projection onto $k$, acts on every transverse vector. Lemma 2.4 therefore compares the entire two-dimensional equation, leaving Lemma 2.6 to estimate both the particular growing solution and the propagation of arbitrary directions.
r5-reference-additive-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_4: The interval must contain the prescribed crossing, which can occur on the normalized scale $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$. In §7, with $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$, the full normalized interval has length at most $CL_{j+1}^4$, $L_{j+1}\le(\log\mu)^2$, and $\delta$ is bounded by $\mu^{-1/16}$ times a fixed power of $\log\mu$. An estimate $CT^C\delta$ is therefore absorbable uniformly in the induction; an estimate exponential in $T$ would not follow from these bounds.

r5-reference-reference-peak-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: The scalar variable is the logarithmic derivative of the second component, $Y=\alpha_2'/\alpha_2$. It is initially defined near launch, where $\alpha_2(0)=1$. The proof proceeds in the opposite direction, constructing $Y$ globally and setting $\alpha_2=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y)$. This ensures that no zero of $\alpha_2$ interrupts the comparison.
r5-reference-reference-peak-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: Set $v=\sqrt\varepsilon\,\tau$. Then $\int_0^\infty\cos\varphi\,d\tau=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\int_0^\infty(1+v^4/4)^{-1/2}\,dv$. Its tail after $\tau_m$ is at most one. In (2.14) the correction $e$ changes this integral by at most $O(\sqrt\varepsilon)$, and the square-root prefactor costs $\tfrac12\log\varepsilon+O(1)$ in the logarithm. Thus most of the logarithmic gain is accumulated on the turning scale $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, although the maximum is later, at $\tau_m\asymp\varepsilon^{-1}$.

r5-reference-relative-comparison-overvie.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: The comparison does not estimate the difference of two large amplitudes in absolute size. It divides both by the positive reference amplitude and measures the remaining direction error by $l$ in (2.15). In the reference equations $l$ can only decay, and the variation it produces in $h$ is bounded by half its decrease in absolute value. This gives a bounded forward propagator before any perturbation estimate is made.
r5-reference-relative-comparison-overvie.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: The estimate on the scaled quotient $q=\alpha_1/\alpha_2$ is important even when the physical velocity direction is nearly $E_2$: multiplication of its small $E_1$ component by the preceding shear leaves an order-one contribution to $f_2$ in (2.20). The other conclusion of Lemma 2.6, the bound for the propagator on the entire transverse plane, is used in §5 to estimate forced oscillatory corrections relative to the growing seed.

r5-reference-couplings-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_7: The first new coupling must stay positive even before the crossing. Indeed $p_{\rm w}=2\nu_+|\mathbf a|/|k|$, so the leading affine pressure Hessian has central eigenvalue $-2\nu_+|\mathbf a||k|$ when $F'(0)=1$. The localized construction uses the same sign on the envelope and the shallow negative part of $F_h'$ to bound the Hessian from above. This bound is needed to solve the mean correction for the next parent.
r5-reference-couplings-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7:
For the next wave it matters that $
u_+$ is close to $
u$, not merely positive, while its ratio with $\eta_+$ can be prescribed. At a crossing $
u_+$ becomes the frozen first coupling of the successor; the error $|
u_+/
u-1|\le\varepsilon$ ensures that repeated transfers do not make this coupling tend to zero. The weaker relative accuracy for the small ratio still suffices to choose a crossing.

r5-reference-crossing-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: The comparison horizon is chosen before the amplitude is normalized and before the crossing is selected. At the reference peak the ratio is at least $\varepsilon/18$, and at $2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$ it is at most $3\varepsilon_+/4$. Since $\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ and $\nu_+>0$ throughout, continuity yields a nonempty closed set of crossings in this bracket. Section 6.2 takes its least element; no monotonicity is needed.
r5-reference-crossing-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8: The crossing supplies three quantities at the same time: the direction $E_{3,+}$ of the following normal, the ratio $\varepsilon_+$, and the shear for its growth rate $r_+=\sqrt{2\sigma_+\nu_+}$. The upper and lower strength estimates in Proposition 2.8 are both useful: a large $r_+$ shortens the next physical growth interval, while an upper bound on $r_+$ limits the normalized length on which the next comparison must be proved.

additive.prescribed-wave-data.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The equations here only use the gradients at a fixed particle, not an affine solution of Euler on an open set. In §7 oddness fixes the particle at zero, and for wave $j$ the older gradient is $B=\nabla U_{j-2}(t,0)$ while $M=\nabla U_{j-1}(t,0)$. The error $E_c$ accounts for the difference between the latter gradient and the older gradient plus the principal shear of wave $j-1$.

r2a1.wave.gradient.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The pair $(k_p,\mathbf a_p)$ evolves over $B$, whereas $(k,\mathbf a)$ evolves over $M$. The rank-one addition annihilates $\mathbf a_p$, and its transpose annihilates $k_p$, by perpendicularity. It therefore does not act on its own wave, but it acts on the new one. The frame of the preceding wave depends on $B$ alone; $E_c$ enters only the new wave equations.
r2a1.wave.gradient.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r: In units of $r$ the preceding shear is $(S\sigma_p/\sigma)E_2\otimes E_1$. In the normal equation its transpose acts on $\lambda\zeta_2/S$, and in the amplitude equation the shear acts on $\alpha_1/S$. Both resulting coefficients are $-\sigma_p/\sigma$ in the respective scaled equations. The opposite placement of the factors $S^{-1}$ in (2.3) retains both transfers.

r2a1.wave.new-vector.TorusEuler.Paper.NewWaveVector: The normal equation is homogeneous in $k$. Also $2k(k\cdot M\mathbf a)/|k|^2$ is invariant under a positive rescaling of $k$. Thus changing the launch frequency $\lambda$ multiplies the normal throughout the slab, but leaves the amplitude evolution and coupling ratio unchanged. Frequency is free in this central calculation and enters the strength $|k||\mathbf a|$.

r2a1.wave.amplitude.TorusEuler.Paper.AmplitudeVector: The term $p_{\rm w}k$ is chosen so that $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'=-2k\cdot M\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|k|^2=0$. It preserves the moving transverse plane. Since $\mathbf a\cdot k=0$, it contributes nothing to $(|\mathbf a|^2)'=-2\mathbf a\cdot M\mathbf a$ directly, but it changes the amplitude direction, on which the subsequent growth depends.

r2a1.wave.frozen-couplings.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The preceding shear may change over the interval. Freezing its initial value $\sigma=\sigma_p(t_0)$ makes $r$ and $S$ constant, so differentiating the scaled coordinates introduces no derivatives of those factors. The shear drift remains in the coefficient $\sigma_p(t)/\sigma$.

The entry $B_{12}$ contributes once through $-M\mathbf a$ and once through the rotation $\dot E_1$ in the equation for $a_1$. This accounts for $-2\nu a_2$ in the model; the shear then maps $a_1$ into the second amplitude equation. Lean uses indices $(0,1)$ for $B_{12}$.

In the model the rotation of the frame contributes the same $-\eta k_3$ as the gradient to $\dot k_2$. The factor $2$ in $-2\eta k_3$ gives $\zeta_2^{\prime}=-\varepsilon\zeta_3$ after scaling, since $2S\eta/r=\varepsilon$. Its subsequent transfer into $\zeta_1$ is the origin of $\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$.

The positivity assumptions are on the two launch entries, not on every entry of $B$. Together with the nonzero preceding pair they give $r,S,\varepsilon>0$. Subsequent values of $B_{12},B_{32}$ are controlled by the relative variations in (2.6), and need not be constant.

additive.time-scales.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The initial growth is due to two transfers, $-2\nu a_2$ into $a_1$ and $-(\sigma-\nu)a_1$ into $a_2$. The geometric mean of their rates is $r\sqrt{1-1/(2S^2)}$. Scaling $a_1$ by $S$ and changing the clock by $r$ makes both leading coefficients equal to $-1$.

The quantity $S=\sigma/r=r/(2\nu)$ measures the loss in recovering a general physical amplitude from the scaled plane coordinates. It is determined by the preceding wave, not by the launch frequency $\lambda$ of the present wave. In §7 the inherited bounds on $\sigma$ and $\nu$ give $CS\le C\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}L_j$, a parent-scale cost in the transverse inverse.

The small positive ratio controls how long amplification can continue and whether it can be repeated. In the model with $\eta=0$, the normal stays along $E_3$ and pressure vanishes; the growing mode is exponential, but $E_{1,+}\cdot M E_{2,+}=0$, so it supplies no first coupling for a successor. Positive $\varepsilon$ permits turning and a positive first coupling, at the cost of eventually ending the amplitude growth.

There are two time lengths to distinguish: the reference comparison uses $T$ in units of $r^{-1}$, while the later endpoint problem uses a physical time slab. A comparison through normalized time $T$ requires the parent on $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. The time cutoff changes on the shorter interval $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$; hence its derivative costs $Cr$ in physical time.

r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.Paper.zeta: The rescaling retains the small normal component on which the large shear acts. Indeed $-(\sigma_p/r)(k\cdot E_2)/\lambda=-(\sigma_p/\sigma)\zeta_2$. The model gives $\zeta_2'=-\varepsilon\zeta_3$, so the two equations produce the finite quadratic displacement of the first normal component.
r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.Paper.alpha: The chosen physical launch $-E_1/S+E_2$ becomes the pair $(-1,1)$, the exact initial direction of the reference solution (not the exact frozen eigenvector at finite $S$). The reciprocal scalings also give $k\cdot\mathbf a=(\lambda/S)\zeta\cdot\alpha$. This is why perpendicularity has no small coefficients although the physical lengths retain the weights $S^{-2}$.
r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.scaled_waveV: Inverting the scaling gives $\zeta_1=k\cdot E_1/\lambda$, $\zeta_2=S k\cdot E_2/\lambda$, $\zeta_3=k\cdot E_3/\lambda$. Only the middle component is magnified. The distinction is essential: $\zeta_2$ has a nonzero reference limit, but the physical projection $k\cdot E_2/\lambda$ tends to zero.
r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.U: The library uses $U=-\alpha_1$, $V=\alpha_2$, so the prescribed launch is $(U,V)=(1,1)$. The minus sign makes the limiting second equation $V'=U$ and gives the reference slope $Y=U/V$ wherever $V>0$. The paper retains the signed physical component $\alpha_1$ instead.
r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.V: The unscaled amplitude coordinate is $V=\alpha_2$. For the chosen launch, Lemma 2.6 proves $V>0$ and bounds $|\alpha_1|/V$ and $|\alpha_3|/V$. Since $|\mathbf a|/V=\sqrt{1+S^{-2}[(\alpha_1/V)^2+(\alpha_3/V)^2]}$, those bounds compare the physical length with this single component. Positivity is needed before using that quotient.

r2a1.wave.initial-coordinates.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coordinate_i: The initial value $\zeta=(0,0,1)$ is independent of $S$ and $\lambda$. Thus the difference of the finite and reference normal equations has zero initial data. All of its subsequent error comes from the coefficient differences.

r2a1.wave.norm-factor.TorusEuler.Paper.scaledNormSq: At reference inputs the squared frequency factor is $m_0=1+x^2=\cos^{-2}\varphi$, where $x=\tan\varphi$. It is not $|\zeta_0|^2=1+x^2+\varepsilon^2\tau^2$: the last term here comes from the magnified middle component and is suppressed by $S^{-2}$ in $m$. This is the length that enters the denominator of pressure.
r2a1.wave.norm-factor.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.wave_norm_sq_: The denominator $m$ is positive whenever $k\ne0$, but the two-coordinate amplitude equation also requires $\zeta_3\ne0$. The latter condition concerns the chart, not the normal itself. Lemma 2.4 proves $\zeta_3\ge1/2$ on the comparison interval, and hence $m\ge1/4$ as well.

r2a1.wave.third-coordinate.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.amplitude_dec: The inverse of the two-component projection on the transverse plane sends $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ to $\alpha_1S^{-1}(E_1-\zeta_1 E_3/\zeta_3)+\alpha_2(E_2-\zeta_2 E_3/(S\zeta_3))$. Both basis vectors are perpendicular to $k$. Lean uses $U=-\alpha_1$ and $V=\alpha_2$, so the third physical component is $(\zeta_1U-\zeta_2V)/(S\zeta_3)$. This is a coordinate chart for all transverse amplitudes, not just the growing one.

r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle: In the reference limit the normal direction is $\sin\varphi E_1+\cos\varphi E_3$ and the wave number is $\lambda/\cos\varphi$. An order-one turn occurs at $\tau\asymp\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, while the reference amplitude peak has $\cos\varphi\asymp\varepsilon$ and $\tau\asymp\varepsilon^{-1}$. Thus a large gain, a nearly complete turn, and a prescribed successor crossing are different events.
r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef: At finite shear the projected slope is $\zeta_1/\zeta_3$, not $\zeta_1$. With $x=\tan\varphi$ and $\zeta_3\ge1/2$, its error from $x$ is at most $2(|\zeta_1-x|+x|\zeta_3-1|)$. Thus even the projected slope has a polynomial comparison error; the actual normal also has the out-of-plane component $\lambda\zeta_2/S$.
r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle_mem: The choice $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ gives $\cos\varphi>0$ on every finite interval. More quantitatively $\cos\varphi\ge T^{-2}$ on $[0,T]$ under $\varepsilon\le1$ and $T\ge2$. The same lower bound controls division by $\cos\varphi$ in (2.15) and converts the additive error in the third coupling into an error relative to its small reference value.
r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.tan_referenceAngle: Writing $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, the branch choice gives $\cos^2\varphi=1/(1+x^2)$ and $\sin2\varphi=2x/(1+x^2)$. Thus the trigonometric coefficients of the reference equation can be expressed as rational functions of $x$; this is how the lower-level calculations use the tangent identity.
r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x: Since $x=\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, a late cosine of order $\varepsilon_+$ requires $x\asymp\varepsilon_+^{-1}$ and hence $\tau\asymp(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$. In particular the target ratio influences the required comparison horizon of the present wave even though it determines the gain of its successor.

r2a1.wave.model-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.ModelCase: The matrix entries are fixed in a moving frame, not in spatial coordinates: $B=\nu E_1\otimes E_2+\eta E_3\otimes E_2$. Even with these two constants fixed, $B$ varies as the preceding frame rotates. The model is an assumption on the central wave equations, not an assertion that this matrix by itself solves the affine Euler equations.
r2a1.wave.model-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.modelEntries: For the older gradient, only the column $BE_2=\nu E_1+\eta E_3$ is nonzero. Adding the preceding shear gives $ME_1=\sigma E_2$ as well, while $ME_3=0$. The rotation of the frame follows from the former column; the large transfer between the first two components follows from the latter addition.

r2a1.wave.constant-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: The model sets $B_{33}=0$ for the entire interval. By (2.2), $(\log\sigma_p)'=0$ in either clock, so the ratio $\sigma_p/\sigma$ is identically one. This is the coefficient of the leading shear term after rescaling; the general case must control its drift instead.
r2a1.wave.constant-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3: The preceding normal and amplitude have logarithmic length derivatives $-B_{11}$ and $-B_{22}$ in physical time. In the model both entries vanish, so each length is constant, not just their product. For general trace-free $B$ their sum is $B_{33}$; this gives the strength equation used in the next lemma.

r2a1.wave.model-vector-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: Put $\mu=1/(2S^2)$. The last two rows preserve $\zeta_3^2+\mu\zeta_2^2=1$; also $\zeta_1+(1+\mu)\zeta_3/(\varepsilon\mu)$ is constant. The initial data therefore give $\zeta_3=\cos(\varepsilon\sqrt\mu\,\tau)$, $\zeta_2=-\sin(\varepsilon\sqrt\mu\,\tau)/\sqrt\mu$ and $\zeta_1=(1+\mu)(1-\zeta_3)/(\varepsilon\mu)$. Expanding the cosine at fixed $\tau$ gives the quadratic first component in (2.4).
r2a1.wave.model-vector-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.model_case_equa: Differentiating $k\cdot E_i$ includes the rotation term $k\cdot\dot E_i$. It doubles the $\eta$ contribution in $\dot k_2$ and adds $\nu$ to the preceding shear in $\dot k_1$. The linked derivation assumes the frame equations of Lemma 2.2; the numbered theorem supplies them.

r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: The pressure contribution to the scaled pair is $\Pi(\zeta_1,\zeta_2/S^2)^T$. One factor $S^{-1}$ comes from the middle physical projection of $k$ and the other from the scaling used to define $\Pi$. Only the first pressure component survives at leading order. The other $S^{-2}$ term in the second equation is from eliminating $\alpha_3$ using perpendicularity.
r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearPressure:
In physical coordinates the three terms in $k\cdot M\mathbf a$ are $
u k_1a_2$, $\sigma k_2a_1$ and $\eta k_3a_2$. On inserting (2.3) these become $
u\lambda\zeta_1\alpha_2$, $2
u\lambda\zeta_2\alpha_1$ and $\eta\lambda\zeta_3\alpha_2$. Using $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$ gives the displayed $\Pi=\lambda Sp_{m w}/r$.
r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix: The pressure nearly cancels the direct driving term at large $x=\tan\varphi$: $-1+x(x+\varepsilon)/(1+x^2)=(\varepsilon x-1)/(1+x^2)$. The additional first diagonal entry is $-2\varepsilon\tau x/(1+x^2)$. Thus the limiting system has both a reduced, eventually reversed driving term and a damping term, even though the second scaled equation retains only its direct shear term.
r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix_mulVe: In the matrix of the finite system the second diagonal entry is $\varepsilon\zeta_2/(2S^2\zeta_3)+\zeta_2(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)/(S^2m)$. Thus the factor $S^{-2}$ alone is not sufficient for a uniform limit: both reciprocal factors must stay bounded. The limiting normal gives $\zeta_3\to1$ and $m\to1+\tan^2\varphi$ on a fixed slab.

r2a1.wave.uniform-strong-shear-limit.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: Uniformity here is on a fixed interval in the normalized time. In the exact model $\zeta_3=\cos(\varepsilon\tau/(\sqrt2S))$; even convergence of this one coordinate requires $\varepsilon T/S\to0$ if the interval is allowed to grow. This example explains why the order of the choices in Lemma 2.3 matters. The varying-background argument instead uses the explicit smallness condition (2.7).
r2a1.wave.uniform-strong-shear-limit.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.strongShear_lim: Once the uniform normal error is less than $1/2$, one has $\zeta_3\ge1/2$ and $m\ge1/4$ throughout the interval. Then each entry of the amplitude matrix is a continuous rational function of the uniformly converging coordinates and $S^{-2}$ on a region with denominators bounded away from zero. The coefficient limit holds for every amplitude vector; there is no need to estimate an amplitude solution first.

r2a1.wave.reference-system.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix: Write $s=\cos\varphi$. The trace of the reference matrix is $2(\log s)'$, so the determinant of two solutions is proportional to $s^2$. Taking the columns to be $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$ and $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ gives the determinant $-a_{\rm ref}(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)$. This is the combination used in (2.15) to measure departure from the reference direction, rather than absolute amplitude error.
r2a1.wave.reference-system.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.referenceMatr: The library uses $U=-\alpha_1$, $V=\alpha_2$, so its system is $U'=-dU+cV$, $V'=U$. With this sign choice the growing solution starts at $(1,1)$ and the slope is $Y=U/V$ instead of $-\alpha_1/\alpha_2$. The two matrices are conjugate by $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$.
r2a1.wave.reference-system.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.referenceSystem: The algebraic forms $c=(1-\varepsilon x)/(1+x^2)$ and $d=2\varepsilon\tau x/(1+x^2)$ are useful even at large $x$: their denominator is the squared reference wave-number factor, not an additional approximation. With $x=\tan\varphi$ they become the two trigonometric coefficients in (2.5).

r2a1.wave.frame-gives-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_2_3_of: The frame equations in Lemma 2.2 are in physical time. Their specialization gives the rotating frame, while $(\log\sigma_p)'=B_{33}=0$ keeps the coefficient of the preceding shear constant. The proof of Lemma 2.3 invokes this frame lemma before passing to the normalized time; the normal and amplitude equations alone would not specify the derivatives of their moving coordinates.
r2a1.wave.frame-gives-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.model_case_equa: The model frame rotates with angular velocity $-\eta E_1-\nu E_3$: crossing this vector with each $E_i$ gives the three displayed frame derivatives. Its derivative is zero since the two contributions along $E_2$ cancel. Thus the frame rotates around a fixed spatial axis even though the two nonzero entries of $B$ are specified in that frame. The new normal evolves over $M$ and does not in general follow this rotation.
r2a1.wave.frame-gives-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_2: Equation (2.2) has $\dot E_3=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2$. The model leaves only $\eta E_2$ here; likewise $\dot E_1=-\nu E_2$ and $\dot E_2=\nu E_1-\eta E_3$. The same lemma controls $\log\sigma_p$ through $B_{33}$, giving constancy of the shear on integrating.

r2a1.wave.physical-model-vector.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.model_case_equa:
For the middle component the gradient term is $-k\cdot ME_2=-
u k_1-\eta k_3$ and the rotation term is $k\cdot\dot E_2=
u k_1-\eta k_3$. Thus the $
u k_1$ terms cancel and $-2\eta k_3$ remains. The same calculation gives the other rows; the linked theorem states their scaled versions in normalized time.

r2a1.wave.physical-model-amplitude.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.model_case_equa:
For the first amplitude component, $-E_1\cdot M\mathbf a=-
u a_2$ and $\mathbf a\cdot\dot E_1=-
u a_2$, giving the factor two in the growth mechanism. For the second, the corresponding sum is $-(\sigma-
u)a_1-\eta a_3$. The linked scaled equations substitute the pressure and use perpendicularity to express $a_3$ through the other two components.

r2a1.wave.scale-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.nu_div_rate: There are two appearances of the identity $2\nu S/r=1$. It makes the first scaled amplitude transfer equal to $-\alpha_2$ and fixes the reference value of $2Sb_{12}$. The same factor of two arises in each calculation from the sum of a gradient term and a frame-rotation term.
r2a1.wave.scale-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.eta_div_rate: The identity $\eta/r=\varepsilon/(2S)$ occurs with two different weights. Multiplication by $2S$ produces the order-one term $-\varepsilon\zeta_3$ in $\zeta_2'$, whereas division by $S$ produces $\varepsilon\zeta_2/(2S^2)$ in $\zeta_3'$. The same physical entry can therefore turn one scaled component strongly and another weakly.
r2a1.wave.scale-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.rate_sq: Substitute $k_2=\lambda\zeta_2/S$ and $a_1=\alpha_1/S$ before taking the limit. Then $\sigma k_2a_1=(\sigma/S^2)\lambda\zeta_2\alpha_1=2\nu\lambda\zeta_2\alpha_1$. This accounts for the factor two inside the numerator of $\Pi$ even when the two physical projections are very small.

r2a1.wave.gronwall-limit.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.zeta_bounds: For $\mu=1/(2S^2)$ the difference of the finite and reference normals solves $d'=A_\mu d+(\mu\varepsilon\tau,0,-\mu\varepsilon^2\tau)$ with $d(0)=0$. The library bounds the forcing by $\mu\varepsilon T(1+\varepsilon)$ and the finite matrix by $2+\varepsilon$ in the maximum norm, assuming $0\le\mu\le1$. The resulting Gronwall estimate is sufficient for the fixed-$T$ limit because the forcing tends to zero with $\mu$.
r2a1.wave.gronwall-limit.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.strongShear_lim: The finite model's exact cosine and sine give more directly $|\zeta_3-1|\le\varepsilon^2\mu\tau^2/2$ and $|\zeta_2+\varepsilon\tau|\le\varepsilon^3\mu\tau^3/6$, with $\mu=1/(2S^2)$. The corresponding first-component bound is $|\zeta_1-\varepsilon\tau^2/2|\le\mu\varepsilon\tau^2/2+(1+\mu)\mu\varepsilon^3\tau^4/24$. These follow from the exact model equations; the linked proof uses Gronwall, which is sufficient on each fixed interval.

r2a1.wave.coefficient-limits.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.strongShear_lim: The limit of $m$ is $1+x^2$, where $x=\tan\varphi$. The first row contains the two pressure coefficients $2x(-\varepsilon\tau)/(1+x^2)$ and $x(x+\varepsilon)/(1+x^2)$. The second row has only the direct shear term $-\alpha_1$ in the limit. The uniform lower bounds for the denominators justify taking all these limits on the same interval.
r2a1.wave.coefficient-limits.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.referenceSystem: After substituting $x=\tan\varphi$, the pressure contribution to the first off-diagonal entry is $x(x+\varepsilon)/(1+x^2)$. Combining it with $-1$ cancels the quadratic numerator and leaves $(\varepsilon x-1)/(1+x^2)$. This identity, not an estimate of two terms separately, gives the sign reversal of the reference driving coefficient.

c8-reference-system-name.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix: The reference system is a matrix equation for arbitrary transverse amplitudes, whereas the reference solution is the solution with initial pair $(-1,1)$. The latter supplies a positive scalar amplitude by which all the other solutions can be divided. The normalized system in Lemma 2.6 then yields a bound for general initial vectors, not just the one used to construct the next wave.

c8-reference-vector-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef: For arbitrary initial components $(u,v,w)$, the reference evolution over elapsed time $h$ is $(u-hv+\varepsilon h^2w/2,\ v-\varepsilon hw,\ w)$. Equivalently the coefficient matrix $A_0$ satisfies $A_0^3=0$. A perturbation injected into the third component can travel through two other equations, but no reference transfer returns to that component. This gives the degree-two propagator used in the polynomial comparison.
c8-reference-vector-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.zeta_bounds: The estimate in `zeta_bounds` includes the case $\mu=0$. Its three right-hand sides then vanish, identifying the solution of the limiting equations with $\zeta_0$ on the interval. For $\mu=1/(2S^2)>0$ the same estimates bound the deviation of the finite model. This is a coordinate estimate, independent of the amplitude.

r2a1.wave.physical-error.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio: The smallness of the error has to be judged in the scaled equations. A term such as $E_{c,32}$ in the normal equation is multiplied by $S/r=1/(2\nu)$, not just $1/r$; it can compete with the smaller turning coupling even when negligible compared with the large preceding shear. The first two terms of $\delta$ likewise control the couplings relative to their own launch values. In the general Lean definition the suprema can be taken on a larger compact physical interval containing the comparison slab.

additive.finite-smallness.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.additiveCompariso: The tolerance used in the coupling calculation is smaller than a fixed absolute error: the second coupling itself may be of order $T^{-2}\nu$. If a preceding estimate is $CT^p\delta$, then (2.7) bounds it by $(C/C_0)\varepsilon T^{p-C_0}$. Taking $C_0\ge p+2$ and $C_0\ge8C$ gives the later tolerance $\varepsilon T^{-2}/8$. This is why the exponent in (2.7) is left sufficiently large.
additive.finite-smallness.TorusEuler.Paper.FiniteSmallness: The first inequality makes the reference ratio small; the second imposes the accuracy of the finite-shear comparison. In particular the model with constant moving entries and $E_c=0$ still has $\delta\ge\nu/r=1/(2S)>0$. Thus even the exact finite-shear model must have $S\ge C_0T^{C_0}/(2\varepsilon)$ to meet (2.7). The reference limit, where $S^{-1}=0$, is not itself a finite physical wave.

r2a1.wave.strong-shear-bounds.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r: At activation $B_{12}=\nu$, so the third term of (2.6) is at least $\nu/r=1/(2S)$. Consequently $S^{-1}\le2\delta$ and, since $\delta\le1/4$, $S^{-2}\le4\delta^2\le\delta$. Strong shear is therefore a consequence of the comparison hypotheses, not another assumption.
r2a1.wave.strong-shear-bounds.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio: The stronger conclusion $S\ge T^2$ is used to pass back from the two scaled amplitude components to the physical vector. For instance $|\alpha_3|/S\le 2(|\zeta_1||\alpha_1|+|\zeta_2||\alpha_2|)/S\le C| (\alpha_1,\alpha_2)|$. Thus the forward coordinate change is bounded independently of the comparison interval; its inverse is allowed the factor $S$ that appears in the transverse propagator bound.

r5-waves-parameter-ratio.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.ε: The target ratio of wave $j-1$ becomes the input ratio of wave $j$. Thus at the launch of wave $j\ge2$ we have $\varepsilon^{-1/2}=L_j$ in the gain estimate, while its own target ratio is $L_{j+1}^{-2}$. The two logarithmic gains belong to successive switches.

r2a1.wave.coefficient-list.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.scaledAmplitu: The reference evaluation is performed after grouping the coefficients. In particular $B/r$ tends to zero in the model, but $2Sb_{12}$ and $2Sb_{32}$ tend to $1$ and $\varepsilon$, not zero. Substituting $B/r=0$ before this grouping would remove the two couplings that drive amplification and turning.

r2a1.wave.vector-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: The second estimate compares the physical wave number to its own, changing reference value. If $d=m\cos^2\varphi-1$, then $|k|/(\lambda/\cos\varphi)=\sqrt{1+d}$ and the deviation of this quotient from one is $|d|/(1+\sqrt{1+d})$. Hence the comparison gives useful relative accuracy even at the late times when $|k|$ is much larger than $\lambda$.
r2a1.wave.vector-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_4: The second bound in (2.10) is the one used in Proposition 2.8: at a late crossing, $\eta_+/\nu_+=\varepsilon_+$ is comparable to $\cos\varphi$, so $|k|\asymp\lambda/\varepsilon_+$. The amplitude comparison is still needed to control $|\mathbf a|$. Bounds on the two quantities separately explain why a very small coupling ratio can be selected after the velocity amplitude has already decreased.
r2a1.wave.vector-comparison.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.additiveCompariso: The auxiliary theorem `additiveComparison` bounds the sum of the three coordinate errors and the matrix error in $(U,V)$. The paper's additional length conclusion uses $m-m_0=(\zeta_1-x)(\zeta_1+x)+(\zeta_3-1)(\zeta_3+1)+S^{-2}\zeta_2^2$. The coefficient $S^{-2}$ makes the last term small even though the scaled middle coordinate is not close to zero.

r2a1.wave.safe-coordinates.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: The normal equation is solved and estimated first. Its third component stays within $1/2$ of one, which gives both reciprocal bounds $1/\zeta_3\le2$ and $1/m\le4$. Thus no estimate of an amplitude, or assumption that its second component is positive, is needed to define the reduced matrix.
r2a1.wave.safe-coordinates.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.waveVector_c: In particular $\zeta_3\ge1/2$ has a use beyond keeping the amplitude chart regular. The preceding vorticity points along $E_3$, while the vorticity of the new wave is perpendicular to $k$. In §8 the projection along $k/|k|$ eliminates the latter contribution and retains at least $\sigma_p/(2\sqrt m)$ of the preceding vorticity. Since $\sqrt m\le3T^2$ here, the retained projection costs only a polynomial in the normalized interval length.
r2a1.wave.safe-coordinates.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.norm_zeta_le: The coordinate bounds used in Lean give $|\zeta_1|\le T^2$, $|\zeta_2|\le T$ and $|\zeta_3|\le3/2$. Hence $|\zeta|\le\sqrt{T^4+T^2+9/4}\le3T^2$ for $T\ge2$. This is a bound on the scaled coordinates used in the polynomial estimates; the physical length is controlled separately by $m$.

r2a1.wave.amplitude-comparison-system.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: This equation compares matrices on a two-dimensional plane chart. It is not an inhomogeneous equation with a force of size $CT^C\delta$ independent of the amplitude: the error is multiplied by the current amplitude. The Lean operator norm is that for the maximum norm on the pair, so entrywise bounds of size $d$ give operator norm at most $2d$.
r2a1.wave.amplitude-comparison-system.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.alpha_system_of: In the raw equations Lean evolves $(U,V)=(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. Conjugating their matrix by $J=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$ gives the matrix in the paper, with the error replaced by $J\mathcal E J$. Since $J$ is an isometry for the maximum norm, the bound on the error is unchanged. The coordinate-change theorem assumes the raw derivative equations.
r2a1.wave.amplitude-comparison-system.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.additiveCompariso: The auxiliary theorem gives a single continuous error operator $R$ after fixing the physical window and the transported normal, but before quantifying over transverse amplitudes. Its coordinates are $U=-\alpha_1$, $V=\alpha_2$. It is a coefficient comparison, with the normal error also estimated; relative bounds for the growing amplitude require the subsequent reference-solution argument.

r2a1.wave.one-common-error.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: The order of the quantifiers is useful: fix the parent and the normal, choose the continuous error operator, and then take any transverse amplitude. This lets us propagate vectors with arbitrary initial direction, even when their second component is zero. Only the selected growing solution is later divided by its own second component.

r2a1.wave.clock-chain-rule.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.hasDerivWith: All time-dependent quantities are evaluated at $t=t_0+\tau/r$ before differentiation. In particular the rotation of $E_i$ is divided by $r$, just as the gradient term is. The relative factors in the projected equations would be incorrect if one changed the clock for $k$ and $\mathbf a$ but not the frame. The linked chain rule applies within the closed time intervals.

additive.normalized-coefficient-bounds.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r: Because $2S/r=1/\nu$, one has $2Sb_{12}=B_{12}/\nu$ and $2Sb_{32}=\varepsilon B_{32}/\eta$. The first two terms of $\delta$ therefore bound their deviations from $1$ and $\varepsilon$, while the third term gives $|b_{ij}|\le\delta$ in the orthonormal frame. The extra factor $\varepsilon\le1$ in the third-coupling deviation only improves the bound.
additive.normalized-coefficient-bounds.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.normalized_fact: The Lean package also bounds the normalized error gradient by $\delta/S$: $\|E_c/r\|\le\|E_c\|/(2\nu S)\le\delta/S$. This is stronger than a plain $\delta$ bound and compensates for the factor $S$ in the scaled equations. The two surviving older entries are compared with $1$ and $\varepsilon$, respectively.

r2a1.wave.strength-bound.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati: The logarithmic derivative is $b_{33}$ after changing the clock. Consequently $e^{-T\delta}\le\sigma_p/\sigma\le e^{T\delta}$, and for $T\delta\le1$ this gives $|\sigma_p/\sigma-1|\le2T\delta$. The error in the leading shear coefficient is thus relative to its frozen value, which may be very large.
r2a1.wave.strength-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.strengthRatio_b: Put $z=\int_0^\tau b_{33}$. On $0\le z\le1$, convexity gives $e^z-1\le(e-1)z$, and for $-1\le z\le0$ one has $1-e^z\le|z|$. Thus $|e^z-1|\le2|z|\le2T\delta$. This estimates the relative drift of the large shear coefficient without estimating either wave length separately.
r2a1.wave.strength-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: The drift estimate is not an additional comparison of the new amplitude. It controls the coefficient $\sigma_p/\sigma$ that multiplies $q$ in the new coupling calculation (2.20). It also shows that a strong preceding shear does not disappear during the present wave's amplification interval: $\sigma_p\ge e^{-T\delta}\sigma$. Section 8 uses this same logarithmic strength equation to estimate the preceding vorticity between activations.

r2a1.wave.second-third-vector-equations.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_w: In the second row, rotation of the preceding frame cancels the $B_{12}$ contribution and adds another $-B_{32}$ to the coefficient of the third normal projection. Scaling gives $-2Sb_{32}\zeta_3$, close to $-\varepsilon\zeta_3$. The third row has coefficient $(b_{32}-b_{23})/S$ on $\zeta_2$, and hence no surviving reference term. The linked equations also allow $E_c$, separated in the paper below.

r2a1.wave.first-vector-equation.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_w: The large entry $S\sigma_p/\sigma$ in $M/r$ acts on $\zeta_2/S$ in the transposed-gradient equation. Its contribution to $\zeta_1'$ is $-(\sigma_p/\sigma)\zeta_2$. The remaining terms in this row contain small $b_{ij}$ or $b_{ij}/S$, so the reference row is just $\zeta_1'=-\zeta_2$.

r2a1.wave.scaled-error-matrix.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_w: The extra gradient changes the normal coefficient by $-PE_c^TP^{-1}/r$, where $P=\operatorname{diag}(1,S,1)$ acts in the preceding frame. Its norm is at most $(S/r)|E_c|=|E_c|/(2\nu)$ because $\|P^{-1}\|=1$. The factor $S$ is paid once, explaining the normalization of $E_c$ in (2.6).

r2a1.wave.polynomial-vector-error.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.polynomial_w: Write $u,v,w$ for the three normal errors. Their reference equations with residuals are $w'=r_3$, $v'=-\varepsilon w+r_2$, $u'=-v+r_1$. With zero initial errors and $|r_i|\le R$, successive integration gives $|w|\le RT$, $|v|\le2RT^2$, $|u|\le3RT^3$. The actual residual bound is $R=D(2T^2+M)$, where $M=\sup(|u|+|v|+|w|)$. Hence $M\le6DT^3(2T^2+M)$, and $12DT^3\le1$ gives $M\le24DT^5$. The polynomial loss comes from the two successive transfers, not from an estimate of a general linear system by Gronwall.
r2a1.wave.polynomial-vector-error.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.waveVector_poly: The preceding-strength drift contributes an error of order $T\delta$ to the first row of the normal equation. The frame calculation bounds the residuals by $5T\delta$ times the sum of the coordinate magnitudes. The triangular estimate then gives $24(5T\delta)T^5=120\delta T^6$, at most $1/2$ by the smallness hypothesis.
r2a1.wave.polynomial-vector-error.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_2_4_of: The first variation-of-constants estimate has a residual involving the unknown actual vector $\zeta$, not only the reference vector. Writing $\zeta=\zeta_0+(\zeta-\zeta_0)$ produces a term $CT^C\delta\sup|\zeta-\zeta_0|$ on the right; (2.7) permits moving it to the left. This closes the normal estimate before any division by $\zeta_3$ in the amplitude equation.

r2a1.wave.relative-wave-norm.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.normFactor_cos_: Write $x=\tan\varphi$ and $e_0$ for the coordinate error. The linked estimate assumes $x\le T^2/4$, which follows here from $\varepsilon\le1/2$, and $e_0\le1/2$. Factoring $\zeta_1^2-x^2$ and $\zeta_3^2-1$ bounds each by $T^2 e_0$; the remaining term $S^{-2}\zeta_2^2$ is at most $2\delta T^2$. Division by $1+x^2$ gives $|m\cos^2\varphi-1|\le2T^2(e_0+\delta)$.
r2a1.wave.relative-wave-norm.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_2_4_of: The length estimate gives $\lambda/(\sqrt2\cos\varphi)\le |k|\le\sqrt{3/2}\lambda/\cos\varphi$. Its reciprocal therefore has the same relative control. In particular, at a late crossing where $\cos\varphi\asymp\varepsilon_+$, the wave number has gained a factor comparable to $\varepsilon_+^{-1}$, not merely $\varepsilon^{-1}$ at the reference peak.

r2a1.wave.pressure-coefficients.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.pressureU: The pressure numerator is linear in the two remaining amplitude components. At fixed $k$ write $\mathbf a=\alpha_1v_1+\alpha_2v_2$, where $v_1=(E_1-\zeta_1 E_3/\zeta_3)/S$ and $v_2=E_2-\zeta_2 E_3/(S\zeta_3)$. Then $F_i=(S/\lambda)k\cdot(M/r)v_i$. This recovers each displayed row by applying $M/r$ to one transverse basis vector. In Lean `pressureU` is $-F_1$ because $U=-\alpha_1$; the paper's formulas here have $E_c=0$.
r2a1.wave.pressure-coefficients.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.pressureV: To obtain $F_2$, set $\alpha_1=0$, $\alpha_2=1$ in the transverse amplitude. The vector is $E_2-\zeta_2 E_3/(S\zeta_3)$; the preceding shear annihilates it. The two surviving reference contributions come from $BE_2$, namely $\zeta_1Sb_{12}$ and $\zeta_3Sb_{32}$. Their sum is $(x+\varepsilon)/2$.

r2a1.wave.projected-amplitude.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.normalized_am: The same scalar pressure coefficient feeds both projected equations. Its matrix on the pair is the outer product $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2/S^2)^T\,2(F_1,F_2)/m$, of rank at most one. It is the factor $S^{-2}$ in the second row that removes the pressure from the second reference equation. The frame-rotation terms are separate from this rank-one contribution.
r2a1.wave.projected-amplitude.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.alpha_system_of: The signed matrix used by the library becomes the paper's matrix under conjugation by $J=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$. Only the off-diagonal signs change. This operation preserves the maximum norm, so the bound on the matrix difference transfers without changing its constant.

r2a1.wave.exact-amplitude-matrix.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.rawMatrix: The raw matrix takes two different gradients as inputs: $A=M/r$ acts on the new amplitude, and $b=B/r$ rotates the preceding frame. For example, the direct and rotation terms in the first paper row add to $-S(A_{12}+b_{12})\alpha_2$, reducing to $-2Sb_{12}\alpha_2$ when $E_c=0$. In the signed first row of `rawMatrix` the coefficient has the opposite sign. The same distinction between the two matrices is retained when adding $E_c$.

r2a1.wave.reference-pressure-values.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.scaledPressur: At reference inputs, $F_1=\zeta_{0,2}=-\varepsilon\tau$ comes from the preceding shear, while $F_2=(x+\varepsilon)/2$ comes from the older gradient. The library has `pressureU` equal to $-F_1$ because it uses $U=-\alpha_1$. The factor two in $2(F_1\alpha_1+F_2\alpha_2)/m$ is applied afterwards.

r2a1.wave.reference-matrix-values.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.scaledMatrix_: In signed coordinates the reference matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-d&c\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, with $c=(1-\varepsilon x)/(1+x^2)$ and $d=2\varepsilon\tau x/(1+x^2)$. Thus the boxed terms retain two distinct effects of pressure, the damping $-d$ and the change of driving from $1$ to $c$. Reversing the first coordinate gives (2.5).
r2a1.wave.reference-matrix-values.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.referenceSystem: The linked identity is an evaluation at the reference inputs, not an estimate of the finite matrix. In the paper's signs the only nonzero entries are $-d,-c,-1$, where $d=\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi$ and $c=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)$. The next paragraph controls the error in replacing the actual entries by these values.

r2a1.wave.polynomial-sensitivity.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.errorOperator: The independent inputs include the reciprocals $1/\zeta_3$ and $1/m$. After this choice, each matrix entry is a fixed-degree polynomial. In subtracting two products of degree $d$, replace one factor at a time; each summand has one small input difference and $d-1$ bounded factors. Thus a box of radius $M$ and input errors at most $\rho$ give a bound of the form $CM^p\rho$ with fixed $p$. The formal theorem gives this bound for the operator norm as well as the underlying entrywise estimates.
r2a1.wave.polynomial-sensitivity.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_2_4_of: The divisions are regular: $|1/\zeta_3-1|\le2|\zeta_3-1|$ and $|1/m-1/m_0|=|m-m_0|/(mm_0)\le4|m-m_0|$ since $m_0=\cos^{-2}\varphi\ge1$. These are the remaining input differences needed for the polynomial coefficient estimate. The conditional proof of Lemma 2.4 combines them with the frame and normal estimates.

r2a1.wave.strain-error.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.norm_errorOpe: The direct extra term in the amplitude equation at a fixed normal is $(2P_k-\mathrm{Id})E_c\mathbf a$. The reflection $2P_k-\mathrm{Id}$ preserves physical length; the cost of $E_c$ comes only from reconstructing the transverse vector and taking the scaled projections. The Lean bound $6S\|E_c/r\|\le3\delta$ uses these two operations. The error in the normal itself has already been treated, so it must not be counted as another direct forcing here.

r2a1.amp.reference-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix: The frozen reference matrix at launch has eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$, with eigenvectors $(-1,1)$ and $(1,1)$. At later times it varies. In particular the growing initial direction need not remain an instantaneous eigendirection; its actual evolution is measured by the slope $Y=-\alpha_1/\alpha_2$.
r2a1.amp.reference-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.driving_referen: The driving coefficient vanishes when $\varepsilon\tan\varphi=1$, or $\tau=\sqrt2/\varepsilon$. This is much later than the turning scale $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ for small $\varepsilon$, but still before the amplitude peak at $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon$. In the scalar equation $\alpha_2''+d\alpha_2'=c\alpha_2$, the sign change concerns $c$, not $\alpha_2'$. The latter remains positive until the later zero of the logarithmic slope.

r2a1.amp.reference-initial-data.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceU_z: The reconstructed reference pair in the library is $(U,V)=(Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$. Since $a_{\rm ref}(0)=1$, imposing $Y(0)=1$ gives $U(0)=1$ and hence the paper's $\alpha_1(0)=-1$. This fixes direction, while the normalization of $V$ fixes size.
r2a1.amp.reference-initial-data.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_z: The scalar exponential has $V(0)=1$ independently of the equation for $Y$. This is the size normalization; every positive multiple gives the same initial direction and logarithmic slope. The reference solution uses the unit normalization so later quotients by $a_{\rm ref}$ compare amplitudes with the prescribed unit launch.

r2a1.amp.reference-rate.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivWith: For continuous $Y$, differentiating $\exp(\int_0^\tau Y)$ gives $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$, including the right derivative at zero. Its positivity is automatic, unlike the positivity of the second component of an arbitrary solution. The Riccati equation is needed only to verify the first amplitude equation after reconstruction.

r2a1.amp.riccati-problem.TorusEuler.Paper.ReferenceSlope: Where $\alpha_2>0$, eliminating $\alpha_1$ gives $\alpha_2''+\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi\,\alpha_2'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)\alpha_2$. Dividing by $\alpha_2$ and using $\alpha_2''/\alpha_2=Y'+Y^2$ gives (2.12). The scalar equation depends on the direction of the pair, not its overall normalization. The proof below constructs the slope globally before reconstructing a positive second component.
r2a1.amp.riccati-problem.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.referenceSlope_: The algebraic formulation uses $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$, so that the driving coefficient is $s^2(1-\varepsilon x)$ and the damping is $2\varepsilon\tau xs^2$. Since $s=\cos\varphi$, substituting these expressions leaves the same Riccati equation and initial condition on the half-line.

r2a1.amp.reference-reconstruction.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_am: Given the scalar solution $Y$, let $V=a_{\rm ref}$ and $U=YV$. Then $V'=U$ and $U'=(Y'+Y^2)V=cV-dU$, with $c$ the driving and $d$ the damping coefficient in (2.5). The quadratic term has canceled, so this is the signed linear system. The reconstruction uses the Riccati equation; the additional condition $Y(0)=1$ selects the reference initial pair.

r2a1.amp.reference-amplitude.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAmplitude: The positive reference amplitude supplies the weight for the subsequent forced problems. Its quotient between normalized times $\tau_1\le\tau_2$ is $\exp(\int_{\tau_1}^{\tau_2}Y)$. Lemma 2.6 compares the physical amplitude quotient with this one; after rescaling the peak to $\lambda^{-3/4}$, the propagator bound in physical time becomes $CS\gamma(t)/\gamma(t')$ for $t'\le t$. Thus the transverse corrections are estimated relative to the seed at each time, rather than relative to its small launch value.
r2a1.amp.reference-amplitude.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV: The definition $a_{\rm ref}=\exp(\int Y)$ normalizes the initial second component to one and guarantees positivity on every finite interval. In the signed library coordinates the reference vector is $(Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$. Dividing by this positive scalar is legitimate even after the peak, and does not require that the first component or its logarithmic rate keep a fixed sign.

lem-2-4-parameter.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: The global reference problem needs only $0<\varepsilon\le1$; there is no prescribed finite $T$ and no $\delta$ or $S$ in this statement. This separates the scalar existence and peak calculation from the comparison of actual waves. In Lean the theorem gives existence and then uniqueness and the listed estimates for every solution of the scalar initial-value problem.
lem-2-4-parameter.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: At a zero of $Y$, the ansatz gives $\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi=2(1+e)$. In particular $\varepsilon\tau\ge2$, and the Riccati equation there gives $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-(\varepsilon\tau)^2/2)<0$. All zeros are therefore downward crossings. The ansatz gives $Y<0$ by $\varepsilon\tau=3$, yielding existence and uniqueness of the peak.

r2a1.amp.reference-existence-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: It is safer to construct the bounded correction $e$ than to begin by dividing by a possibly vanishing amplitude. Its equation is $e'=\cos\varphi(-2e-e^2+\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi/2)$. At $e=0$ the derivative is nonnegative, and at $e=\varepsilon/8$ it is nonpositive since the source is at most $\varepsilon/4$. This invariant interval gives continuation on every finite time interval. The amplitude reconstructed by exponentiation never vanishes.
r2a1.amp.reference-existence-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: The upper bound $Y\le1$ controls the amplitude accumulated in the first normalized unit. It follows from the Riccati equation at $Y=1$, since the driving term is at most one and the damping is nonnegative. For the lower bound use the ansatz: $\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi/4\le\min(\varepsilon\tau/4,1/\tau)\le1/2$. In particular $Y\ge-1/2$, and the weaker formal bound $|Y|\le1$ suffices to control the relative amplitude coordinates.

r2a1.amp.reference-ansatz.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: The ansatz can also be read as a change of dependent variable and clock. With $s=\cos\varphi$, put $a_{\rm ref}=\sqrt{s}\,W(\theta)$, $\theta'=s$, $\theta(0)=0$. Since $Y=(\log a_{\rm ref})'$, (2.13) gives $W_\theta/W=1+e$. The correction equation is equivalent to $W_{\theta\theta}=(1+\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi/2)W$, with $W(0)=W_\theta(0)=1$. The coefficient lies between one and $1+\varepsilon/4$; the square-root factor accounts for the geometric loss as the normal turns.
r2a1.amp.reference-ansatz.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: At the peak the ansatz gives $\varepsilon\tau_m=2(1+e(\tau_m))/\sin\varphi(\tau_m)$. Since $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)\le\varepsilon/2$ and $e\le\varepsilon/8$, this is $2+O(\varepsilon)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. After the peak the integral remaining in (2.14) is bounded, so the amplitude quotient is comparable to the square root of the cosine quotient. The reference strength instead contains the inverse square root, because the wave number is $\lambda/\cos\varphi$.

r2a1.amp.reference-amplitude-formula.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: The two factors in (2.14) have opposite effects on the amplitude: the exponential grows and the square root of the cosine decreases. For the reference shear, however, multiplication by $|k|=\lambda/\cos\varphi$ changes the latter factor into $(\cos\varphi)^{-1/2}$. Both factors then grow. It is the amplitude, not the shear, that has a maximum at $\tau_m$.
r2a1.amp.reference-amplitude-formula.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: In the time $\xi=\int_0^\tau\cos\varphi\,d\tau'$, the factor $a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$ grows at rate $1+e$. The total available effective time is $c_*\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, where $c_*=\sqrt2\int_0^\infty(1+v^4)^{-1/2}\,dv$ by $v=\sqrt{\varepsilon/2}\,\tau$. The bound on $e$ changes the logarithmic gain by at most $O(\sqrt\varepsilon)$, even over the whole half-line. In particular a very long wait for the next crossing does not produce another large exponential gain.

r2a1.amp.unique-zero.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: At the zero of $Y$, (2.13) gives $\varepsilon\tau_m=2(1+e(\tau_m))/\sin\varphi(\tau_m)$. The stated bracket implies $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)=O(\varepsilon)$, so in fact $\varepsilon\tau_m=2+O(\varepsilon)$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. The peak occurs with the normal nearly parallel to $E_1$, long after it has reached angle $\pi/4$ at $\sqrt{2/\varepsilon}$.
r2a1.amp.unique-zero.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: At any zero, (2.12) reduces to $Y'=s^2(1-(\varepsilon\tau)^2/2)$, with $s=\cos\varphi$. The ansatz first rules out zeros for $\varepsilon\tau\le2$. All remaining zeros have negative derivative; once the first is crossed, the function cannot return to zero from below. The opposite signs at $2/\varepsilon$ and $3/\varepsilon$ give existence.

r2a1.amp.reference-signs-maximum.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: The maximum in this lemma is that of the second scaled component of the reference solution. Later, (2.18) compares the actual physical length with this component pointwise. Taking maxima preserves the two multiplicative inequalities, provided the comparison interval contains $\tau_m$; it does not locate the maximizing time of the physical length.
r2a1.amp.reference-signs-maximum.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: For the reference strength, the logarithmic derivative is $Y-(\log\cos\varphi)'=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\tfrac12(\log\cos\varphi)'>0$. In particular the decrease in amplitude after $\tau_m$ is more than offset by the increase in wave number. Later we will use the finite-shear comparison to estimate the actual strength at a crossing; monotonicity of the actual strength is not required.

r2a1.amp.reference-gain.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: The gain is a ratio of amplitudes, so one can use it in reverse. Given a desired maximum $A=\lambda^{-3/4}$ on the comparison slab, solve with the growing launch direction and multiply by $A/\max|\mathbf a|$. The frame and the crossing equation are unchanged. It is the resulting small initial amplitude, rather than an arbitrarily large final velocity, that is needed in §6.2.
r2a1.amp.reference-gain.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: The lower bound uses the interval ending at $b=\sqrt{2/\varepsilon}$, when $\varphi=\pi/4$. On that interval $\cos\varphi\ge1/\sqrt2$ and $1+e\ge1$. The gain in the exponential is therefore at least $b/\sqrt2=\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ in the logarithm, at a cost of only $\tfrac14\log2$ from the square-root prefactor. The large gain is already established before the later turn of the amplitude.

r2a1.amp.angle-and-clock-derivatives.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivAt_s: Writing $s=\cos\varphi$ and $x=\tan\varphi$, we have $s'/s=-xx'/(1+x^2)=-\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$. Thus the coefficient of $Y$ in (2.12) is $2s'/s$, and the correction in (2.13) is $s'/(2s)$. The latter is the logarithmic derivative of the square-root prefactor in (2.14).

r2a1.amp.ansatz-proof.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY: Another way to obtain the ansatz is to set $s=\cos\varphi$, $d\xi=s\,d\tau$ and $a_{\rm ref}=\sqrt{s}\,f(\xi)$. Then $Y/s-s'/(2s^2)=f_\xi/f$. In the scalar second-order equation obtained from (2.5), this substitution eliminates the first derivative of $f$. The ansatz sets its logarithmic derivative equal to $1+e$.

r2a1.amp.integrated-ansatz.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_r: Between times $a$ and $b$, the integral in (2.14) is replaced by its increment $\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi$. The prefactor is replaced by $\sqrt{\cos\varphi(b)/\cos\varphi(a)}$. Choosing $a=\tau_m$ will remove the entire gain accumulated before the peak from the estimate for the retained amplitude.

r2a1.amp.deviation-equation.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivWith: In the time $d\xi=\cos\varphi\,d\tau$, the equation for $e$ has no small prefactor. If $f=a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$, then $f_\xi/f=1+e$ gives $f_{\xi\xi}=(1+\tfrac12\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi)f$, with $f(0)=f_\xi(0)=1$. Its coefficient differs from one by at most $\varepsilon/4$. The corresponding constant-coefficient growing solution would be $e^\xi$.
r2a1.amp.deviation-equation.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_ze: The launch value $e(0)=0$ follows from $Y(0)=1$, $\cos\varphi(0)=1$ and $(\log\cos\varphi)'(0)=0$. Thus the ansatz starts with the exact growing eigenvector of the frozen launch matrix; no initial error has to be absorbed into $e$.

r2a1.amp.deviation-forcing.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_mul_s_sq_l: The forcing in the parentheses is $(\varepsilon/2)x/(1+x^2)$ with $x=\tan\varphi$. It is at most $\varepsilon/4$, with equality at $x=1$. At $e=\varepsilon/8$ the linear term $-2e$ alone balances this upper bound, and the term $-e^2$ has the favorable sign.

r2a1.amp.global-deviation.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_ex: At $e=0$ the derivative is nonnegative, while at $e=\varepsilon/8$ it is strictly negative for $\varepsilon>0$ and finite $\tau$. The solution remains in this bounded interval. On every finite interval the coefficient is continuous and the vector field is locally Lipschitz in $e$, so there can be no finite-time obstruction to continuation.
r2a1.amp.global-deviation.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: Solve the equation for $e$ first and define $Y$ by (2.13). Then $a_{\rm ref}=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y)$ is positive, and direct substitution shows that $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$ solves (2.5) with the required data. This order avoids assuming that the second component of the reference solution never vanishes in order to derive a global equation for its quotient.

r2a1.amp.upper-rate.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_abs_: To bound the positive part of $Y$, the equation at $Y\ge1$ gives $Y'\le1-Y^2\le0$. On the negative side (2.13) gives $Y\ge-\min\{\varepsilon\tau/4,1/\tau\}\ge-\sqrt\varepsilon/2$. The paper needs only the resulting uniform bound $|Y|\le1$, which will also bound the entries of the coordinate change after the peak.

r2a1.amp.positive-before-turn.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_p: The sign of the driving coefficient and the sign of $Y$ need not change at the same time: at $\tau=\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, the first term of (2.12) vanishes but $Y>0$. By then the remaining effective growth time $\int_{\sqrt2/\varepsilon}^{\infty}\cos\varphi\,d\tau$ is at most $\sqrt2$. The large exponential gain has already occurred; the balance of this remaining gain with the decreasing cosine determines the peak.

r2a1.amp.sine-strict.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_mul_s_lt_o: For finite $x=\tan\varphi$, $1-\sin^2\varphi=(1+x^2)^{-1}>0$. The strictness, rather than just $\sin\varphi\le1$, rules out a zero at the lower endpoint $\varepsilon\tau=2$.

r2a1.amp.negative-at-three.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_n: At $\tau=3/\varepsilon$, one has $\tan\varphi=9/(2\varepsilon)\ge9/2$, hence $\sin\varphi>3/4$. The subtracted term in $Y/\cos\varphi$ is then $>9/8$, while $1+e\le9/8$. This gives the other strict endpoint sign without an asymptotic estimate.

r2a1.amp.unique-turn-proof.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_turn: All zeros must occur with $\varepsilon\tau>2$, where the differential equation at $Y=0$ gives $Y'<0$. At every zero the function therefore crosses from positive to negative values. Together with the opposite signs at $2/\varepsilon$ and $3/\varepsilon$, this proves existence, uniqueness and the signs on the two sides.

r2a1.amp.gain-proof.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_gain: At $b=\sqrt{2/\varepsilon}$, $\tan\varphi(b)=1$. The integral in $\log a_{\rm ref}(b)$ is at least $b/\sqrt2=\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, since $e\ge0$, and the logarithm of the prefactor is $-\tfrac14\log2$. The maximum is no smaller than this value.

r2a1.amp.normalized-coordinates.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalize: Equivalently, $\alpha_2=a_{\rm ref}h$ and $\alpha_1=-a_{\rm ref}(Yh+l\cos\varphi)$. For solutions of the reference system, $l=dh/d\xi$ in the time $d\xi=\cos\varphi\,d\tau$. This gives a reason for the factor $1/\cos\varphi$ in the definition: the relative amplitude and its derivative in effective growth time are the two coordinates. They are defined even when $\alpha_2=0$.

r2a1.amp.normalized-h-derivative.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.hasDerivW: Differentiating $\alpha_2/a_{\rm ref}$ uses $\alpha_2'=-\alpha_1$ and $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$. The two terms combine to $(-\alpha_1-Y\alpha_2)/a_{\rm ref}=l\cos\varphi$. The reference growth disappears from the equation for $h$.

r2a1.amp.normalized-l-decay.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangula: Liouville gives $a_{\rm ref}^2l\cos\varphi$ proportional to $\cos^2\varphi$. On substituting (2.14), this says that $(a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi})^2l$ is constant. In the effective time $d\xi=\cos\varphi\,d\tau$, this is the constant Wronskian of $f=a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$ and $\alpha_2/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$. In particular $l$ decays like the inverse square of the growing factor $f$.

r2a1.amp.triangular-system.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.hasDerivW: In the time $d\xi=\cos\varphi\,d\tau$, the equations read $h_\xi=l$, $l_\xi=-2(1+e)l$. For arbitrary initial data the total transfer into the first coordinate is at most half the decrease in $|l|$. This follows by integrating $|l|\le-\tfrac12\partial_\xi|l|$; it gives a uniform estimate without a lower bound on the speed of the effective clock.

r2a1.amp.reference-normalized-state.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalize: The distinguished growing initial data give $h=1$, $l=0$. Since this is an equilibrium of the triangular system, the comparison with the actual wave reduces to controlling the displacement from $(1,0)$ in the perturbed system, rather than the difference of two exponentially large amplitudes.

ref-l-does-not-increase.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangula: The multiplier of $l$ is $[f(\tau_1)/f(\tau_2)]^2$, where $f=a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$. Since $f$ is increasing, this is at most one even when $a_{\rm ref}$ is decreasing. For fixed $\varepsilon$ it need not tend to zero: the integral of $\cos\varphi$ on the half-line is finite. Bounded forward propagation is the property needed below.

If $d$ denotes the multiplier of $l$ and $q$ the off-diagonal transfer, then $(2q+d)'=-2e\cos\varphi\,d\le0$ and $2q+d=1$ at the initial time. Thus $q\le(1-d)/2$. This is the argument in the linked coefficient bound; no positive lower bound for $\cos\varphi$ is required.

r2a1.amp.transfer-from-decay.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangula: An initial direction error $l_1$ contributes $ql_1$ to the relative amplitude and $dl_1$ to the later direction error, with $q\ge0$ and $0<d\le1$. The inequality $2q+d\le1$ means that the amount transferred into the amplitude is at most half the direction error lost. It is not necessary for $|h|$ itself to decrease.

From $d'=-2(1+e)\cos\varphi\,d$ and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ one obtains $(1-d)/(2(1+\varepsilon/8))\le q\le(1-d)/2$. The linked bound needs only the upper inequality, which uses $e\ge0$. The lower inequality, for the reference solution of Lemma 2.5, also shows that a nonzero initial $l$ can transfer an absolute fraction of its size to $h$ during the first unit of time.

ref-l1-contraction.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangula: The estimate is a forward contraction in the sum norm, with operator norm exactly one: the first column of the propagator is $(1,0)$, and the sum of the nonnegative entries in its second column is $q+d\le1$. It does not give a corresponding bound for backward evolution, for which the multiplier of $l$ is inverted.

r2a1.amp.uniform-reference-propagator.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.normalize: The uniform Euclidean bound follows by changing norms in two dimensions, not by applying Gronwall to the raw system. In fact the sum-norm estimate gives $\|\Psi_0\|\le\sqrt2$. The paper uses the convenient constant two.

r2a1.amp.polynomial-error.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.integrated: In raw coordinates the growth rate would give an estimate of order $\exp(CT)$ for the propagator. In normalized coordinates the reference propagator has norm at most two, and a raw coefficient error of size $\theta$ has integrated conjugated size at most $4T^3\theta$ in the maximum operator norm. Thus the comparison requires polynomial smallness rather than exponential smallness of the coefficient error.

r2a1.amp.comparison-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: The actual amplitude solves a linear system whose coefficients differ from the reference coefficients by $CT^C\delta$. The ratio $\varepsilon$ and the strength $\sigma$ used to define its reference system and its clock are their launch values; neither is assumed constant for the physical parent. The bound (2.7) must hold up to the end of the prescribed comparison slab, not just up to the amplitude peak.
r2a1.amp.comparison-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: The prescribed amplitude is not normalized to have unit physical length: its length at launch is $\sqrt{1+S^{-2}}$. Rather, $(-1,1)$ are the initial scaled components, so the normalized reference coordinates start exactly at $(1,0)$. The small geometric length correction is accounted for when passing back to $|\mathbf a|$.

r2a1.amp.positive-second-amplitude.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: The second component is positive because $\alpha_2=a_{\rm ref}h$ and $h\ge1/2$. The physical amplitude therefore has a strictly positive projection on the preceding direction $E_2$, not necessarily on the other two frame vectors. This is what fixes the orientation in the formulas for the new unit amplitude and its cross product with the normal.
r2a1.amp.positive-second-amplitude.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: The change (2.15) is available before any positivity of $\alpha_2$ has been proved. The estimate for $(h,l)$ can therefore be obtained on the whole slab without stopping at a hypothetical first zero of $\alpha_2$. Only afterward do we use $h\ge1/2$ to divide by $\alpha_2$.

r2a1.amp.amplitude-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: The first estimate is a direction estimate in the scaled coordinates. In the physical frame the tilt of the amplitude along $E_1$ is only $q/S$, but the shear maps it into $E_2$ with coefficient $\sigma_p q/S$. A further factor $S^{-1}$ in a coupling pairing brings this to the scale $\sigma_p/S^2\asymp\nu$. Thus a good approximation of the physical length alone would not determine the successor's couplings.
r2a1.amp.amplitude-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: The two estimates concern different parts of the reconstruction. From (2.15), $q+Y=-l\cos\varphi/h$, which measures the error in the direction. From transversality, $z=-(\zeta_1q+\zeta_2)/\zeta_3$, so the length correction is $|\mathbf a|/\alpha_2=(1+S^{-2}(q^2+z^2))^{1/2}$. Both estimates follow once the normalized state is close to $(1,0)$.

r2a1.amp.log-amplitude-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: Exponentiating (2.18) gives a two-sided multiplicative comparison with the reference amplitude at every time. Applied at two times, this gives an error factor between $e^{-2\varepsilon}$ and $e^{2\varepsilon}$ in the ratio of their amplitudes, regardless of whether the reference amplitude is increasing or decreasing between them.
r2a1.amp.log-amplitude-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: Using transversality to write $z=\alpha_3/\alpha_2$, we have $\log(|\mathbf a|/a_{\rm ref})=\log h+\tfrac12\log(1+S^{-2}(q^2+z^2))$. The first error is due to the perturbed evolution, and the second to reconstruction in the physical frame. Both are small independently of the size of $a_{\rm ref}$.

r2a1.amp.onto-transverse-transport.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: In fact differentiating $k\cdot\mathbf b$ gives $-2k\cdot M\mathbf b+p_{\rm w}|k|^2=0$, with $p_{\rm w}$ evaluated for $\mathbf b$. The same identity holds when solving the linear equation backwards. Hence the flow restricts to an isomorphism between the two moving transverse planes; the estimate for its norm below concerns forward time only.
r2a1.amp.onto-transverse-transport.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: In §5 the same estimate is needed for every initial vector and for sources that need not lie in the growing direction. At a label $a$, the map $D_aX$ identifies the fixed plane $k_*^\perp$ with the moving plane $\kappa^\perp$. In these coordinates the origin estimate gives a propagator bounded by $\mathsf D^3\gamma(t)/\gamma(t')$. The generator at nearby labels is then compared with the one at zero by variation of constants; the amplitude weights cancel in the integral.

r2a1.amp.transport-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: The factor $S$ arises because an arbitrary transverse vector can initially be directed along $E_1$. In the launch frame, data $\mathbf b=E_1$ give $(h,l)=(0,-S)$. The reference triangular system transfers part of $l$ into $h$, and $h$ is the coefficient of the growing $E_2$ component after division by $a_{\rm ref}$. Thus the large factor in the conversion to normalized coordinates is relevant for general data, even though it is absent for the chosen launch mode. Lean uses the explicit upper constant $252\exp(1)$.
r2a1.amp.transport-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: For example, in physical time a transverse forcing $g$ with zero initial data gives $|\mathbf b(t)|\le CS\gamma(t)\int_{t_0}^t |g(t')|/\gamma(t')\,dt'$. There is no extra gain from integrating a forcing already proportional to $\gamma$. If a source is originally given in normalized time it must first be converted to physical time using $d\tau=r\,dt$. The hierarchy in §5 uses physical-time sources.

r2a1.amp.arbitrary-amplitude-coordinates.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.amplitude_dec: The transverse plane is two-dimensional, but it changes with $k$. Since $\zeta_3\ge1/2$, the graph formula $\beta_3=-(\zeta_1\beta_1+\zeta_2\beta_2)/\zeta_3$ is valid throughout the interval. Lean reconstructs the physical vector using the pair $(-\beta_1,\beta_2)$.

r2a1.amp.comparison-matrices.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.unscaledC: The first row of $R$ extracts $\beta_2$; the second extracts the component that vanishes when $\beta_1=-Y\beta_2$ and divides it by the cosine. In Lean the first raw coordinate is $U=-\beta_1$, which accounts for the sign difference in the matrix.

The inverse sends $(h,l)$ to $(-Yh-l\cos\varphi,h)$ before multiplying by $a_{\rm ref}$. All its entries are bounded since $|Y|\le1$ and $0<\cos\varphi\le1$. Only the forward change of coordinates incurs an inverse-cosine loss. Lean returns the sign-reversed first component.
r2a1.amp.comparison-matrices.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalize: The determinant of $R$ is $1/\cos\varphi$; its inverse has bounded entries. The poorly scaled direction is the excess of $-\beta_1$ over $Y\beta_2$, whose natural unit in (2.15) is $a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi$. Thus the factor in the condition number comes from measuring the direction on a finer scale, not from a small reference amplitude.

r2a1.amp.comparison-conjugation.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.hasDerivW: Put $P=R/a_{\rm ref}$ and let $N_0$ be the reference matrix. The coefficient in the new coordinates is $P'P^{-1}+PN_0P^{-1}+P\mathcal EP^{-1}$. The first two terms are exactly the matrix in (2.16); in the last term the scalar $a_{\rm ref}$ cancels. Hence even the perturbation is multiplied only by the condition number of $R$, which is polynomial in $T$.

r2a1.amp.inverse-cosine-bound.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.inv_sq_windo: On the prescribed slab, $1/\cos\varphi=\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4}\le\sqrt{1+T^4/4}\le T^2$. There is no need for the reference angle to stay away from $\pi/2$ by an absolute margin.

cmp-conjugated-error-bound.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.norm_norm: In the maximum operator norm, the row sums of $R$ and $R^{-1}$ give $\|R\|\le(1+|Y|)/\cos\varphi$ and $\|R^{-1}\|\le1+|Y|$ (using $\cos\varphi\le1$). The bound $|Y|\le1$ then gives $\|R\mathcal ER^{-1}\|\le4T^2\|\mathcal E\|$.

r2a1.amp.variation-of-constants.TorusEuler.linearODE_variation_of_consta: For an impulse at time $u$, its contribution at $\tau_2$ is obtained by applying the reference propagator $\Psi_0(\tau_2,u)$ to the error matrix acting on the actual state at $u$. Integrating these contributions gives the displayed identity. Because $\Psi_0$ is bounded for every ordered pair of times, the estimate involves the integral of the error coefficient rather than the integral of the large raw growth rate.

r2a1.amp.perturbed-propagator-budget.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.normalizedState: With $D=\int_0^T\|R\mathcal ER^{-1}\|$ and $P=\sup_{\tau_1\le\tau_2}\|\Psi(\tau_2,\tau_1)\|$, variation of constants gives $P\le2+2DP$. If $D\le1/4$, we obtain $P\le4$ by absorbing the last term. The linked Lean result instead uses the bound $2\exp(2D)$ with $D$ an integrated majorant; in either case the exponential involves the small conjugated error, not $T$ itself.

r2a1.amp.normalized-initial-state.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalize: For the chosen data the displacement from the reference state, $w=(h-1,l)$, starts at zero. Writing $\Delta=R\mathcal ER^{-1}$, its equation has the same perturbed matrix as the full normalized system, with inhomogeneous term $\Delta(1,0)^T$. There is no term proportional to the exponentially large raw reference solution.

r2a1.amp.normalized-error-budget.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.normalized_clos: The unperturbed term is exactly $(1,0)$. In the integral, the reference propagator has norm at most two and the perturbed state has norm at most four. Thus $\sup|(h-1,l)|$ is bounded by eight times the integrated conjugated error in the paper's norms. The corresponding Lean maximum-norm estimate uses $4D\exp(2D)$ for an integrated majorant $D$.

r2a1.amp.positive-ratio-identity.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.raw_ratio_: The identity actually gives $|\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y|=\cos\varphi\,|l/h|$. In particular the scaled direction error is bounded by $CT^C\delta\cos\varphi$, even when the reference first component passes through zero. This stronger form follows from (2.15); the linked Lean quotient estimate drops the cosine factor. The finer scale is natural for the small successor turning coupling.

The ratio follows by dividing $-\alpha_1-Y\alpha_2=a_{\rm ref}l\cos\varphi$ by $\alpha_2=a_{\rm ref}h$. The equality only needs a nonzero denominator; the bound on the quotient additionally needs the lower bound on $h$. The sign convention in the Lean raw coordinate is $-\alpha_1$.

r2a1.amp.physical-norm-identity.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.orthonorma: If $q=\alpha_1/\alpha_2$ and $z=\alpha_3/\alpha_2$, orthonormality gives $|\mathbf a|/\alpha_2=\sqrt{1+S^{-2}(q^2+z^2)}$ for $\alpha_2>0$. The geometric correction is quadratic in the small physical tilts. Neither tilt is being set to zero in the equations for the couplings.

r2a1.amp.geometric-norm-budget.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.norm_bounds_of_: Eliminating the third scaled amplitude component by transversality costs at most a factor of order $T^2$ in $z=\alpha_3/\alpha_2$. Its contribution to $|\mathbf a|^2/\alpha_2^2$ is consequently at most of order $T^4S^{-2}$. The formal bound on the relative length correction is $40T^4S^{-2}$; the inequality $S^{-2}\le\delta$ places it in the comparison budget.

r2a1.amp.physical-log-budget.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.log_growin: The physical norm is $a_{\rm ref}h\sqrt{1+S^{-2}(q^2+z^2)}$. Thus its logarithmic error is the sum of $\log h$, bounded by $2d$ for $|h-1|\le d\le1/2$, and a nonnegative geometric correction bounded by $S^{-2}(q^2+z^2)/2$. The latter is at most $20T^4S^{-2}$ in the formal estimate.

r2a1.amp.coordinate-recovery-cost.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.norm_movi: The vector $L_l$ lies in the $(E_1,E_3)$-plane. At the reference normal it equals $(-\cos\varphi E_1+\sin\varphi E_3)/S$ and has length $1/S$, even near $\varphi=\pi/2$. Lemma 2.4 gives $|L_l|\asymp S^{-1}$ for the actual normal. One recovers $h$ by the $E_2$ projection and then $l$ from the remaining vector $\mathbf b/a_{\rm ref}-hL_h$, costing only $CS$ rather than $CS/\cos\varphi$.

r2a1.amp.physical-propagator-conclusion.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.norm_movingAmpl: The linked estimate has the factor $126S\exp(2D)$ multiplying the ratio of reference amplitudes, where $D$ is the integrated conjugated-error majorant from the initial to the final time. The number $126=9\cdot2\cdot7$ comes from reconstruction, normalized propagation and recovery, respectively. Only recovery carries the factor $S$.
r2a1.amp.physical-propagator-conclusion.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: After peak normalization, $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t)|$ is positive and has maximum one.
