For a parent scale $\mathsf D\ge CS$, the inequality becomes $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$, the first condition in (5.5). The other condition, $\nu_+\ge\mathsf D^{-1}$, follows from Lemma 2.7 if $\mathsf D\ge2/(\nu\varepsilon)$. The same scale controls propagation and the pressure sign.

c8-pressure-coupling-identity.TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient: The pressure coefficient enforces the transverse constraint: differentiating $k\cdot\mathbf a$ gives $-2k\cdot M\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|k|^2$. Since $p_{\rm w}=2\nu_+|\mathbf a|/|k|$, it is the sign of the normalized coupling, not a lower bound on the small wave amplitude, that fixes the sign of the pressure. The Hessian contains two more powers of the wave number.
c8-pressure-coupling-identity.TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_cente: For the affine profile the central pressure Hessian is $-2\nu_+\sigma_+ E_{1,+}\otimes E_{1,+}$, where $\sigma_+=|\mathbf a||k|$. When $\nu_+>0$, as established below, its nonzero eigenvalue is negative. In the localized profile it is the lower bound $F_h'\ge-Ch$ that controls positive curvature of this leading tensor. The large negative central curvature is allowed by the upper quadratic-form bound used for the endpoint inverse in §4; the slow derivatives and correction pressures must still be estimated.

r2a1.amp.coupling-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_7: For the next comparison $M$ becomes the older gradient, and $\mathbf a\otimes k$ becomes the preceding shear. Since $(\mathbf a\otimes k)E_{2,+}=0$, that shear changes the strength without changing either of the pairings defining $\nu_+,\eta_+$. The completed periodic parent has an additional central gradient error $E_{c,+}$ from (T4). It belongs in the error term of the next comparison, not in the pair whose ratio is prescribed exactly.
r2a1.amp.coupling-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7: In the two-entry model at launch, $E_{1,+}=E_3$ and $E_{3,+}=-(E_1+S^{-1}E_2)/\sqrt{1+S^{-2}}$. The $E_1$ contribution to the second pairing is $-\nu$, but the preceding shear contributes $\sigma/S^2=2\nu$, so their sum is positive before division by $1+S^{-2}$. The launch direction from Lemma 2.6 is essential to this sign.

r2a1.amp.new-wave-frame.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame: The ordered cross product makes $E_{3,+}$ the direction of the new leading vorticity, because a gradient $\mathbf a\otimes k$ contributes $k\times\mathbf a=\sigma_+E_{3,+}$. It is also the direction chosen for the successor's normal at launch. The sign of the third coupling depends on this order; it cannot be changed independently of the frame.

r2a1.amp.coupling-definitions.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: Here $M$ is the gradient over which the current wave is evolved. Thus $\nu_+$ both determines its pressure coefficient and is the older-gradient entry to be frozen when the successor is launched. The corrected gradient at that launch also contains the new rank-one shear and an error. The shear annihilates $E_{2,+}$; the error is controlled separately by (2.6) in the next step.

The second entry is the projection of the same vector $ME_{2,+}$ onto the oriented third direction. At a successor launch this is the coupling that turns the successor's normal, while $\nu_+$ drives its growth. The ratio is formed only after checking that $\nu_+>0$.

lem-2-5-positive-coupling.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_7:
At launch in the two-entry model $
u_+=\eta/\sqrt{1+S^{-2}}$. Thus the uniform lower bound must initially be on the small scale $\eta=\varepsilon
u$. The late estimate is on the larger scale $
u$; it is used for the coupling inherited by the successor.
lem-2-5-positive-coupling.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7: For $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\le1$, $Y>0$ gives a reference lower bound $\varepsilon$ for $\nu_+/\nu$. In the complementary range the reference value is $1+O(\varepsilon^2)$, hence also at least $\varepsilon$ when (2.7) holds with sufficiently large $C_0$. The additive comparison error is smaller than this common margin.

lem-2-5-late-time.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_7: The condition $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\ge1$ is equivalent to $\tau\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, the time when the driving coefficient in (2.5) changes sign. It precedes the amplitude maximum. In particular the entire bracket used in Proposition 2.8 will be in the range of (2.19), even though the start of that bracket is chosen using the amplitude rather than the couplings.

r2a1.amp.late-coupling-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_7: The first coupling is inherited multiplicatively: at the $j$th crossing $|\nu_j(t_{j+1})/\nu_{j-1}(t_j)-1|\le\varepsilon_{j-1}$. Taking logarithms costs at most $2\varepsilon_{j-1}$, and the geometric decrease of the ratios makes their sum at most $4\varepsilon_1$. Starting from $2\pi$ therefore keeps the frozen first couplings between $\pi$ and $4\pi$. A fixed relative error at every step would not give such a uniform conclusion.
r2a1.amp.late-coupling-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7: The two errors are measured initially in units of $\nu$. The reference first entry is close to one in these units, but the reference third entry is of order $s=\cos\varphi$. The stronger $O(\varepsilon)$ relative comparison of the latter follows from an additive error at most $\varepsilon T^{-2}/8\le\varepsilon s/8$. Only after this comparison is the quotient formed; its denominator is close to one in the late range.

r2a1.amp.coupling-ratio-coordinates.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.normalized_co: At the reference normal, $z=-xq+\varepsilon\tau$ with $x=\tan\varphi$. Substituting $q=-Y$ from (2.13) yields $z_0=(1+e)\sin\varphi+\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau(1+\cos^2\varphi)$. This component can grow after the amplitude peaks. In comparing $z$ at a fixed reference normal, however, the direction error $q+Y=-\cos\varphi\,l/h$ is multiplied by $x$, giving only $\sin\varphi\,l/h$ in $z-z_0$.

r2a1.amp.coupling-amplitude-and-norm.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.amplitude_dec: The vector $\mathbf a/\alpha_2$ has coordinates $(q/S,1,z/S)$ in the preceding frame. It is not yet a unit vector: its length is $n$. Keeping this distinction produces the factors $n$ and $n^2$ in the two coupling formulas.
r2a1.amp.coupling-amplitude-and-norm.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.orthonorma: The factor $n^2-1$ is quadratic in the physical tilts and can be estimated in the perturbation budget. This does not permit dropping the tilts from the matrix product: an $E_1$ component of size $S^{-1}$ acted on by the preceding shear has size $\sigma/S$, and a further projection of size $S^{-1}$ brings it to the coupling scale $\sigma/S^2=2\nu$.

r2a1.amp.scaled-forcing.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.forcing: The term in $f_2$ coming from the preceding shear is $(\sigma_p/\sigma)q$, because $M$ acts on the first component $q/S$ with coefficient $\sigma_p$ and we divide by $r$. Thus $\sigma_p/(rS)$ remains close to one, even though $q/S$ is small. This surviving term accounts for the quadratic expression in the second coupling.

r2a1.amp.coupling-cross-product.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.cross3_frame_: In the cross-product pairing the first and third coordinates multiply $f_1/S$ and $f_3/S$. The middle coordinate already contains $S^{-1}$ and multiplies $f_2$. All terms therefore contribute on the same scale $r/S=2\nu$. In particular the middle-coordinate term cannot be dropped when passing to the reference values.

r2a1.amp.rational-couplings.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.normalized_co: Each of the two scalar products has an overall factor $r/S$ after the scaled components are substituted. Dividing by $\nu$ gives the common factor two. The denominator is $\sqrt m\,n$ for the normal pairing and $\sqrt m\,n^2$ for the cross-product pairing, since the latter contains the amplitude twice. Both formulas are homogeneous of degree zero in the positive amplitude scale.

r2a1.amp.strain-coupling-error.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.normalized_co: For unit vectors the contribution of $E_c$ to either normalized entry is at most $\|E_c\|/\nu$. In (2.6) this is part of $\delta$. Lean works with the gradient divided by $r$ and multiplies the bound by $2S=r/\nu$ to convert it back to the old-coupling scale.

cmp-reference-forcing.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.referenceForc: The reference values $(1/2,-Y,\varepsilon/2)$ are those of the scaled forcing $f$, not of the physical gradient product. For the second entry, the factor $\sigma_p/\sigma$ tends to one and $q$ tends to $-Y$. Keeping this term is necessary for the cancellation in the next display.

r2a1.amp.reference-coupling-values.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.couplingNumer: The middle component of the cross product contributes $(q-xz)q$, since the reference forcing has $f_2=q$. On using $z=-xq+\varepsilon\tau$, this becomes $(1+x^2)q^2-\varepsilon\tau xq$. The terms $2Y^2/\cos\varphi$ and $2\varepsilon\tau Y\sin\varphi$ in the second entry are precisely these two terms with $q=-Y$ and the common factor $2\cos\varphi$ restored.
r2a1.amp.reference-coupling-values.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceNu: The reference first entry is $\cos\varphi(x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon\tau Y)$, where $x=\tan\varphi$. At the reference peak $Y=0$ the shear term in this pairing vanishes, leaving $\sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi=1+O(\varepsilon^2)$. Away from the peak its contribution is retained in the estimate, since the physical first component of the amplitude need not vanish.
r2a1.amp.reference-coupling-values.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceEta: At fixed $\varepsilon$, the ansatz gives $Y\sim-1/\tau$ and $\cos\varphi\sim2/(\varepsilon\tau^2)$. The three contributions to the second reference entry then approach $\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon$ and $-2\varepsilon$. An estimate of their magnitudes would give an error of order $\varepsilon$ even at arbitrarily late times. We need their sum on the much smaller scale $\cos\varphi$.

r2a1.amp.coupling-cancellation.TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators: With $s=\cos\varphi$ and $u=\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi/2$, the second expression divided by $s$ can be written as $2(Y/s+u)^2-1+\varepsilon\tan\varphi-2u^2$. The first square is $2(1+e)^2$ by (2.13). The last two terms must be combined before estimating them; bounding them separately loses the small cosine scale.

r2a1.amp.coupling-cancellation-calculati.TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators: The large terms have a common factor determined by the clock: $2u^2=\varepsilon\tan\varphi\sin^2\varphi$. Their difference is consequently $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\cos^2\varphi=\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$. In the late range $\cos\varphi\le\varepsilon$ this remainder is at most $\varepsilon^2$ in the expression already divided by $\cos\varphi$.

r2a1.amp.reduced-reference-couplings.TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators: For the reference coefficients with an arbitrary tilt $q$, the second entry divided by $s=\cos\varphi$ is $2(q/s-u)^2-1+\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$, where $u=\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi/2$. In the distinguished solution $q=-Y$, so $q/s-u=-(1+e)$. In normalized coordinates $q/s-u=-(1+e+l/h)$; thus the cancellation is stable to an error $O(|l/h|+(l/h)^2)$ on this relative scale. The remaining finite-shear and coefficient errors require the separate comparison below.

r2a1.amp.late-reference-estimates.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_co: In the late range $x=\tan\varphi\ge1/\varepsilon$, the errors in the first entry have three sources: $1-\sin\varphi\le\varepsilon^2$, $\varepsilon\cos\varphi\le\varepsilon^2$, and $\varepsilon\tau\cos^2\varphi\le\sqrt2\varepsilon^2$. The second entry has an error of order $\varepsilon$ after division by the cosine. The Lean bounds are $7\varepsilon^2$ and $2\varepsilon$, respectively.

r2a1.amp.early-reference-positive.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceNu_: In the early range $\varepsilon\tau\le\sqrt2$, the sign $Y>0$ allows us to drop the third term of the first reference entry. For $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ and $\varepsilon\le1$, $\sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi\ge\varepsilon(\sin\varphi+\cos\varphi)\ge\varepsilon$. This proves a lower bound even at launch, where $\sin\varphi=0$.
r2a1.amp.early-reference-positive.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.referenceNu_low: The linked implication isolates the step using positivity: $Y>0$ makes $2\varepsilon\tau Y\cos\varphi\ge0$, and the remaining two terms are at least $\varepsilon$. It assumes the sign of $Y$; the turning-time bracket of Lemma 2.5 is what supplies it here.

r2a1.amp.coupling-perturbation.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.normalized_co: The rational formulas are estimated before forming the ratio of the two couplings. The denominators $\zeta_3$, $\sqrt m$ and $n$ are bounded below, and all scaled coordinates and coefficients have polynomial bounds in $T$. The linked estimate quantifies this continuity by $256T^8\kappa+2\delta$ in its scaled-gradient error variables. The potentially small turning entry itself is never a denominator in this calculation.

r2a1.amp.coupling-budget-absorption.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.coupling_err: The perturbation must be small compared with the reference turning entry even at $\tau=T$. As $\cos\varphi\ge T^{-2}$, a bound $CT^p\delta\le\varepsilon/(8T^2)$ gives an error at most $\varepsilon\cos\varphi/8$. Condition (2.7) permits this by taking $C_0$ larger than $p+2$ and $8C$. The two additional powers are needed when comparing the turning coupling relative to the cosine.

r2a1.amp.positive-actual-coupling.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7: The lower bound is relative to the central lengths: with $\mathsf D\ge2/(\nu\varepsilon)$ it gives $k\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|k||\mathbf a|$. In §5.4, relative changes of size $d$ in $k$ and $\mathbf a$ and an absolute change of size $d$ in $M$ change this contraction by at most $4\mathsf D d|k||\mathbf a|$ (central lengths on the right). Thus $d\le(8\mathsf D^2)^{-1}$ suffices for positivity on the envelope, without needing an exponentially small radius to match the launch amplitude.

r2a1.amp.actual-relative-couplings.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.actual_coupl:
Write $N=
u_+/
u$ and $H=\eta_+/
u$. The separate estimates in Lean give $|N-1|\le\varepsilon$ and $|H/s-1|\le3\varepsilon$, where $s=\cos\varphi$. Subtracting one from $(H/N)/s$ gives $(H/s-N)/N$, so the error is at most $4\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)\le1/2$ for $\varepsilon\le1/16$. The denominator here uses the late estimate $N\ge1-\varepsilon$, not merely its global lower bound.
r2a1.amp.actual-relative-couplings.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.actual_coupling:
The linked implication uses the early lower bound for the first entry and the separate late estimates of both entries. In the late range the division is by $
u_+/
u$ close to one, so the error for $\eta_+/
u_+$ remains relative to $\cos\varphi$. The global positive lower bound alone would lose a factor of order $\varepsilon^{-1}$ in that division.
r2a1.amp.actual-relative-couplings.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7: For the iteration the first inequality of (2.19) is needed with its actual error $\varepsilon$, since successive changes of $\nu$ must be summable. For locating a crossing the second inequality need only give comparability with the cosine. It is not necessary to control the derivative or monotonicity of the physical quotient.

r2a1.amp.crossing-definition.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: The crossing is an equality for the actual wave over $M$, not for its reference approximation. At physical time $t_0+\tau/r$, freeze $\sigma_+=|\mathbf a||k|$ and the two entries of $M$ in the new frame. The successor uses $k_{\rm new}=\lambda_{\rm new}E_{3,+}$ at that time and its clock has rate $r_+=\sqrt{2\sigma_+\nu_+}$. The corrected parent's additional central error is not included in the exact ratio.

lem-2-6-inherited-assumptions.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: Write $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$ in §7. The full comparison interval is $[t_j,S_j]$, of length $2\tau_j=2\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^3$. Its prescribed crossing bracket ends at normalized time $2L_jL_{j+1}$, since $\varepsilon= L_j^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_+=L_{j+1}^{-2}$. The lower bound $r_j\gtrsim\mu^{1/8}$ places this endpoint before $t_j+\tau_j$; the second half of the interval leaves room for the successor's construction.
lem-2-6-inherited-assumptions.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8: The two previous lemmas have different roles. Lemma 2.7 provides the ratio whose crossing is located; Lemma 2.6 compares the physical amplitude with its reference value both at the crossing and at the maximum. The normal estimate from Lemma 2.4 then converts amplitude into retained shear.

lem-2-6-successor-smallness.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: The target must be below the ratio at the reference maximum, not just smaller than the input ratio. The proof obtains the lower bound $\varepsilon/18$ at $\tau_m$ and uses $\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ for a strict margin. In the induction $\varepsilon_j/\varepsilon_{j-1}=(L_j/L_{j+1})^2=K_{j+2}^{-2}$, so the required separation is much weaker than that supplied by the frequency schedule.

lem-2-6-crossing-existence.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteReturn: The strict inequalities give an interior crossing. Its level set in the closed late bracket is nonempty and compact, so the physical construction can select its least element. `finiteReturn` describes existence and the strength estimates; the least-crossing choice is part of `GrowingCrossing`. Neither requires monotonicity of the actual ratio or excludes earlier crossings outside the bracket.
lem-2-6-crossing-existence.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: The peak time serves two purposes. Since $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon>\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, the late comparison (2.19) holds throughout the crossing bracket. Also the reference amplitude has attained its maximum by the left endpoint, so its subsequent decay can be estimated by integrating (2.14) from $\tau_m$. Neither argument identifies the maximizing time of the actual amplitude.
lem-2-6-crossing-existence.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8: At the left endpoint $\rho=\eta_+/\nu_+\ge\varepsilon/18>\varepsilon_+$; at the right endpoint $\rho\le3\varepsilon_+/4<\varepsilon_+$. Since the first coupling stays positive, the quotient is continuous. The use of the intermediate value theorem is important: the comparison in Lemma 2.7 does not control the derivative of $\rho$.

r2a1.amp.all-crossings-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: Fix the entire comparison slab first, so that $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ is known before choosing a crossing. Positive rescaling multiplies $A$ and $\sigma_+$ by the same constant, preserves both unit directions and leaves the two couplings unchanged. It therefore preserves every crossing and the ratio in (2.23), but changes the strength passed to the next wave.

lem-2-6-strength.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteReturn: At the crossing $|\mathbf a|/A\asymp\sqrt{\varepsilon_+/\varepsilon}$, with $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$, while $|k|/\lambda\asymp1/\varepsilon_+$. Compared with the values at the reference peak time, the former loses a factor of order $\sqrt{\varepsilon_+/\varepsilon}$ and the latter gains $\varepsilon/\varepsilon_+$. The retained gradient scale thus grows like $\sqrt{\varepsilon/\varepsilon_+}$ relative to its value at that time.
lem-2-6-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: The denominator is the launch frequency times the maximum physical amplitude on the prescribed slab; it is a gradient scale. The numbered Lean statement gives explicit lower and upper coefficients $e^{-1}/4$ and $18e^3$ for $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$. The older `finiteReturn` statement uses the weaker lower coefficient $(18e^3)^{-1}$; the induction needs only absolute comparability.
lem-2-6-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8: Substituting $A=\lambda_j^{-3/4}$, $\varepsilon=L_j^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_+=L_{j+1}^{-2}$ gives $\sigma_j\asymp\lambda_j^{1/4}L_jL_{j+1}$ at the crossing. The next growth rate is therefore $r_{j+1}\asymp\lambda_j^{1/8}\sqrt{L_jL_{j+1}}$. Both bounds on the strength are useful: in §7 the lower bound on the rate fits the next crossing into its short physical interval, while the upper bound controls the length of the normalized interval in (2.7).

lem-2-6-early-gain.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: The interval in (2.24) is the time during which the cutoff varies, of physical length $1/r$. The estimate must hold throughout that interval, not merely at launch. The crossing used for the successor is later than $2/\varepsilon>1$, so the full rank-one shear is present throughout the successor's active interval as long as it lies inside the present slab.
lem-2-6-early-gain.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8: For wave $j$, the choice $\varepsilon^{-1/2}=L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ gives $\gamma\le e^3\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$ while the cutoff varies. Since $|\widetilde\chi'|\le Cr_j$, this controls $\|\widetilde\chi'\gamma\|_\infty$, the activation factor in (5.48), by $Ce^3r_j\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. The expansion depth $P=6K_{j+1}$ gives the other factor $\lambda_j^{-2P/3}=\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. Both errors can then pay the frequency and parent losses in the physical residual estimate.

ret-proof-turning-bracket.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_turn: The entire interval $[\tau_m,T]$ lies in the range $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\ge1$ because $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon>\sqrt2/\varepsilon$. The estimates of (2.19) can thus be used not only at the two endpoints but at any crossing found in this late interval.

ret-proof-horizon-lower.TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.eight_d: With $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$, the target restriction gives $H\ge 2\sqrt{32}/\varepsilon>8/\varepsilon>\tau_m$. The hypothesis $T\ge H$ is needed because the actual comparison is only proved on the prescribed slab. A reference estimate at a later time would not suffice for a crossing of the actual ratio.

r2a1.amp.late-clock-coupling-bounds.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.inv_two_mul_: For $x=\tan\varphi\ge1$, the estimate $\sqrt{1+x^2}\le2x$ gives $\cos\varphi\ge1/(2x)$. Since $x(\tau_m)\le9/(2\varepsilon)$, (2.19) yields $\rho(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon/18$, where $\rho=\eta_+/\nu_+$. This strict margin above $\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ avoids any need to estimate the ratio at the actual amplitude maximum.
r2a1.amp.late-clock-coupling-bounds.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.s_le_inv_x: The identity $\cos\varphi=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}\le1/x$ for $x>0$ gives the opposite comparison. Unlike the lower bound it does not require $x\ge1$; it is used at the right endpoint, where the tangent is chosen explicitly.
r2a1.amp.late-clock-coupling-bounds.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.couplingRati: Writing $\rho=\eta_+/\nu_+$, the inequalities say $1/2\le\varepsilon\tau^2\rho\le3$ throughout $[\tau_m,T]$. The two bounds locate the ratio on the scale $1/(\varepsilon\tau^2)$ without requiring any control of its derivative. At a crossing this immediately bounds its normalized time by multiples of $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$.

r2a1.amp.crossing-upper-endpoint.TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.x_cross: At $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$ the reference tangent is $2/\varepsilon_+$, hence $\cos\varphi(H)\le\varepsilon_+/2$. The error factor in (2.19) allows the actual ratio to exceed the cosine by as much as $3/2$. The extra factor in the choice of $H$ leaves the strict bound $3\varepsilon_+/4$.

r2a1.amp.continuous-crossing.TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_: Continuity is applied to the actual quotient, which is well defined on the whole interval by the lower bound on $\nu_+$. The strict endpoint inequalities bracket the prescribed value, rather than bracketing a zero of a derivative. In particular the proof does not require the actual ratio to decrease throughout the bracket.
r2a1.amp.continuous-crossing.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.continuousOn_ph: Continuity of the normal and amplitude, their nonvanishing, and continuity of $M$ give continuity of the two unit-vector pairings. Dividing by $\nu_+$ is legitimate because Lemma 2.7 bounds it away from zero. The linked continuity result concerns the entries separately, before this division.

r2a1.amp.crossing-clock-scale.TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_: At any late crossing the tangent bounds give $1/\sqrt{2\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}\le\tau\le\sqrt{3/(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)}$. Thus the elapsed physical time is comparable to $1/(r\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+})$, no matter which crossing in the bracket is chosen. In the induction the upper bound fits the next activation into the present slab, and a lower bound on the elapsed time is also used in §8 for the vorticity integral.

r2a1.amp.exponential-amplitude-compariso.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.reference_: From (2.18), exponentiation of the bound on the logarithm gives $e^{-\varepsilon}a_{\rm ref}\le|\mathbf a|\le e^\varepsilon a_{\rm ref}$. The linked implication requires positive amplitudes; Lemma 2.6 ensures this and the bound at every time of the slab.

r2a1.amp.reference-maximum.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_l: Because $T\ge H>\tau_m$ and $Y$ has the two stated signs, the maximum of $a_{\rm ref}$ on $[0,T]$ is its global maximum. The argument compares this value with the actual maximum, without differentiating the finite-shear norm to find its maximizing time.

r2a1.amp.ratio-to-actual-maximum.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_ra: Put $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ and $A_m=a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$. The lower estimate in (2.18) at $\tau_m$ gives $A\ge e^{-\varepsilon}A_m$, and the upper estimate at every point of the slab gives $A\le e^\varepsilon A_m$. Dividing the pointwise amplitude estimates by these opposite bounds gives an error factor at most $e^{2\varepsilon}$ in the ratios to the maxima. No comparison of the maximizing times is needed.

r2a1.amp.reference-ratio-decomposition.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_r: The exponential in this ratio measures only the gain accumulated after the peak. Its logarithm is between zero and two even when the target ratio tends to zero. Consequently the amplitude loss is comparable to $\sqrt{\cos\varphi(\tau)/\cos\varphi(\tau_m)}\asymp\tau_m/\tau$, whereas the wave number grows quadratically in $\tau$. No exponentially small factor from launch is lost a second time.
r2a1.amp.reference-ratio-decomposition.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.referenceV_rati: The ratio identity itself holds for any ordered pair of nonnegative times. Taking the lower limit $\tau_m$ bounds the integral by an absolute constant on the entire remaining half-line. This is important: using a lower limit on the earlier scale $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ could still leave an integral of order $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$.

r2a1.amp.reference-tail-integral.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_ta: The remaining gain is uniformly bounded because the integral starts at the peak, where $\varepsilon\tau_m\ge2$. More precisely, for $\tau\ge\tau_m$, $\int_{\tau_m}^\tau\cos\varphi\,d\tau'\le (2/\varepsilon)(1/\tau_m-1/\tau)\le1$. The bound is uniform even when the target ratio is much smaller than the input ratio.

r2a1.amp.wave-number-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.wave_norm_compa: Equation (2.10) gives $|k|\asymp\lambda/\cos\varphi$; the linked late estimate writes the same scale as $\lambda\tan\varphi$. Notice also that the $E_3$ component of $k/\lambda$ remains bounded below by $1/2$. In §8, projecting the vorticity onto $k/|k|$ therefore retains a component comparable to $\cos\varphi$ of the preceding wave's vorticity, while eliminating the new wave's leading curl.

r2a1.amp.late-strength-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.amplitude_late_: After the peak, $|\mathbf a|/A\asymp\tau_m/\tau\asymp1/(\varepsilon\tau)$, where $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$. In the same interval $|k|/\lambda\asymp\varepsilon\tau^2$. Their product is therefore comparable to $\tau$ at each late time, not just at a crossing. Continuing beyond the peak trades a factor linear in time in velocity amplitude for a quadratic increase in wave number.
r2a1.amp.late-strength-comparison.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_la: In the late interval the strength and the turning ratio obey $\varepsilon(\eta_+/\nu_+)\,[|\mathbf a||k|/(\lambda A)]^2\asymp1$, with $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$. This follows by multiplying the squared strength bound, of order $1/(\varepsilon\cos\varphi)$, by the ratio bound in (2.19). Specifying the next ratio therefore fixes the scale of the available strength, independently of which late crossing is selected.

r2a1.amp.turning-clock-scale.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_bounds_of_: The tangent at the peak is of order $1/\varepsilon$, so the cosine there is of order $\varepsilon$. More precisely, the zero relation in (2.13) yields $\varepsilon\tau_m=2+O(\varepsilon)$ and hence $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)=(\varepsilon/2)(1+O(\varepsilon))$. It is this small peak cosine, not the launch value one, that normalizes the retained amplitude.

ret-proof-early-gain-conclusion.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_in: The early bound in (2.24) compares with the maximum over the full slab. Indeed $Y\le1$ gives $a_{\rm ref}\le e$ in the first unit of time, while the reference maximum is at least $\exp(\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1)$. The two uses of (2.18) add at most $2\varepsilon\le1$ to the logarithm of their ratio. This accounts for the constant three in the exponent.

r5-localization-transport-phase-envelope.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject: Along $x=X(t,a)$ both $g(a)$ and $F_h(k_*\cdot a)$ are constant. The material derivative of the leading wave is consequently $g(a)F_h(k_*\cdot a)\mathbf a_t(t,a)$, with no error from differentiating the transported cutoff or phase.
r5-localization-transport-phase-envelope.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.lea: The material equation treats $gF_0$ as a constant on each trajectory. But at a fixed time the neighboring amplitudes and the envelope can vary; the divergence of the leading field is $(F_0\mathbf d\cdot(g\mathbf a))^\natural$. Orthogonality to the normal cancels the phase derivative, not this slow divergence.

r5-localization-amplitude-path.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryTransverse_: For each fixed label replace the affine gradient by $M(t,a)$. Since the transported normal satisfies $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$, the same transverse amplitude equation applies on that trajectory. The cited ODE result permits a forcing as well; the seed uses the homogeneous case. Smooth dependence on $a$ is a separate ingredient of the localized construction.

r5-localization-divergence-correction.TorusEuler.divergence_completedWaveOn: Taking the divergence of the leading wave gives $(F_0\,\mathbf d\cdot(g\mathbf a))^\natural$, since the term $gF_0'\,\kappa\cdot\mathbf a$ vanishes. We preserve the desired oscillation by making it the fast curl of a potential; the slow curl then cancels the displayed defect exactly, with support still in the label envelope.

localized.flow.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn: Only the kinematics of the parent are used in transporting the wave. In particular, $\partial_tD_aX=MD_aX$ follows by differentiating $X_t=U\circ X$, even when $U$ has a momentum residual. This permits the same wave equations on every successive approximate solution.

r2.s34.lagrangian-coefficients.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn: The label $a$ always denotes the position at time zero, even for waves that are activated later. In particular $M(t,a)$ samples the parent at its current position, and differentiating at fixed $a$ means following the parent, not holding $x$ fixed.
r2.s34.lagrangian-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.meanGradient: The matrix $M$ acts on physical vectors, although its argument is a label. In particular $\partial_tD_aX=D_a(U\circ X)=M D_aX$. It is $M$, not $M D_aX$, that enters the local affine amplitude equation (3.2).
r2.s34.lagrangian-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformation: A displacement $v$ of a label becomes $D_aXv$ in physical space. For a scalar profile at fixed phase, the label gradient is therefore $(D_aX)^T$ times the physical gradient. Solving for the latter gives precisely the inverse transpose in $\mathbf d$.
r2.s34.lagrangian-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformationInv: Writing $G=D_xX^{-1}$ at $X(t,a)$, the identity $X^{-1}\circ X=\operatorname{Id}$ gives $G D_aX=\operatorname{Id}$. Thus the coefficient in $\mathbf d$ is $G^T$. The reverse derivative in the formal definition implements precisely the inverse in the paper.

localized.lattice-equivariance.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVect: The fields $X(t,a+n)$ and $X(t,a)+n$ satisfy the same trajectory equation and have the same initial value. Thus $D_aX$, its inverse, and $M$ are periodic in the labels. The carrier $k_*\cdot a$ need not be periodic; the envelope will be used to handle precisely this remaining obstruction.

localized.transported-covector.TorusEuler.labelWaveVector: Under the planar stretch $X(a_1,a_2)=(2a_1,a_2/2)$, the phase $a_1+a_2$ becomes $x_1/2+2x_2$. Its normal changes from $(1,1)$ to $(1/2,2)$. The inverse transpose gives this change and preserves the pairing with transported tangent vectors. `labelWaveVector` uses the same rule for the derivative of the flow at each label.
localized.transported-covector.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_transportedPhas: Test the rule on a shear, where transposing the forward map gives the wrong sign. If $X(a_1,a_2)=(a_1+s a_2,a_2)$, the phase $a_1$ becomes $x_1-s x_2$ and has gradient $(1,-s)$. The forward transpose would give $(1,s)$. The example distinguishes transporting a phase gradient from multiplying by the forward transpose. Differentiating $\theta(t,X(t,a))=\phi(a)$ with respect to $a$ gives $(D_aX)^T\nabla_x\theta=k_*$. This is the inverse-transpose law for the wave vector. The local chain rule assumes the differentiable reverse map; invertibility is furnished by the flow.

localized.profile-graph.TorusEuler.transportedProfile: At fixed $(t,a)$ the phase mean integrates over the whole circle, whereas $f^\natural$ samples just the phase $k_*\cdot a$. A profile with zero phase mean need not have zero spatial mean after evaluation. In the expansion the mean and oscillatory equations are separated before this evaluation.
localized.profile-graph.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject: The trajectory identity says that $f^\natural(t,X(t,a))$ is a function of $t$ at fixed $(a,s)=(a,k_*\cdot a)$. Thus the fast phase contributes no material time derivative even if $\kappa$ varies strongly in time. In the spatial chain rule it is the changing label that makes the phase derivative appear.
localized.profile-graph.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule: For a scalar profile the spatial derivative is $G^T\nabla_a f+\kappa\partial_s f$ with $G=(D_aX)^{-1}$. It is important to apply the fixed-phase derivative to the coefficients before evaluating at $s=\phi(a)$; differentiating the evaluated profile as if $s$ were fixed would miss the second term.

localized.graph-chain-rules.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule:
At fixed time, a physical displacement $v$ changes the label by $D_xX^{-1}v$ and the phase by $\kappa\cdot v$. Along $x=X(t,a)$ neither changes. In particular $
abla_x\cdot A_1^
atural=(\mathbf d\cdot A_1+\kappa\cdot\partial_sA_1)^
atural$, whereas the material derivative is simply $(A_{1,t})^
atural$.

r2.s34.phase-lattice.TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_modOne_line: The phase is measured in cycles: translation by the $j$th coordinate vector changes $s$ by $(k_*)_j$, which is invisible modulo one exactly when that component is an integer. A real normal can still be used because the wave vanishes where opposite label faces are identified.

localized.cell-extension.TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile: On a translated cell write the label as $a+n$ with $a$ in the original cell. Continue the profile as $f(t,a+n,s)=f(t,a,s-k_*\cdot n)$, so its value at $s=k_*\cdot(a+n)$ equals $f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$. The zero collar makes this continuation smooth and the evaluated field periodic; the real carrier itself need not be periodic.
localized.cell-extension.TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_localizedTr: In the labels, the field obtained after evaluation is periodic by construction. The inverse flow takes $x+n$ to $X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)+n$, so this periodicity is preserved in physical coordinates. This uses equivariance of the flow, not integrality of the wave vector.
localized.cell-extension.TorusEuler.contDiff_localizedTransported: Across a cell face the representative of the label may jump by a lattice vector, and hence the carrier may jump by a noninteger phase. The oscillatory field and all its derivatives vanish in a collar of the face. The repeated field is therefore smooth across the join before composition with $X(t,\cdot)^{-1}$.

localized.covector-equation.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.hasDerivWithinA: Differentiating $(D_aX)^T\kappa=k_*$ at fixed $a$ gives $(D_aX)^T(\kappa_t+M^T\kappa)=0$, using $\partial_tD_aX=MD_aX$. Invertibility gives $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. This is the affine normal equation on each particle path, regardless of how $M$ varies across paths.

localized.seed-equation.TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator_a: Write the correction to $-M\mathbf a$ as $p_{\rm w}\kappa$. Differentiating $\kappa\cdot\mathbf a$ gives $-2\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|\kappa|^2$. There are two equal terms because the normal itself moves by $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. Canceling them determines the pressure coefficient in (3.3).
localized.seed-equation.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryTransverse_: At a fixed label $M(t,a)$ and the nonzero $\kappa(t,a)$ are prescribed by the parent. Equation (3.2) is then linear in $\mathbf a$, with operator $-(I-2P_\kappa)M$. The linked existence result allows a transverse source, here set to zero. The seed is assembled across labels using the smooth dependence of this ODE on its coefficients and initial data.

localized.seed-transversality.TorusEuler.oscillatory_transverse_of_ini: Differentiation gives $\partial_t(\kappa\cdot\mathbf a)=-\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a-\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a+2\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=0$. A transverse forcing would also have zero pairing with $\kappa$. Thus the same calculation applies to the higher forced oscillations, not only to the seed.

localized.leading-profile-pressure.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.lea: The leading profile is obtained by multiplying the amplitude ODE by $gF_0$. This is an exact cancellation at fixed $(a,s)$. Spatial localization thus introduces no additional material time derivative, even though derivatives of $g$ and of the seed in neighboring labels remain in the spatial terms.

The phase derivative of $\mathsf p[A_1]$ is $-p_{\rm w}gF_0$, so its fast gradient cancels the part of the amplitude acceleration along $\kappa$. Its slow gradient is $-P_0\mathbf d(p_{\rm w}g)$; it need not be zero when the amplitude or envelope varies between particles. This term enters the next level in (5.25).

localized.leading-on-trajectory.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject: On a trajectory, $g(a)F_0(k_*\cdot a)$ is fixed while $\mathbf a(t,a)$ evolves. A particle at a zero of $F_0$ has zero leading velocity along its parent path even though the velocity gradient there may be large. The formula is for the leading profile, before curl completion.

localized.homogeneous-momentum.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.pap: Put $b=g\mathbf a$, so $A_1=bF_0$. Before completion and switching, the two uncanceled terms are $F_0^2(b\cdot\mathbf d)b$ and $-P_0\mathbf d(p_{\rm w}g)$: the fast self-advection vanishes by $b\cdot\kappa=0$. Although $A_1$ is mean free, $F_0^2$ is not. The quadratic terms therefore also enter the mean equation at level two.

localized.curl-graph.TorusEuler.curl_transportedProfile: The potential is chosen so that its fast curl is the prescribed transverse velocity. The other curl, $\mathbf d\times Q$, is then a determined correction and may have a normal component. The sum is a curl in physical space, so cancellation of its divergence is exact rather than an estimate of a small divergence.

localized.completion-definition.TorusEuler.wavePotential: For $z\perp\kappa$, $\kappa\times(\kappa\times z)=-|\kappa|^2z$. Hence the inverse of the fast cross product on the transverse plane is $z\mapsto-\kappa\times z/|\kappa|^2$. One can take its periodic phase primitive because $V$ has zero mean, and the inverse cross product gains one power of $|\kappa|^{-1}$.
localized.completion-definition.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: The slow curl $C[V]$ is obtained by differentiating $Q[V]$ at fixed $s$. In particular it is not the curl of the graph-evaluated potential: that curl also contains the prescribed velocity $V$. Since $Q[V]$ carries $|\kappa|^{-1}$, the slow correction in (5.31) costs one label derivative but no factor $|\kappa|/h$.

localized.normalized-primitive.TorusEuler.phasePrimitive: For a periodic mean-zero $f$, set $J(s)=\int_0^s f(r)\,dr$. The primitive used here is $J-\int_0^1J(r)\,dr$. Subtracting a constant in phase preserves the derivative but removes a phase-independent component from the potential and hence from its slow curl.
localized.normalized-primitive.TorusEuler.periodic_phasePrimitive: The necessary condition for a periodic primitive is that its input have zero integral over a period. Here $J(s+1)-J(s)=\int_0^1f=0$. Zero mean of the primitive itself is a different condition: it selects one of the periodic primitives.

localized.fast-curl.TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl: In differentiating $Q[V]$ in phase, $\kappa$ is held fixed. Hence $\kappa\times\partial_s Q=-\kappa\times(\kappa\times V)/|\kappa|^2=V$ by transversality. If $V$ had a normal component, the same formula would return only its projection onto $\kappa^\perp$.

localized.completed-velocity-longitudina.TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential: The fast curl is exactly $V$, so the graph evaluation of $V+C[V]$ equals $\nabla_x\times Q[V]^\natural$. The identity is exact, irrespective of the size of $\mathbf d\cdot V$. One may therefore estimate the correction in size while preserving divergence cancellation without a residual.
localized.completed-velocity-longitudina.TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o: For the leading wave, (3.6) reads $\kappa\cdot C[A_1]=-P_0(s)\,\mathbf d\cdot(g\mathbf a)$. Thus the phase velocity introduced by the completion can be computed from the slow divergence of the envelope and seed. In particular the mean of a fast interaction satisfies $\langle(\kappa\cdot C[V])\partial_s Y\rangle_s=\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$ by integration by parts; this is used at (5.42).
localized.completed-velocity-longitudina.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: Apply the full slow-fast divergence to the completed field. The slow curl has zero slow divergence, and the transverse $V$ has zero fast divergence. Thus the remaining two terms give $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$. This is a derivative identity; obtaining (3.6) without an additive function of the labels uses the zero phase mean of $C[V]$.

localized.divergence-of-curls.TorusEuler.divergence_curl: The linked divergence-of-curl theorem is the ordinary spatial identity, proved by symmetry of mixed second derivatives. To use it before phase evaluation, observe that $[\widetilde{\mathbf d}_i,\widetilde{\mathbf d}_j]=(\mathbf d_i\kappa_j-\mathbf d_j\kappa_i)\partial_s=0$, since $\kappa_j=\mathbf d_j\phi$ and the $\mathbf d_i$ commute. The same mixed-derivative cancellation then applies at every phase.
localized.divergence-of-curls.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: The variable coefficients in $\mathbf d$ do not introduce a commutator: $\mathbf d_i$ is $\partial_{x_i}$ conjugated by $X$ at fixed $s$. Consequently the mixed second derivatives in $\mathbf d\cdot(\mathbf d\times Q)$ cancel, even though $D_aX$ varies with $a$.

localized.longitudinal-derivative.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: The derivative on $Y$ in a product $(\kappa\cdot C[V])\partial_sY$ can be moved to $\kappa\cdot C[V]$ inside a phase average. Its derivative is $-\mathbf d\cdot V$, so the mean is $\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$. The fast interaction need not be small pointwise for this reduction to hold; it is the averaged interaction that loses the fast derivative in (5.42).

localized.completion-zero-means.TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o: The right side of $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$ has zero mean, because $\mathbf d$ commutes with the phase average and $\langle V\rangle_s=0$. The normalized potential also gives $\langle C[V]\rangle_s=0$. These two mean identities justify taking the zero-mean primitive, with no free phase-independent term.
localized.completion-zero-means.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: The potential is normalized by its mean, not by its value at $s=0$. For instance the primitive of an odd periodic oscillation is even and need not vanish at zero. Choosing its mean to be zero avoids introducing an unintended phase-independent curl.

The slow curl commutes with phase averaging because the coefficients of $\mathbf d$ are independent of $s$. Since $\langle Q[V]\rangle_s=0$, completing $V$ does not change its phase mean. This allows the mean equation to be solved separately from the curl completion of the oscillations.

localized.leading-potential.TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadin: In this formula $\mathbf a$ and $\kappa$ are orthogonal, so $|Q[A_1]|=|gP_0|\,|\mathbf a|/|\kappa|$. Unlike the leading velocity, the potential uses $P_0$ and need not vanish at $s=0$. Its slow curl is therefore not required to have zero central gradient, a contribution that is estimated separately in (5.50).

localized.completion-derivative-cost.TorusEuler.norm_wavePotential_le: For a mean-free profile with $\sup_s|V|\le B$ at a fixed label, the primitive before mean subtraction has norm at most $B$ on a period of length one. Its mean has norm at most $B$ as well. Hence $\sup_s|Q[V]|\le2B/|\kappa|$. The frequency gain comes from the inverse cross product, not from assuming that the phase primitive is an integral over a period of length $h$.
localized.completion-derivative-cost.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: In differentiating $Q[V]$, each $\mathbf d_j$ acts on $\partial_s^{-1}V$ or on the coefficient $\kappa/|\kappa|^2$. The latter varies on the parent scale: $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$. This is why the coefficient estimates in (5.8) and a single additional label derivative of $V$ suffice for the inverse-frequency estimate (5.31).

localized.completion-support.TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile: The relevant support is the set of labels where at least one phase of $V$ is nonzero. If $V(t,a,\cdot)=0$, the entire phase primitive is zero at that label. It would not suffice to know $V(t,a,k_*\cdot a)=0$, since the primitive uses other phases at the same label.
localized.completion-support.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: Outside the closed label support the potential is zero in a neighborhood at every phase, so its slow curl is also zero there. The same argument applies on the open interval before activation. This support statement concerns the oscillation and its completion; it does not localize the phase-independent correction found by the endpoint inverse.

localized.even-seed.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.even_materialGr: Oddness of $U$ and uniqueness give $X(t,-a)=-X(t,a)$ and $X(t,0)=0$. Differentiating the two odd maps $X$ and $U$ gives even matrices $D_aX$ and $D_xU\circ X$. Hence $M$ and $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$ are even; the seed ODE has the same coefficients at opposite labels.
localized.even-seed.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.eve: At activation, the center amplitude is projected onto $\kappa(t_0,a)^\perp$ at each label. Since the normal is even, the projection is the same at $a$ and $-a$. The two seed equations then have the same coefficients and initial value, so their solutions are equal by uniqueness.

localized.odd-completed-wave.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: Use joint reflection $(a,s)\mapsto(-a,-s)$. For an odd $V$ under this reflection the zero-mean phase primitive is even: reflection reverses the phase derivative, and the mean fixes the integration constant. With $\kappa$ even, $Q[V]$ is even; differentiation at fixed phase by the even inverse deformation makes $\mathbf d\times Q[V]$ odd.
localized.odd-completed-wave.TorusEuler.odd_transportedProfile: The inverse flow is odd, so physical reflection sends $(a,k_*\cdot a)$ to $(-a,-k_*\cdot a)$. Joint oddness of the completed profile becomes oddness of its evaluation. The symmetric cell extension preserves this relation across the torus.

localized.time-cutoff.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff: The multiplier $\widetilde\chi$ commutes with both the slow curl and phase integration, and with all spatial derivatives after evaluation. Its derivative enters the residual as $\widetilde\chi'(A_1+C[A_1])$. It is this whole completed wave, rather than $A_1$ alone, whose size during activation is needed.
localized.time-cutoff.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first: At the first step the seed is defined from time zero, so there is no earlier interval to fill by zero. The formal first cutoff takes $t_0=0$ and is identically one, eliminating $R_{\widetilde\chi}$.

localized.switched-profiles.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.gen: In the initial cell the switched transverse profile is $V_1=\widetilde\chi g\mathbf a F_h(s)$. On a cell translated by $n$, its independent phase is shifted by $-k_*\cdot n$. The extension preserves the value on the phase graph, and the smooth multiplier preserves the zero collar at the cell faces.

The phase pressure must be switched by the same factor as the leading velocity. In (3.4), $V_{1,t}+MV_1+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p_1=\widetilde\chi\,0+\widetilde\chi' A_1$. When the slow curl is included the extra switching term is $\widetilde\chi'(A_1+C[A_1])$, as in (3.8).
localized.switched-profiles.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Physi: Since $\widetilde\chi$ depends only on $t$, $Q[\widetilde\chi A_1]=\widetilde\chi Q[A_1]$ and $C[\widetilde\chi A_1]=\widetilde\chi C[A_1]$. The whole completed wave is thus switched by a scalar, without introducing a spatial cutoff derivative in addition to those already included in $C[A_1]$.

localized.flat-zero-extension.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.con: For an interior activation time, all derivatives of a smooth function identically zero for $t<t_0$ vanish at $t_0$. Every derivative of the product with the seed contains such a factor, including the undifferentiated cutoff. The extension of the switched profile by zero is therefore smooth even though the seed is defined only on the active slab.
localized.flat-zero-extension.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_flatActivation_smu: This auxiliary flat-multiplier lemma gives smooth zero extension for a smooth seed on the future side of $t_0$ and a globally smooth flat cutoff. The slab version is used directly for (3.7); in both cases flatness removes any boundary term from differentiating the extension.

localized.switch-residual.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Physi: At the switching times the relevant estimate is on $|\widetilde\chi'|\gamma$, not $|\widetilde\chi'|$ alone. Section 6 switches while $\gamma\le\exp(3-\varepsilon^{-1/2})$, with $|\widetilde\chi'|\le Cr$. Thus a cutoff whose time derivative is large can still give a small momentum residual, since it acts before the seed has been amplified.

localized.central-localized-gradient.TorusEuler.hasFDerivAt_inductionPrimaryW: At the central particle the product rule has two terms: one differentiates $g\mathbf a$ and is multiplied by $F_h(0)=0$; the other differentiates the phase and is multiplied by $g(0)F_h'(0)=1$. The exact central derivative is therefore $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$ for the leading oscillation alone. After switching it acquires the scalar $\widetilde\chi(t)$.

localized.affine-pressure-control.TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian: The affine coefficient and normal do not depend on space, so differentiating $-p_{\rm w}P_h(k\cdot x)$ twice leaves just $-p_{\rm w}F_h'(k\cdot x)k\otimes k$. The localized version also differentiates the coefficient and transported normal, as displayed in (5.51).
localized.affine-pressure-control.TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u: When $p_{\rm w}\ge0$, the sole potentially nonzero eigenvalue of the leading Hessian is $-p_{\rm w}|k|^2F_h'$. Its positive part is bounded by $(h/2)p_{\rm w}|k|^2$, while at phase zero its negative value is $-p_{\rm w}|k|^2$. The estimate does not require the latter to be small.

localized.lemma31.existential-profile.TorusEuler.paperLemma31_waveProfile: Both the velocity and the pressure profiles are selected by one bump. The first integration of its normalized slope gives the odd periodic velocity factor; the second gives the even zero-mean pressure factor. The constants in the lemma depend on the fixed bump and on the derivative order, not on the width subsequently used for a wave.
localized.lemma31.existential-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_3_1: The numbered Lean statement chooses explicit functions `waveProfile` and `wavePressurePrimitive`; it asserts that this pair satisfies `ProfileFamily`. Thus the existential choice in the paper is resolved once, before the frequency or derivative order of a particular wave is chosen.
localized.lemma31.existential-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_3_1: The numbered theorem establishes the chosen smooth pair $F_h,P_h$ and their bounds at every admissible width. In particular there is no change of profile when a higher derivative order is requested; only its constant $C_j$ changes.
localized.lemma31.existential-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.ProfileFamily: `ProfileFamily` is the collection of hypotheses and uniform estimates imposed on a supplied pair $(F_h,P_h)$. It distinguishes the periodic primitive relation from the estimates on the slope and height. The numbered lemma establishes these properties for the explicit bump family, rather than assuming them of an arbitrary profile.

localized.lemma31.uniform-estimates.TorusEuler.paperLemma31_waveProfile: In the norm used in Section 5, a phase derivative carries a factor $h$. Lemma 3.1 consequently gives $\|(h\partial_s)^jF_h\|_\infty\lesssim_j h$ also for $j=0,1$. After evaluation the corresponding derivative is $\kappa\partial_s=(\kappa/h)(h\partial_s)$. These are different estimates: the first is uniform in the profile width and the second contains the physical frequency.
localized.lemma31.uniform-estimates.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_3_1: The constants may depend on the derivative order but not on $h$. This lets one take arbitrarily narrow profiles while controlling any prescribed finite number of scaled phase derivatives. It does not assert that a single constant controls all orders simultaneously.
localized.lemma31.uniform-estimates.TorusEuler.Paper.ProfileFamily: The uniformity in this specification is over the width and phase, not over the derivative order: $C_j$ may depend on $j$. This suffices because the construction controls each finite derivative order separately while using the same $F_h$ at a given step.
localized.lemma31.uniform-estimates.TorusEuler.lemma31_waveProfile: For this fixed family, the amplitude and all fixed-order scaled derivatives are $O(h)$, but the unscaled derivative at zero equals one. Both features follow from the same theorem. There is no need to select a different profile when a higher derivative estimate is required.

localized.lemma31.bump-choice.TorusEuler.waveBump: Lean uses $\psi(s)=\operatorname{smoothTransition}(1-64s^2)$. It is even, equals one at zero, and is zero for $|s|\ge1/8$. The rescaled bump therefore occupies an interval of length $h/4$ in a period, so $c_h\le h/4$.

localized.lemma31.slope-formula.TorusEuler.waveSlope: The mean subtraction enforces $\int_0^1F_h'=0$; the denominator then enforces $F_h'(0)=1$. Outside the bump the slope is $-c_h/(1-c_h)$. Its magnitude is proportional to the mass of the narrow bump, not to its height, which is what permits the small adverse pressure curvature.
localized.lemma31.slope-formula.TorusEuler.waveProfile: Integrating the normalized slope from zero determines $F_h(0)=0$. Because the slope has zero period integral, this primitive closes up after one period. Its derivative is precisely the normalized slope, not the original bump.
localized.lemma31.slope-formula.TorusEuler.hasDerivAt_waveProfile: The integrated periodic slope is continuous (indeed smooth) across the joins. The fundamental theorem of calculus therefore identifies the derivative of $F_h$ at every real phase with that slope. On the centered cell it has the displayed bump formula.

localized.lemma31.parity-periodicity-pri.TorusEuler.odd_waveProfile: Integrating the even slope from zero gives an odd $F_h$. Periodicity then also gives $F_h(1/2)=0$ and $\int_0^1 F_h=0$. The second identity is what permits a periodic pressure primitive, whereas $F_h(0)=0$ eliminates the slow contribution to the central velocity gradient.
localized.lemma31.parity-periodicity-pri.TorusEuler.periodic_waveProfile: For any starting phase $s$, $F_h(s+1)-F_h(s)=\int_s^{s+1}F_h'=0$. This uses zero mean of the slope; zero mean of $F_h$ itself is a second property, obtained from oddness.
localized.lemma31.parity-periodicity-pri.TorusEuler.wavePressurePrimitive: The primitive of an odd periodic $F_h$ with zero mean is even when normalized by its mean. In particular $P_h'(0)=0$, but $P_h(0)$ need not be zero. At the origin this distinction eliminates the mixed terms in (5.51), without eliminating the slow coefficient Hessian multiplied by $P_h(0)$.
localized.lemma31.parity-periodicity-pri.TorusEuler.periodic_wavePressurePrimitiv: There are two integrations in the construction. The mean-free slope gives periodic $F_h$; the odd periodic $F_h$ has zero mean, giving periodic $P_h$. Subtracting a constant from the latter then sets its mean to zero.
localized.lemma31.parity-periodicity-pri.TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePressurePrimiti: The mean-zero condition fixes a phase-dependent decomposition. Replacing $P_h$ by $P_h+C$ changes the localized pressure by $-C(p_{\rm w}g)^\natural$, whose slow spatial gradient need not vanish. This differs from subtracting a spatial constant from the total Eulerian pressure, which leaves the momentum equation unchanged.

localized.lemma31.amplitude-integration.TorusEuler.hasDerivAt_waveProfile_zero: Only the value of the bump at zero is used for the normalization: $F_h'(0)=(1-c_h)/(1-c_h)=1$. This ratio is exact for all $0<h\le1$, so the central gradient does not carry an $O(h)$ normalization error.
localized.lemma31.amplitude-integration.TorusEuler.deriv_waveProfile_bounds: The minimum of the normalized slope is $-c_h/(1-c_h)$, and the maximum is one. Since $c_h\le h/4\le1/4$, the lower bound $-2c_h\ge-h/2$ holds for this bump. The paper keeps the more general constant $C$ in the profile lemma.
localized.lemma31.amplitude-integration.TorusEuler.norm_waveProfile_le: Integrate the lower bound $F_h'\ge-2c_h$ along the two intervals $[0,s]$ and $[s,1]$. Since $F_h(0)=F_h(1)=0$, this gives $-2c_hs\le F_h(s)\le2c_h(1-s)$. Thus $\|F_h\|_\infty\le2c_h\le h/2$ for the chosen bump; the narrow positive slope does not force a large height.

localized.lemma31.higher-derivatives.TorusEuler.exists_iteratedDeriv_waveProf: For $j\ge2$ the derivative $\partial_s^jF_h$ is $h^{1-j}\psi^{(j-1)}(s/h)/(1-c_h)$ on the centered cell. The constant subtracted from the bump has disappeared. The same formula extends through the periodic joins because these derivatives vanish near the faces, giving the uniform estimate with constants of the fixed bump.
localized.lemma31.higher-derivatives.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_3_1: After differentiating the slope once the constant background has disappeared. The remaining derivatives are those of the single fixed bump at $s/h$, with one factor $h^{-1}$ for each differentiation. The denominator is uniformly bounded below and the bump is identically zero near the period joins.
localized.lemma31.higher-derivatives.TorusEuler.lemma31_waveProfile: In terms of the scaled phase variable, the estimate is $h^j\|\partial_s^jF_h\|_\infty\le C_jh$. The higher profile norms can thus have the same small size as the velocity, even though physical derivatives through the phase will later cost $|\kappa|/h$.

sec4.initial-first-variation.TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation: Differentiate $X_\delta(0,a)=a$ in $\delta$ to obtain the zero initial trace. In contrast, differentiating $\partial_t X_\delta(0,a)=u(0,a)+\delta b(0,a)$ gives the initial slope $\xi_t(0,a)=b(0,a)$. These two identities explain which initial datum is fixed and which is to be selected.

sec4.select-initial.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: This is a linear boundary-value problem even when the parent is not an exact Euler flow. The initial position determines $\xi(0)=0$, while (1.5) gives $\xi_t(0)=b(0)$. We solve for the latter so that $\xi(T)=0$. The uniqueness statement compares solutions with the same force and parent on the same entire slab.

sec4.actual-parent.TorusEuler.Paper.MeanParentFlow: The parent in the iteration is the truncated velocity $U$, with defect $R_U$ in its Euler equation. Linearization over this field still gives $B_t+MB+\mathbf d q=\bar f$; the force at the first mean level includes $-R_U\circ X$. The effective coefficient in the displacement problem is $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$, so the inverse can be constructed before the parent's residual has been removed.

sec4.volume-preserving.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.det_labelDeriva: The deformation of a small volume element is governed by $F_t=MF$, $F=D_aX$. Jacobi's determinant formula gives $(\det F)_t=\operatorname{tr}M\det F=0$ since $u$ is incompressible; $F(0)=I$ fixes the determinant at one. This gives both the change of measure and the divergence transformation used in the inverse.

sec4.coefficients.TorusEuler.endpointHessian: Differentiating $F_t=MF$ gives $F_{tt}=(M_t+M^2)F$, with $F=D_aX$. Hence $F_{tt}+H^\# F=0$. In particular each column of $F$ satisfies the homogeneous vector ODE at a fixed label, though it does not have the two zero endpoint traces of an admissible displacement. The coefficient $H^\#$ depends only on the parent flow, and (4.3) expresses it in terms of the pressure and residual.
sec4.coefficients.TorusEuler.kineticForm: Since $Kv\cdot v=|D_aXv|^2=|B|^2$, $K$ measures the physical velocity correction in label coordinates. The energy in (1.8) instead involves $|\xi_t|^2=|M\xi+B|^2$. The cross term in this last square is accounted for by the vorticity form and the boundary derivative in (4.7).
sec4.coefficients.TorusEuler.vorticityForm: Although $\Omega$ is skew, $\Omega z_t\cdot z$ need not vanish. For example, with a constant planar coefficient $\Omega e_1=\omega e_2$, $\Omega e_2=-\omega e_1$, take $z=r(\cos\theta-1,\sin\theta)$ with $\theta$ increasing from $0$ to $2\pi$. The integrated skew term is $-2\pi\omega r^2$ and changes sign if the path is reversed. Thus positivity of $K$ alone is insufficient for the path estimate.
sec4.coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.meanGradient: The matrix $M$ differentiates $u$ in physical space and then evaluates at the particle. In the convention $M_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i(t,X)$, the chain rule gives $D_a(u\circ X)=MF$. Hence $M$ itself is not the label derivative of $u\circ X$; the distinction is used in differentiating the deformation equation.
sec4.coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.meanGradientRate: The rate $M_t$ is the material derivative of the physical gradient. Differentiating the material acceleration adds another term: $\nabla[(\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla)u]\circ X=M_t+M^2$. Thus $H^\#$ is the negative gradient of material acceleration evaluated at the particle. Even when $u_t=0$, both terms in this formula can occur.
sec4.coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.meanHsharp: The identity $H^\#=-F_{tt}F^{-1}$ makes independence of the chosen $p$ in (4.3) transparent. If $p$ is changed by a smooth function $r$, then $R$ changes by $\nabla r$, leaving $D^2p-\nabla R$ unchanged. For the later truncated parent, the choice of pressure is made to render its residual divergence free.
sec4.coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.meanKinetic: The bound on $F^{-1}$ controls the *smallest* singular value of $F$: $|Fw|\ge D_-^{-1}|w|$. It follows that $w\cdot Kw\ge D_-^{-2}|w|^2$. Volume preservation gives $\det K=1$, but by itself supplies no such lower eigenvalue bound; the latter is needed when solving the spatial equation at fixed time.
sec4.coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.meanVorticity: Using $F_t=MF$ we have $\Omega=F_t^TF-F^TF_t$ and $\Omega_t=F^T(H^\#-(H^\#)^T)F$. For an exact Euler parent, the Hessian is symmetric, so $\Omega$ is constant in time (the pulled-back vorticity form). For an approximate parent, (4.3) gives $H^\#-(H^\#)^T=((\nabla R)^T-\nabla R)\circ X$. The inverse allows the resulting time dependence of $\Omega$.

sec4.inverse-bound.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent: The coefficient parent in Lean includes fields $F,G$ with $GF=FG=I$ and $\|G\|\le D_-$. This separates invertibility of the deformation from coercivity of the displacement equation. For an actual flow the two identities follow from its inverse map; the coefficient-level energy proof uses these identities without having to reconstruct the flow itself.
sec4.inverse-bound.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse: A bound on $F^{-1}$ gives the ellipticity constant $D_-^{-2}$ for $K$. For the full path form there is an additional loss, because $v=F^{-1}(\xi_t-M\xi)$ rather than $F^{-1}\xi_t$. Equations (4.6) and (4.8) therefore give $[2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2]^{-1}$ as the coercivity constant on $v$. These are the two distinct constants passed to Theorem A.1.
sec4.inverse-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformationInv: Differentiate $X(t,\cdot)^{-1}\circ X(t,\cdot)=\operatorname{Id}$ at $a$. This gives $F^{-1}(t,a)=D_xX(t,\cdot)^{-1}|_{x=X(t,a)}$. The inverse derivative must be evaluated at the current position rather than the original label; this is the expression used by `meanDeformationInv`.
sec4.inverse-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: For the stationary shear of §1.1, or any constant multiple of it, $M$ is constant along each trajectory and $M^2=0$. Thus $H^\#=0$, whereas $F=I+tM$ and $F^{-1}=I-tM$ can be arbitrarily large as the shear is increased. The curvature hypothesis cannot replace the inverse-deformation bound, even for exact Euler parents.

sec4.flow-identities.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.labelDerivative: The flow equation implies $\partial_tF(t,a)=M(t,a)F(t,a)$ and $F(0,a)=I$. In particular $F(t,a)F(s,a)^{-1}$ transports a homogeneous displacement from $s$ to $t$. This is the same fundamental matrix that weights the forcing $b\circ X$ in the solution of (1.5).
sec4.flow-identities.TorusEuler.derivWithin_kineticForm_sub_v: From $F_t=MF$ we get $K_t=F_t^TF+F^TF_t$ and $\Omega=F_t^TF-F^TF_t$. Hence $K_t-\Omega=2F^TF_t$, and $Kv_t+2F^TF_tv=(Kv)_t-\Omega v$. This identity permits integration of the momentum equation with no time derivative on the source or on $\Omega$.

sec4.residual.TorusEuler.momentumResidual:
With the pressure convention $\Delta p_U=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla U)^2)$ in §5.1, $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$ since $\operatorname{div}((U\cdot
abla)U)=\operatorname{tr}((
abla U)^2)$. Thus $R_U$ is the actual defect of the projected Euler equation. Its gradient enters (4.3), whereas the field itself is canceled by the first mean source.

sec4.residual-gradient.TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHe: The pressure condition in Theorem 7.1 is chosen so that (4.3) can be used even after truncation. If the parent has frequencies at most $2\mathsf D$, then $R_U$ has frequencies at most $4\mathsf D$ and $\|\nabla R_U\|_\infty\le C\mathsf D\|R_U\|_\infty$. In the induction the parent velocity has frequencies at most $2\mu^5$ and the preceding residual has size $\lambda^{-3}$, giving $H^\#\le(2/N+C\mu^5\lambda^{-3})I\le I$.

sec4.displacement-derivative.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_endpointDisp: The quantity $Fz_t=\xi_t-M\xi$ is the velocity relative to the motion of the parent: if $z$ is constant along time then the physical displacement changes by $M\xi$ alone. This is the product rule used to change variables in the energy, and it remains valid for a Sobolev path with smooth $F$.

sec4.first-variation-equation.TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation: One can identify the label displacement directly by composing the perturbed flow with the inverse of the parent flow. At first order, $X^{-1}\circ X_\delta=\operatorname{Id}+\delta z+O(\delta^2)$. Thus $z=F^{-1}\xi$ and $Fz_t=b\circ X$ by (1.5) and (4.4). Since the relative map preserves volume, $\operatorname{div}_a z=0$.

sec4.deformation-invertible.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.labelDerivative: No curvature assumption is needed to pass between the two endpoint conditions. Differentiating the inverse-flow identities gives $F^{-1}F=FF^{-1}=I$; hence $F(t,a)z(t,a)=0$ if and only if $z(t,a)=0$. In particular, a zero terminal displacement is independent of which of these two coordinate systems is used.

sec4.terminal-primitive.TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_eq_neg_term: The map $v\mapsto Jv$ is a bijection between $L^2$ paths with zero integral and $H^1_0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ displacements. Its inverse is differentiation. In particular $Jv(t)=-\int_t^T v$ for such paths, which gives the terminal Poincaré bound and also the adjoint identity $J^*v=-Jv$ used in Appendix A.

sec4.poincare.TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_terminal_po: Cauchy–Schwarz on the tail interval gives $|z(t)|^2\le(T-t)\int_t^T|v(s)|^2\,ds$. The displayed bound replaces the tail norm by the full $L^2$ norm. It holds for the absolutely continuous representative of an $H^1$ path, at every time and at any fixed label.

After bounding by the full time integral, the only factor depending on $t$ is $T-t$, whose integral is $T^2/2$. The argument applies to the physical displacement $\xi$ as well as to $z$ since $F$ preserves the two zero traces. It is the estimate for $\xi$ that bounds the curvature contribution below.

sec4.norm-equivalence.TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelVelocit: From (4.4), $\|z_t\|_2\le D_-(\|\xi_t\|_2+\|M\|_\infty\|\xi\|_2)$. The terminal Poincaré inequality bounds $\|\xi\|_2$ by $(T/\sqrt2)\|\xi_t\|_2\le\|\xi_t\|_2$. Squaring gives (4.6) for differentiable paths; the Sobolev version uses the same inequality almost everywhere.
sec4.norm-equivalence.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.integral_norm_: For an $L^2$ path $v$ with zero integral, take its absolutely continuous primitive $z$. Then $Fz$ has weak derivative $MFz+Fv$ by the Sobolev product rule. The same Poincaré and triangle inequalities give (4.6) in this class. Thus the estimate can be used for a time-path solution of Appendix A, before recovering its continuous representative.

sec4.label-energy.TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy: The integral is the quadratic form of the integrated operator acting on $v=z_t$. With $Jv=z$, time integration by parts gives $\int_I J(\Omega v)\cdot v=-\int_I\Omega v\cdot z$, since $z$ vanishes at the endpoints. This is why the minus sign of the integral in (4.9) produces a plus sign in the mixed energy here.

sec4.energy-algebra.TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_eq: After the two $|M\xi|^2$ terms cancel, the mixed terms are $-\xi_t\cdot M\xi-\xi\cdot M\xi_t$. This is $-\partial_t(\xi\cdot M\xi)+\xi\cdot M_t\xi$. The remaining square-matrix term $\xi\cdot M^2\xi$ therefore combines with the last term into $-\xi\cdot H^\#\xi$. The identity uses neither symmetry of $M$ nor an equation for the parent.

sec4.integrated-energy.TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelEnergy_: The integrated boundary term is $-[\xi\cdot M\xi]_0^T$, which vanishes at both ends. To pass from smooth velocities to $L^2$ velocities of zero integral, subtract the time mean from each smooth approximant. Their primitives retain the two traces, and the operations $v\mapsto FJv$ and $v\mapsto MFJv+Fv$ are continuous in $L^2$. This gives (4.7) without a classical time derivative of $v$.

sec4.hardy-hypothesis.TorusEuler.paper_mean_hardy: The hypothesis is an upper bound on the symmetric part of $H^\#$, not on $\|M_t+M^2\|$. For instance a large negative eigenvalue does not reduce the lower bound in (4.7). The construction in §3 exploits exactly this asymmetry: a large negative contribution to the pressure Hessian is compatible with a small upper bound.
sec4.hardy-hypothesis.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_4_1: The test functions in the statement are all $H^1_0$ paths at a single label. Lean expresses this class using $v\in L^2(I)$ with $\int_Iv=0$, then reconstructs the path as $Jv$. These descriptions are equivalent; neither imposes a momentum equation on the test path.
sec4.hardy-hypothesis.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_4_1: We need the lower bound before integrating over the labels, since Appendix A freezes all the time-dependent coefficients at a single label. In this calculation $z$ is an arbitrary vector-valued path with zero traces; it need not extend to a divergence-free field on the torus. The spatial constraint is imposed later by projection.

sec4.hardy-hessian.TorusEuler.paper_mean_hardy: It is $\xi=Fz$ that appears in the potential term of (4.7). Its end traces vanish, so $\int H^\#\xi\cdot\xi\le\int|\xi|^2\le(T^2/2)\int|\xi_t|^2$. Estimating $\xi$ instead via $\|F\|\|z\|$ would introduce an unnecessary parent-deformation factor into the curvature restriction.
sec4.hardy-hessian.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_4_1: One can choose any fixed label $a_0$ before choosing the time path $z$. This gives the same inequality for the coefficient family frozen at $a_0$ for every Fourier coefficient of a spatial field. In particular it also covers time paths taking values in any transverse plane; no spatial divergence constraint is needed to establish this lower bound.
sec4.hardy-hessian.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_4_1: For a more general upper bound $H^\#\le hI$, $h\ge0$, the same argument gives the factor $hT^2/2$. Thus the condition used here is a sufficient fixed-endpoint coercivity condition, not a sharp threshold for invertibility. Taking $h=1$ and $T\le1$ leaves at least half the derivative energy, uniformly over all stages.

sec4.hardy-coercive.TorusEuler.paper_mean_hardy: Writing $\mu=[2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2]^{-1}$, (4.6) and (4.8) give $\langle (K-J\Omega)v,v\rangle_{L^2_t}\ge\mu\|v\|_{L^2_t}^2$ for $\int_Iv=0$. This is the path-space lower bound, independent of the spatial projection. It estimates the norm of an entire path; a separate spatial inversion will be needed to estimate its endpoint values.
sec4.hardy-coercive.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_4_1: A lower bound only after integrating in $a$ would control the global $L^2$ norm, but would not necessarily control the operator obtained by freezing at an arbitrary $a_0$. Lemma A.2 requires the latter. The quantifiers of Lemma 4.1 give precisely the same constant at each frozen label.
sec4.hardy-coercive.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_4_1: On the zero-integral time space, $\mathcal Q J\mathcal Q$ is skew-adjoint, because $J^*v=-Jv$ there. If the parent is exact, $\Omega$ is independent of time and commutes with time integration and $\mathcal Q$; the two skew factors then give a symmetric compressed term $-\mathcal Q J\Omega\mathcal Q$. For an approximate parent this argument fails when $\Omega$ depends on time. Appendix A uses coercivity, which suffices also in the nonsymmetric case.

sec4.hardy-proof.TorusEuler.paper_mean_hardy: Only the upper bound $H^\#\xi\cdot\xi\le|\xi|^2$ is used. The negative part of the quadratic form need not be estimated. In the induction, the positive contribution from the pressure and the gradient of the residual must be small; the large negative curvature of a steep wave is allowed.
sec4.hardy-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_4_1: The linked proof fixes $a$ and applies `paper_mean_hardy` to the coefficient functions of time there. The density argument has already been established for the full $L^2$ kernel of time integration. In particular the lower bound is available on the Hilbert space of Appendix A, before applying any spatial projection or solving for a force.

sec4.integrated-equation.TorusEuler.paperMeanIntegratedMomentum: Write $F=D_aX$. The integrated equation follows by multiplying momentum along the particles by $F^T$. With $g=F^T(f\circ X)$, its velocity terms are $Kv_t+2F^TF_tv=\partial_t(Kv)-\Omega v$. Integrate from zero, put $L=-Jg$, and absorb the integrated pressure into $\nabla_a\phi$. Now the unknown initial velocity appears only as the time-independent field $c$.
sec4.integrated-equation.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution: For the parent at rest, $K=I$, $\Omega=0$ and (4.9) reduces to $v+L=c+\nabla\phi$. Writing $\overline L$ for the time mean, we obtain $v=-\mathbb P(L-\overline L)$, $c=\mathbb P\overline L$, $\nabla\phi=(I-\mathbb P)L$. Here the zero time mean selects the initial correction, whereas the spatial projection selects the pressure gradient. The same distinction is used in Appendix A for nonconstant coefficients.
sec4.integrated-equation.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e: Given a displacement satisfying (4.9), differentiate in time only to obtain $v=z_t$ in the closed solenoidal space. The two traces imply $z=Jv$ and $\int_Iv=0$. Projecting the original integrated equation, without differentiating its source, gives the velocity formulation in the linked declaration. This direction is useful for uniqueness of solutions expressed as displacements.
sec4.integrated-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.EndpointSystemSolution: The pressure variable at this regularity is a continuous curve $G=\nabla_a\phi$ of periodic gradients, determined by (4.9). No time derivative of the scalar potential is required. The other variables are a continuous solenoidal $v$, its primitive $z$ with two zero traces, and a time-independent solenoidal $c$. The pressure gradient and $c$ can both be recovered once $v$ is found.

sec4.constant-initial.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.c: Evaluating (4.9) at zero with $L(0)=0$ gives $v(0)=c+\nabla_a\phi(0)$. Both $v(0)$ and $c$ are solenoidal. A solenoidal periodic gradient is zero, so in fact $c=v(0)=b(0)$ and $\nabla_a\phi(0)=0$. The first equality is the linked lemma; the conclusion about the gradient follows from the same equation.

sec4.inverse-hypothesis.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent: The hypotheses concern a fixed parent before any source is chosen: smooth coefficients, $F_t=MF$, an inverse bounded by $D_-$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. Lean constructs from these data both pointwise and mixed-path coefficient fields. This is why the same inverse estimate can be used for the different mean sources at every level of a single wave expansion.
sec4.inverse-hypothesis.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: The theorem estimates the response to the integrated datum $L$, for which time continuity is enough. It gives $z\in C^1_tC_a^{0,1/2}$ and a continuous pressure gradient in the integrated equation. To recover (4.11) we need an additional time derivative of $v$ and of the gradient; these follow in the smooth-force clause below.
sec4.inverse-hypothesis.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: In Appendix A the first inverse yields $v\in C_a^{0,1/2}(L_t^2)$. Averaging the projected equation then gives $c$, while the time primitive $J(\Omega v)$ takes values in $C_tC_a^{0,1/2}$. Equation (A.9) is now a spatial equation with a continuous right side, so the fixed-time inverse yields the desired $v\in C_tC_a^{0,1/2}$. Agreement with the first solution is proved by kinetic ellipticity.
sec4.inverse-hypothesis.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse:
Only $\mathbb P\mathcal QL$ determines the velocity. Indeed, replacing $L$ by $L+d+
abla r$ for a time-independent solenoidal $d$ changes the solution to $(v,c+d,
abla\phi+
