abla r)$. By uniqueness the velocity is unchanged. This also shows that its estimate may be applied to the projected datum $\mathbb P\mathcal QL$ in place of $L$.
sec4.inverse-hypothesis.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.p: Once the projected velocity is known, set $h=Kv-J(\Omega v)+L$. Equation (4.9) determines $c=\mathbb Ph$ and $\nabla_a\phi=(I-\mathbb P)h$ at every time. Hence the pressure gradient inherits the spatial Hölder regularity of $h$ without differentiating it. The linked uniqueness result is for this gradient; the scalar potential remains free up to a function of time.
sec4.inverse-hypothesis.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e: The velocity formulation and the displacement formulation give the same solution: $v=z_t$ is solenoidal with zero integral, and conversely $z=Jv$. Thus uniqueness of the projected velocity implies uniqueness of $z$ and, by the decomposition of (4.9), of $c$ and the gradient. This argument needs no time derivative of $L$.

sec4.inverse-polynomial.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse: The coefficient-level theorem uses the sufficient exponent $4\cdot291=1164$. In its notation $D$ bounds $F^{-1}$ and $L$ bounds $M$ (the source is called `src`). If $S=D+L+K_0+K_1+\Omega_0+\Omega_1$, the reciprocal mixed coercivity $2D^2(1+L)^2$ is bounded by $8S^4$; the other controls have no larger degree. Hence an absolute power of the Appendix A scale becomes an absolute power of the parent scale. The numerical exponent is not asserted to be sharp.
sec4.inverse-polynomial.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: The inverse-deformation and strain bounds enter the reciprocal coercivity constants as $D_-^2$ and $2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2$. The spatial norms of $K$ and $\Omega$ then determine how small a neighborhood is needed for freezing coefficients in Lemma A.2. The Lean statement separates the supremum and first-derivative bounds for each coefficient. These are controlled by the norms in (4.10).
sec4.inverse-polynomial.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: The exponent in (4.10) must be absolute for the use in §5.3. On the envelope scale $\ell_*$, the coefficient bound there gives $\ell_*^m(|K|_{m,1/2}+|\Omega|_{m,1/2})\le C_m/A$ for $m\ge1$. Each differentiated-coefficient term in the equation for $\partial_a^\beta v$ therefore loses a factor $A$ from the inverse and gains $A^{-1}$ from that bound. Induction gives $\|v\|_{[n],1/2}\le C_n A\|L\|_{[n],1/2}$, keeping the exponent of the parent size independent of $n$.

sec4.velocity-bound.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse: For a force $f$, $L=-Jg$ with $g=F^T(f\circ X)$, so $\|L\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}\le T\|g\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}$. The inverse gives the same factor $T$ in the bound for $v$ and hence for $b(0)=v(0)$. At other times, the physical correction must also be multiplied by $F$ and composed with the inverse flow.
sec4.velocity-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: The same estimate controls the position error: $z(t)$ is both $\int_0^t v$ and $-\int_t^T v$. Thus $\|z(t)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le A\min(t,T-t)\|L\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}$. In particular the bound for the displacement has an extra factor $T/2$ compared with that for the velocity.
sec4.velocity-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: The mixed norm from (A.8) is sufficient for the primitive: $\|J(\Omega v)(t)-J(\Omega v)(s)\|_{C_a^{0,1/2}}\le |t-s|^{1/2}\|\Omega v\|_{C_a^{0,1/2}(L_t^2)}$. This follows by applying Cauchy–Schwarz both to the values and to spatial increments. Thus the known right side of (A.9) is continuous even before $v$ has been shown continuous in time.

sec4.force-source.TorusEuler.endpointPhysicalForcePrimitiv: Multiplication by $F^T$ is chosen to transform the pressure by the ordinary chain rule: $F^T((\nabla_xq)\circ X)=\nabla_a(q\circ X)$. It transforms the force in the same way, to $g=F^T(f\circ X)$. Thus a gradient component of $f$ gives a label gradient in $g$ and does not affect the velocity selected by the projected inverse.
sec4.force-source.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_integr: Here $g$ is not the physical force in particle coordinates alone. The physical vector along a trajectory is $f\circ X$; the multiplication by $F^T$ puts it into the same covector coordinates as the pressure gradient. In the coefficient-level Lean construction the parameter `force` already denotes $f\circ X$, so it must not be composed with the flow a second time.

sec4.smooth-displacement.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: The proof gains spatial regularity first, using Lemma A.2 at all derivative orders, then obtains $v\in C_tC_a^{k,1/2}$ for every $k$ by (A.9). That equation expresses $v$ using the smooth coefficient inverse and a primitive of $\Omega v$, which now has a time derivative. Repeating the argument gives joint smoothness; it avoids differentiating the original $L^2$ time path.
sec4.smooth-displacement.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.exist: This link goes in the reverse direction from the smoothness assertion. Starting with a smooth correction, integrate its label momentum equation with $L=-Jg$ to get a solution of (4.9). Consequently the uniqueness theorem for integrated data compares any two smooth solutions of the physical problem, including solutions obtained by a different construction.
sec4.smooth-displacement.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: The first clause admits arbitrary continuous integrated data; the smooth-force clause uses $L=-Jg$ with $g$ smooth. The joint regularity part of Theorem A.1 then applies to the same solution. In the Lean statement this regularity is asserted for every integrated solution with smooth data, which is equivalent by uniqueness.
sec4.smooth-displacement.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: After recovering $v\in C_tC_a^{k,1/2}$ for every $k$, differentiate the projected equation to get $S(t)v_t=\mathbb P(\Omega v-K_tv-L_t)$, where $S(t)=\mathbb PK(t)$ on the solenoidal space. Since $S(t)^{-1}$ is smooth in time, this gives $v_t$ in every spatial class. Successive differentiation gives higher time derivatives and thus smoothness of $z=Jv$.

sec4.mean-definition.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The field called `mean` in the smooth solution is $B=b\circ X=Fv$, with physical vector components at the parent particles. Its label-coordinate counterpart is $v=z_t$. In the later wave equations $B$ is paired with the transported wave vector $\kappa$; the endpoint condition instead integrates $F^{-1}B$. This distinction prevents a misplaced deformation factor in either equation.
sec4.mean-definition.TorusEuler.derivWithin_kineticForm_sub_v: For $B=Fv$ the material derivative along $X$ is $B_t=Fv_t+F_tv$, and the linearized strain term is $MB=F_tv$. Multiplying their sum by $F^T$ gives $Kv_t+2F^TF_tv$. This explains the two occurrences of $F_t$ in the strong label equation and hence the definition of $\mathcal D$.

sec4.normalized-pressure.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: The smooth field $G_q=g-\mathcal Dv-Kv_t$ has zero Leray projection. On the torus its Fourier coefficient at nonzero $n$ is parallel to $n$, and its zero coefficient is zero, so it is the gradient of a periodic potential. Requiring the potential's zero Fourier coefficient to vanish makes it unique. This is the instantaneous pressure in (4.11), not the integrated pressure in (4.9).
sec4.normalized-pressure.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2:
There are two pressure gradients: the integrated gradient $
abla_a\phi$ in (4.9) and the instantaneous gradient $
abla_a\mathsf q$ in (4.11). They satisfy $
abla_a\mathsf q=-\partial_t
abla_a\phi$ for smooth forces. The zero-mean convention for $\mathsf q$ concerns its spatial mean at each time, not its average over the interval.
sec4.normalized-pressure.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: For smooth data the gradient in (4.9) is a smooth field, and $-\partial_t\nabla_a\phi=g-\mathcal Dv-Kv_t$. There is no need to choose and differentiate an unnormalized scalar $\phi$; the right side has zero Leray projection and directly determines a normalized periodic potential. This is how the proof supplies a smooth scalar pressure rather than only its gradient.

sec4.strong-label.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.stron: The coefficient-level equation uses $2F^TMF$ for $\mathcal D$, since $F_t=MF$. Its input is the force along the flow; multiplying by $F^T$ gives $g$. The linked identity is thus exactly the strong label form, before using the inverse deformation to recover the Eulerian momentum equation.
sec4.strong-label.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2:
Differentiate (4.9): the left side becomes $Kv_t+K_tv-\Omega v-g$, while the derivative of $c$ is zero. Using $K_t-\Omega=\mathcal D$ and $
abla_a\mathsf q=-\partial_t
abla_a\phi$ gives $Kv_t+
abla_a\mathsf q=g-\mathcal Dv$. The negative primitive of the force is responsible for the positive $g$ on the right.
sec4.strong-label.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: On the solenoidal space, projection of (4.11) gives $v_t=S(t)^{-1}\mathbb P(g-\mathcal Dv)$ with $S(t)=\mathbb P K(t)$. This is an evolution equation once $v(0)$ is known. Its initial value must come from (4.9), since the evolution equation by itself imposes no zero-integral condition on $v$.

sec4.smooth-eulerian.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: The force adapter starts with $f(t,x)$, evaluates it at $X(t,a)$ and solves for the label-coordinate correction. The resulting physical fields are $b(t,x)=F(t,a)v(t,a)$ and $q(t,x)=\mathsf q(t,a)$ at $a=X^{-1}(t,x)$. Smoothness of the actual flow and its inverse transports joint regularity to physical coordinates.
sec4.smooth-eulerian.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.euler: For the reconstruction from coefficient data, $F$ must be the label derivative of $X$, not an arbitrary matrix field satisfying the energy identity. This gives both $\nabla_a\mathsf q=F^T((\nabla_x q)\circ X)$ and the Piola identity for $Fv$. The linked result also identifies $M$ with the gradient of the physical parent along $X$, so the recovered equation is the linearized Euler equation over that parent.
sec4.smooth-eulerian.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: The formula $b=(Fv)\circ X^{-1}$ is the pushforward of the label velocity as a vector field. For the pressure, $q=\mathsf q\circ X^{-1}$ is ordinary scalar composition, hence $(\nabla_x q)\circ X=F^{-T}\nabla_a\mathsf q$. Using the same vector transformation for pressure would not give (4.12).
sec4.smooth-eulerian.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: The pressure normalization survives the change of coordinates: $\int q(t,x)\,dx=\int\mathsf q(t,a)\det D_aX(t,a)\,da=\int\mathsf q(t,a)\,da=0$. This uses the determinant-one property independently of the endpoint coercivity.

sec4.eulerian-equation.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.euler: Multiply (4.11) by $F^{-T}$. The two left-hand terms become $Fv_t$ and $(\nabla_x q)\circ X$, and $F^{-T}\mathcal Dv=2F_tv$. Since $B=Fv$ and $MB=F_tv$, the resulting equation is $B_t+MB+(\nabla_xq)\circ X=f\circ X$. This is (4.12) along the particle trajectories.
sec4.eulerian-equation.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: The flow adapter starts from a physical force $f$ and composes it with $X$ to obtain the label force. In the reverse transformation, $B_t=[(\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla)b]\circ X$, and Piola gives $\operatorname{div}b=0$ from $\operatorname{div}_a v=0$. The argument works even when $u$ is not an exact Euler solution.
sec4.eulerian-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: Adding a periodic gradient $\nabla r$ to the force adds $r-\int r$ to the normalized pressure and leaves $b$ unchanged. Indeed the endpoint and divergence conditions are unchanged and the new pair satisfies (4.12), so uniqueness identifies the velocity. Thus the mean inverse depends only on the solenoidal part of the physical source.
sec4.eulerian-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: The mean solve in (5.27) produces $B_p=b_p\circ X$. In (5.28) it contributes $-(B_p\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$ to the transverse source. Since $B_p$ and $\kappa$ are independent of $s$, this term has zero phase mean. The mean can therefore be found first, and only then inserted into the transverse equation; there is no additional mean unknown to solve for at that level.

sec4.endpoint-selection.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: If the parent and source are odd, the reflected pair $(-b(t,-x),q(t,-x))$ satisfies the same momentum equation and displacement conditions (the parent flow is odd). Uniqueness gives oddness of $b$, and of $B=b\circ X$. This is the argument used for the phase means in the hierarchy, without assuming that the mean is localized in space.
sec4.endpoint-selection.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: For force data $L(0)=0$, and $X(0)=\operatorname{Id}$ gives $F(0)=K(0)=I$. The constant $c$ is therefore precisely $v(0)=B(0)=b(0)$. The formal smooth-force clause records this equality explicitly: the unknown time-independent field in the integrated equation is the initial correction to the Eulerian velocity.
sec4.endpoint-selection.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: Averaging (4.9) after spatial projection gives $c=\mathbb P[\overline{Kv}+\overline L-T^{-1}\int_0^T(T-s)\Omega(s)v(s)\,ds]$, where the bar denotes the time mean. For force data this field is $b(0)$. The formula displays the dependence on the whole interval, including the contribution of the skew term to the selected initial value.

sec4.fixed-time-inverse.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse:
To solve $\mathbb P(Kw)=\mathbb Ph$ on solenoidal fields, write $Kw=h+
abla\psi$. Then $w=K^{-1}(h+
abla\psi)$ and $\operatorname{div}w=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}(K^{-1}
abla\psi)=-\operatorname{div}(K^{-1}h)$. In particular simply applying $\mathbb P$ to $K^{-1}h$ generally does not give the required inverse. The gradient enforces the spatial constraint at that time.
sec4.fixed-time-inverse.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: The fixed-time map $S(t)w=\mathbb P(K(t)w)$ acts on all solenoidal spatial fields, including their constant spatial modes. Testing against $w$ gives $\langle S(t)w,w\rangle\ge D_-^{-2}\|w\|_2^2$. Lemma A.2 upgrades this lower bound to a bounded spatial Hölder inverse. The zero-time-mean condition belongs to the earlier path problem, not to this map.
sec4.fixed-time-inverse.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: The fixed-time inverse supplies a continuous representative: $S(t)^{-1}-S(s)^{-1}=S(t)^{-1}(S(s)-S(t))S(s)^{-1}$, and the inverses are uniformly bounded. The right side of (A.9) is continuous in the spatial norm, so the reconstructed $v$ is continuous. Testing its difference from the original time path at almost every time against that difference gives zero by ellipticity; hence its time integral is still zero.

r2.s34.rescale-endpoint.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.endpointSystem: Set $Z(\tau)=z(T\tau)/T$, $V(\tau)=v(T\tau)$. Then $Z_\tau=V$ and $\int_0^1V=T^{-1}\int_0^Tv=0$. In (4.9), the primitive becomes $T\int_0^\tau\Omega(Ts)V(s)\,ds$. The rescaling therefore leaves the velocity, $c$ and source amplitudes unchanged, and changes the skew coefficient to $T\Omega(T\tau)$.
r2.s34.rescale-endpoint.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.solve42: The rescaling changes the displacement amplitude by $T^{-1}$ so that its derivative $Z_\tau$ equals the original velocity at $t=T\tau$. In particular its supremum norm in the label Hölder space and that of $L$ are preserved. The terminal trace is also preserved, since $Z(1)=z(T)/T$.

r2.s34.apply-appendix-inverse.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.solve42: The normalized data are $K(T\tau)$, $T\Omega(T\tau)$ and $L(T\tau)$. The norms used in Appendix A involve spatial derivatives only, so $K$ keeps the same bounds and the norms of $T\Omega$ can only decrease for $T\le1$. Meanwhile both the path energy and the squared velocity $L^2$ norm are divided by $T$, leaving the coercivity quotient unchanged.
r2.s34.apply-appendix-inverse.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_4_2_of: For the normalized path problem the two bounds required by Theorem A.1 are different: $\kappa=D_-^{-2}$ is the ellipticity of $K$, while $\mu=[2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2]^{-1}$ is the lower bound for the path form on zero-integral velocities. The latter includes the vorticity contribution; the former is used when the time path has to be recovered at each time by a spatial inverse.
r2.s34.apply-appendix-inverse.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_A_1: For a nonzero spatial Fourier mode $n$, $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$ retains only paths in $n^\perp$ whose time integral is zero. For $n=0$ only the time condition remains: a spatially constant velocity is allowed, provided its time integral is zero. Lemma 4.1 supplies coercivity for all these paths at each frozen label, including the zero spatial mode.
r2.s34.apply-appendix-inverse.TorusEuler.kineticForm_elliptic: For every label vector $w$, $|w|=|F^{-1}Fw|\le D_-|Fw|$. Since $w\cdot Kw=|Fw|^2$, this gives $K\ge D_-^{-2}I$. This bound is needed in the second, fixed-time inversion, and follows from the inverse deformation without using $H^\#$.

sec4.coercivity-constant.TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy_coercive: The lower bound for the full time path cannot be proved only for continuous velocities, since the inverse is first constructed in a space of $L^2$ paths. The linked theorem extends the smooth inequality by density in the kernel of time integration. This produces exactly the test class required by the normalized coercivity assumption (A.2).
sec4.coercivity-constant.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.sobolevEnergy_: In the rescaled form, $Z=z/T$ and $Z_\tau=v$ at $t=T\tau$. Thus $\int_0^1(K Z_\tau\cdot Z_\tau+T\Omega Z_\tau\cdot Z)\,d\tau$ is the original energy divided by $T$, and $\int_0^1|Z_\tau|^2\,d\tau$ is also divided by $T$. The coercivity constant is therefore identical for the normalized problem.
sec4.coercivity-constant.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.solve42: In (4.8) the right side controls the physical derivative, whereas Theorem A.1 asks for control of the derivative of the label displacement. Read (4.6) in the direction $\|\xi_t\|_2^2\ge\|v\|_2^2/[D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2]$. The factor $1/2$ from (4.8) then gives exactly the displayed mixed coercivity constant.

r2.s34.endpoint-unique-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.solve42: If two solutions of (4.9) have the same $L$, their velocity difference $w$ satisfies $\mathcal R(K-J\Omega)w=0$ with $w=\mathcal Rw$. Coercivity gives $\mu\|w\|_{L^2_{a,t}}^2\le0$. Hence $w=0$; the initial trace determines the displacement, and the orthogonal spatial decomposition of (4.9) determines the difference of $c$ and the pressure gradient to be zero. No scalar pressure normalization is needed for this uniqueness statement.
r2.s34.endpoint-unique-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_4_2_of: The inverse rescaling is $z(t)=TZ(t/T)$ and $v(t)=V(t/T)$. The field $c$ is unchanged and the gradient is simply composed with $t/T$. This is a bijection on the integrated solution class, preserving the time-uniform velocity and source norms exactly. Hence both uniqueness and the estimate transfer to the original slab without a factor of $T^{-1}$ in the velocity bound.

sec4.polynomial-scale.TorusEuler.paperMean_inverse_scale: In the scale comparison put $S=D+L+C_K+C_\Omega+L_K+L_\Omega\ge1$. The costly term is the reciprocal of mixed coercivity, $2D^2(1+L)^2\le8S^4$, while the reciprocal of pointwise ellipticity is $D^2\le S^2$. The coefficient bounds contribute only linearly. The arithmetic lemma packages these inequalities into a fourth-power bound for the scale entering the Hölder inverse.
sec4.polynomial-scale.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_4_2_of: Let $S$ be the sum in (4.10). Since $D_-\ge1$, we have $S\ge1$. The fixed-time reciprocal ellipticity is at most $S^2$ and the reciprocal path coercivity is $2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2\le8S^4$. The coefficient terms in $Q$ grow at most linearly in $S$. Therefore $Q\le CS^4$; raising to the fixed power of Appendix A gives (4.10) with an enlarged absolute exponent.
sec4.polynomial-scale.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.pow_le_of_le_s: The two inversions in the theorem may initially have different exponents. The arithmetic lemma allows a bound $x\le cS^4$ and an exponent $n\le m$ to be replaced by $x^n\le c^n S^{4m}$ for $S\ge1$. Thus a single absolute power of the parent size can be chosen to dominate both estimates.

sec4.smooth-force-proof.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_integr: The field $X(t,a)$ is a periodic lift, so $X(t,a+m)=X(t,a)+m$ for $m\in\mathbb Z^3$. Thus $f(t,X(t,a))$ and $F(t,a)$ are periodic in $a$. Their transpose-weighted product $g$ is smooth, and integrating in time gives a smooth periodic $L$ with $L(0)=0$. This is the force datum to which the smoothness clause applies.
sec4.smooth-force-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.smooth42: The source $L=-J(F^T(f\circ X))$ is smooth jointly in time and label. The formal proof first obtains smoothness of the displacement from the integrated inverse, then identifies its derivative with the continuous velocity of that inverse. It can therefore differentiate the projected equation to reconstruct the instantaneous pressure.
sec4.smooth-force-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_4_2_of: The smoothness clause is applied on the normalized slab to $L(T\tau,a)$. Composition with the linear change of time preserves smoothness, and the rescaling of $z$ then preserves smoothness on the original slab. This supplies the differentiability needed for (4.11), including the one-sided time derivatives at the endpoints.

r2.s34.smooth-solution-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.solve42: In `solve42` the high-regularity part is supplied by Theorem A.1 on the rescaled slab. Its proof first lifts the spatial regularity of the whole path and then uses (A.9) to bootstrap in time. Only joint smoothness of the displacement is retained at this step of the formal proof; `smooth42` uses its time derivative to reconstruct the instantaneous pressure and physical equation.
r2.s34.smooth-solution-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.smooth42: Rather than differentiating an arbitrary scalar potential from the integrated equation, the Lean proof uses the smooth field $g-(K_t-\Omega)v-Kv_t$. Its Leray projection is zero by differentiation of the projected equation. It is therefore a periodic gradient, and taking its zero-mean potential gives the instantaneous pressure.

sec4.differentiate-integrated.TorusEuler.strongLabelMomentum_of_integr: The derivative of the integrated left side is $Kv_t+K_tv-\Omega v-g$, since $L_t=-g$. The linked lemma assumes that the derivative of the integrated gradient is $-\nabla_a\mathsf q$; the smooth-data argument supplies such a derivative. Now $K_t-\Omega=\mathcal D$ gives (4.11), with the force on the right.
sec4.differentiate-integrated.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.smooth42: Differentiate the spatially projected equation: $\mathbb P(Kv_t+K_tv-\Omega v-g)=0$. The smooth complementary field $g-(K_t-\Omega)v-Kv_t$ is a gradient. Its normalized periodic potential is $\mathsf q$ in (4.11); the time regularity of any initially chosen scalar $\phi$ is immaterial.
sec4.differentiate-integrated.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_4_2_of: There is a harmless normalization issue in setting $\mathsf q=-\phi_t$. The integrated problem specifies only $\nabla_a\phi$, so choose the scalar potential to have zero spatial mean at each time before differentiating. Equivalently, the formal proof differentiates the projected equation and constructs the normalized potential of the smooth field $g-\mathcal Dv-Kv_t$. Both procedures give the same pressure gradient.

sec4.physical-momentum-proof.TorusEuler.eulerianMomentum_of_strongLab: Under multiplication by $F^{-T}$, $Kv_t$ becomes $Fv_t$, $\mathcal Dv$ becomes $2F_tv$, and $\nabla_a\mathsf q$ becomes $(\nabla_xq)\circ X$. Since $B=Fv$ and $MB=F_tv$, the first two velocity terms are $B_t+MB$. This recovers the physical momentum equation along the parent flow.
sec4.physical-momentum-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.smooth42: For the field $b$ defined by $b\circ X=B$, the chain rule gives $B_t=[b_t+(u\cdot\nabla)b]\circ X$. Also $MB=[(b\cdot\nabla)u]\circ X$. Applying these identities after multiplication by $F^{-T}$ proves the Eulerian momentum equation; incompressibility of $b$ is the separate Piola step.

sec4.piola.TorusEuler.divergence_piola_of_contDiffA: For a smooth map of determinant one, the divergence of the pushforward $b=(Fv)\circ X^{-1}$ at $X(t,a)$ is $\operatorname{div}_a v(a)$. To see the identity weakly, change variables in $\int b\cdot\nabla_x\psi\,dx$; the integrand becomes $v\cdot\nabla_a(\psi\circ X)$. The linked Piola theorem gives the pointwise version used here, so the solenoidal constraint is preserved.
sec4.piola.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.smooth42: The divergence constraint is preserved by the vector pushforward $B=Fv$. For $\det F=1$, Piola gives $(\operatorname{div}_x b)\circ X=\operatorname{div}_a v=0$; there is no separate spatial divergence condition on the components of $B$ in labels. Thus the same solenoidal constraint used in (4.9) is sufficient for (4.12).

r2.s34.freeze-kinetic-coefficient.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.fixedTime42: Here time is a parameter, and the Hilbert space in Lemma A.2 is $\mathbb R^3$. The coefficient is just $K(t,a)$ with coercivity $D_-^{-2}$, rather than $K-J\Omega$ on paths. The projection is consequently the spatial Leray projection alone. This gives the fixed-time bound without using the mixed coercivity or a time-mean restriction.
r2.s34.freeze-kinetic-coefficient.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_4_2_of: For fixed $t$, the parameter in Lemma A.2 is $2+D_-^2+\|K(t)\|_{C^1}$. Its fixed power is bounded by a fixed power of the parent sum in (4.10), uniformly in $t$. Enlarging the absolute constant and exponent makes the same $A$ valid for both the fixed-time and the whole-path solves; it does not require the latter coercivity hypothesis for the fixed-time solve itself.
r2.s34.freeze-kinetic-coefficient.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_A_2: Freeze $K(t,\cdot)$ at $a_0$ and let $P_n$ be projection onto $n^\perp$ (the identity at $n=0$). The extended Fourier symbol is $P_nK(t,a_0)P_n+I-P_n$, with lower bound $\min(1,D_-^{-2})$. Its inverse and finitely many angular derivatives are bounded by powers of the parent size. Lemma A.2 then localizes to a radius $r$ with $r^{1/2}\|K\|_{C^1}$ sufficiently small to absorb the coefficient variation. Taking $r$ to be an inverse power gives the polynomial bound.

sec4.fixed-inverse-proof.TorusEuler.exists_endpointSpatialLerayIn: Put $F=D_aX$. Since $|F^{-1}|\le D_-$, we have $|Fw|^2\ge D_-^{-2}|w|^2$, the ellipticity needed in Lemma A.2. Inverting $K=F^TF$ pointwise would not in general give a solenoidal field. The concrete Lean inverse instead inverts $v\mapsto\mathbb P(Kv)$ on solenoidal fields, with a bound of degree $145$ in $4+D_-^2+\|K\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}K$.
sec4.fixed-inverse-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.fixedTime42: Here the inverse is applied to a projected datum $\mathbb Pf$. In `fixedTime42` the bounds for $K$ and its first label derivative are $K_0$ and $K_1$; the torus Lipschitz constant is at most $2K_1$. With ellipticity $D_-^{-2}$, the bound on the composite is $C_2(2+D_-^2+K_0+2K_1)^{p_2}\|\mathbb P\|$. Unlike the inverse for the whole endpoint problem, this estimate needs no lower bound on the displacement energy (4.7).

r2.s34.common-inverse-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_4_2_of: The same coefficient bound $A$ in (4.10) controls the endpoint solve and the inverse at a fixed time. For the force problem put $g=(D_aX)^T(f\circ X)$. The integrated source $L(t)=-\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ obeys $\|L\|_{C_t C^{0,1/2}}\le T\|g\|_{C_t C^{0,1/2}}$. Applying the endpoint bound gives $\|v\|_{C_t C^{0,1/2}}\le AT\|g\|_{C_t C^{0,1/2}}$.

r5-B-purpose-central-gradient.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_9: The next wave does not use merely a lower bound for $|\nabla U|$. It uses the particular matrix $\nabla U_{j-2}+\sigma E_2\otimes E_1$ in the preceding wave’s frame. The bound in (5.50) controls every entry of the difference from this matrix; truncation adds one more small matrix in (6.5).

r5-B-purpose-flow-control.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_10: For the next step the size of $D_aY$ and its inverse enters the parent parameter $\mathsf D$. A direct flow estimate in terms of the large shear could grow exponentially in the wave frequency. Lemma 5.10 obtains a polynomial bound and keeps it valid under the small solenoidal Fourier tail, so the truncated velocity can be used as a parent.

r5-B-purpose-next-coercivity.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_11: For a parent with residual $R_U$, the matrix in the endpoint problem is $H^\#=(D_x^2p_U-D_xR_U)\circ X$, not just the pressure Hessian. The new pressure is recomputed after truncation, and (5.57) bounds the change caused by both $R_V$ and the Fourier tail. The new residual derivative is estimated separately in Section 7 using its finite frequency support.

c8-first-mean-cancels-parent-residual.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.meanSource: The old error is removed in the first mean, not by the cutoff or the next wave's oscillatory equation. Indeed $\bar f_2+f_2=-H_2-R_U\circ X$, so the two new linear equations together cancel precisely those terms, with the supplementary source canceling the newly introduced phase advection. This is the cancellation used in (5.29).

r5-B-prescribed-seed.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsSeed: At the other labels the initial central vector must first be projected onto the local plane $\kappa(t_0,a)^\perp$. Solving the seed equation from those projected data gives a transverse extension, and at $a=0$ the projection is the identity on the central vector. `IsSeed` specifies this smooth extension and its agreement with the central solution.
r5-B-prescribed-seed.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_4: The nonvanishing of $\kappa$ makes the projected initial data smooth in the label, and the linear ODE extends those data in time. The formal Proposition 5.4 includes the existence of this seed before the hierarchy is constructed. Its quantitative comparison with the central solution, used to estimate the hierarchy, is a separate part of Lemma 5.3.

s5.frequency-band.TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand: Differentiating $\cos(2\pi n x)$ keeps the frequency $n$. Squaring it produces a constant and a mode at $2n$. The same bookkeeping says that if $U$ only uses frequencies of length at most $2\mathsf D$, then $\nabla U$ stays in that band and $U\otimes U$ can reach $4\mathsf D$. The band is measured in the spatial variable before composition with the flow.

s5.parent-data.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Parent: The parent is an approximate solution. To construct the next wave we need the band and deformation bounds (5.1) to differentiate its coefficients, the upper bound (5.2) to solve the mean equation, and a sufficiently small inherited residual (5.6). In `Parent` the pressure need only be smooth and periodic, with an odd, band-limited residual satisfying these bounds. The zero-mean Poisson pressure used in the paper is a particular admissible choice and additionally makes $R_U$ divergence free.

s5.parent-frequency.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trunc: The first derivative is already bounded by $\mathsf D$. Since $\nabla U$ has the same band as $U$, Bernstein applied to $\nabla U$ costs only $k-1$ additional factors of $\mathsf D$ for an order-$k$ derivative of $U$. This gives the velocity-jet bound $C_k\mathsf D^k$ without using a bound on the size of $U$ itself. The hierarchy record supplies these inputs separately from the mean geometry.
s5.parent-frequency.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Parent: At step $j$, the preceding cutoff gives a band $2\lambda_{j-1}^5$. Bernstein and the bound $\|U_{j-1}\|_\infty\le\lambda_{j-1}$ give $\|\nabla U_{j-1}\|_\infty\le C\lambda_{j-1}^6$. Thus $\mathsf D=\lambda_{j-1}^9$ covers both the band and the gradient for large initial frequency. The deformation bound is a separate part of (T2), proved using Lemma 5.10 rather than Bernstein.

s5.parent-deformation.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trunc: Write $F=D_aX$. For a label vector $w$, the length of the physical vector $Fw$ is between $\mathsf D^{-1}|w|$ and $\mathsf D|w|$. The metric $K=F^TF$ in the mean equation therefore satisfies $\mathsf D^{-2}I\le K\le\mathsf D^2I$. The same bound on the two changes of coordinates is needed for $F^{-T}k_*$ and for the moving transverse plane. Volume preservation alone would control only the product of the three singular values.
s5.parent-deformation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Parent: The propagator of $Y_t=M(t,a)Y$ from $\sigma$ to $t$ is $F(t,a)F(\sigma,a)^{-1}$, where $F=D_aX$. Hence it has norm at most $\mathsf D^2$. This is the bound used for the highest derivative in the differentiated flow equation below; integrating the strain bound directly would give $e^{T\mathsf D}$ instead of a power of $\mathsf D$.

s5.origin-fixed.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.odd: The reflected curve $-X_{s,t}(a)$ solves the trajectory equation with initial point $-a$, so uniqueness gives $X_{s,t}(-a)=-X_{s,t}(a)$. At $a=0$ the trajectory is fixed. Consequently the strain in the central wave equation is simply $\nabla U(t,0)$, with no moving evaluation point.

s5.even-coefficients.TorusEuler.even_fderiv_of_odd: In $X(t,-a)=-X(t,a)$, differentiation in $a$ gives $-D_aX(t,-a)=-D_aX(t,a)$. The identical argument for $U(t,\cdot)$ makes its gradient even. Since $X$ is odd, the composed gradient $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$ is even as well.
s5.even-coefficients.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.even_materialGr: Both $M$ and $F=D_aX$ are even in $a$. Hence the inverse transpose is even and so is $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$. The sign change of the phase $k_*\cdot a$ under reflection is not a sign change of its physical gradient. In particular the projection in (5.4) and the seed equation are the same at the labels $a$ and $-a$.

s5.parent-pressure.TorusEuler.exists_truncatedParentPoisson:
Let $q=\operatorname{tr}((
abla U)^2)$. Since $q=\operatorname{div}(U\cdot
abla U)$, its integral is zero. Define $\widehat p_U(0)=0$ and $\widehat p_U(\xi)=\widehat q(\xi)/(4\pi^2|\xi|^2)$ for $\xi
e0$. The pressure is smooth, with frequencies at most $4\mathsf D$, and even since $
abla U$ is even. This solves the Poisson equation regardless of the size of the momentum residual.

s5.parent-residual.TorusEuler.momentumResidual: The new equations are in labels, so their inherited source is $R_U\circ X$. Composition preserves the spatial supremum because $X(t,\cdot)$ is a diffeomorphism, but does not preserve finite Fourier support. To estimate derivatives of the source in labels, one needs Bernstein in the Eulerian variables followed by the flow-jet estimate of Proposition 5.1.

s5.projected-residual.TorusEuler.exists_truncatedParentPoisson:
Taking the divergence of the momentum gives $\operatorname{div}R_U=\Delta p_U+\operatorname{tr}((
abla U)^2)=0$. Equivalently the gradient part of $U\cdot
abla U$ is $-
abla p_U$, so $U_t+\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(U\otimes U)$ is the actual defect, not merely its projection. In particular the small residual estimate is a bound on this solenoidal vector field.

s5.residual-fourier-band.TorusEuler.parentResidualFourierBand_of_: All Fourier coefficients of $U$ outside $2\mathsf D$ vanish identically in time, so their time derivatives vanish as well. The tensor $U\otimes U$ has band $4\mathsf D$; both the divergence and the projection preserve that band. This is why the residual has a Bernstein bound even though no separate bound on $U_t$ is imposed in (5.1).

s5.parent-coercivity.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trunc: The parent-geometry constructor takes (5.2) as a hypothesis: it gives $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ along every particle. Neither finite Fourier support nor the strain bound supplies this inequality. For the initial stationary shear in (6.1), $M_t=M^2=0$, so $H^\#=0$; for a later approximate solution one instead uses the pressure increments and the gradient of its residual.
s5.parent-coercivity.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Parent: With $F=D_aX$ and $\xi=Fz$, the label energy is $\int_0^T(|\xi_t|^2-H^\#\xi\cdot\xi)\,dt$: the omitted total derivative has zero boundary term because $z$ vanishes at both ends. The bound $H^\#\le I$ and $\int|\xi|^2\le(T^2/2)\int|\xi_t|^2$ leave at least $\tfrac12\|\xi_t\|_2^2$. Since $z_t=F^{-1}(\xi_t-M\xi)$, this is at least $[2\mathsf D^2(1+\mathsf D)^2]^{-1}\|z_t\|_2^2$. A large negative direction of $H^\#$ increases the energy, so an absolute bound on the Hessian is unnecessary.

s5.endpoint-hypothesis.TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHe: The derivative of the material acceleration along particles is $M_t+M^2$. The differentiated momentum equation therefore gives $-(M_t+M^2)=(D^2p_U-\nabla R_U)\circ X$. For an approximate solution the matrix need not be symmetric; the upper bound concerns its quadratic form. Adding a scalar field to $p_U$ adds its Hessian to both terms of the difference, so the condition is intrinsic to $U$.

s5.transported-covector.TorusEuler.labelWaveVector: The phase is constant along a parent particle: $\theta(t,X(t,a))=k_*\cdot a$. Differentiation in $a$ gives $F^T\nabla_x\theta=k_*$, with $F=D_aX$. Thus the physical normal is $F^{-T}k_*$, not $Fk_*$. Its evolution $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ follows by differentiating the inverse transpose.
s5.transported-covector.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.waveVector: The reference labels for `waveVector` are those at time zero, even if $t_0>0$. The phase is transported by the parent throughout the slab; only the amplitude is switched on at $t_0$. It is the physical normal at that later time whose length defines the launch frequency.

s5.launch-frequency.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Launch: For a prescribed physical unit normal $e$ at launch, take $k_*=\lambda D_aX(t_0,0)^Te$. Then $\kappa(t_0,0)=\lambda e$, as required. The length $\lambda$ is imposed in physical space at launch, not on the constant label vector. No lattice condition on $k_*$ is needed because the oscillation is localized before it is continued periodically.

s5.wave-vector-bounds.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_normalized: If $F_0=D_aX(t_0,0)$ and $F=D_aX(t,a)$, then $\kappa(t,a)=F^{-T}F_0^T\kappa(t_0,0)$. Each of these two factors and its inverse has norm at most $\mathsf D$. This gives $\mathsf D^{-2}\le |\kappa|/\lambda\le\mathsf D^2$; the same argument with $F_0^T$ alone bounds the label vector. In particular $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2\le\mathsf D^4$ throughout the slab.
s5.wave-vector-bounds.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_labelWaveV: At a fixed label, $\mathsf D^{-1}|k_*|\le|\kappa|\le\mathsf D|k_*|$ follows from the inverse transpose and its inverse. The lower inequality is as important as the upper one: it bounds the denominator in the projection and the pressure coefficient. Apply the same inequalities at launch to relate $|k_*|$ to $\lambda$.

s5.profile-width.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.width: The steep portion of $F_h$ occupies a phase interval of size $h$. Since the physical phase gradient is $\kappa$, its local normal thickness at the central particle at launch is $h/\lambda=\lambda^{-3/2}$. More generally the reciprocal of $h/|\kappa|$ is the cost of a fast physical derivative. The radius $\ell_*$ controls a different scale: the extent of the envelope in labels.

s5.origin-normalization.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Origin: Positive rescaling of a nonzero solution of (3.2) leaves its frame and all ratios of its lengths unchanged. It therefore leaves both conditions (5.5) unchanged. The paper chooses the scale to make $\max\gamma=1$; `Origin` requires only nonvanishing and $\gamma(t)\le1$.

s5.seed-nonzero.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: A nonzero solution of the homogeneous seed equation cannot become zero: uniqueness from such a time, including backward uniqueness, would make it identically zero. Therefore $0<\gamma(t)\le1$ on the active interval. The division by $\gamma$ below is legitimate even though its minimum is not bounded uniformly as $\lambda$ increases.

s5.weight-and-coupling.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.weight: The weight is positive on $[t_0,T]$, and division by $\gamma(t)$ compares a correction with the seed at the same time. For a later wave $\gamma(t_0)$ can be very small. A bound on $V/\gamma$ implies a correspondingly small velocity during switching, which is needed for the activation error. Only the label and phase derivatives occur in this norm, and they commute with division by $\gamma$.
s5.weight-and-coupling.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: In the moving frame $E_1=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, the first coupling is $\nu=E_1\cdot ME_2$. In particular $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=\nu|\kappa||\mathbf a|$. This is the scalar whose positivity will give the sign of the leading pressure tensor in (5.51). The amplitude weight $\gamma$ here is unrelated to the frame coefficient of the same name in the frame equations.

s5.projected-activation.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn: `SeedOn` contains the comparison obtained after evolving the projected data. Its bound $|\mathbf a(t,a)-\mathbf a(t,0)|\le C|a||\mathbf a(t,0)|$ is relative at each time, with $C$ a parent-dependent constant. It also gives $\kappa(t,a)\cdot M(t,a)\mathbf a(t,a)\ge(2\mathsf D)^{-1}|\kappa(t,0)||\mathbf a(t,0)|$ on the envelope. The first estimate controls velocity; the second controls the sign of the pressure contribution.
s5.projected-activation.TorusEuler.oscillatoryTransverseProjecti: Let $v=\mathbf a(t_0,0)$. Since $v\perp\kappa(t_0,0)$, the new datum minus $v$ is $-(P_{\kappa(t_0,a)}-P_{\kappa(t_0,0)})v$. Proposition 5.1 bounds the derivative of the direction projection by a parent power. Thus the initial error is $O(\mathsf D^C|a||v|)$, small even relative to a very small $v$.
s5.projected-activation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsSeed: Transversality is an invariant of the seed equation. In fact $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ and $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2P_\kappa M\mathbf a$ give $\partial_t(\kappa\cdot\mathbf a)=-\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a-\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a+2\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=0$. Thus projection is needed at launch only; the ODE preserves the constraint thereafter.

s5.seed-even.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.eve: At opposite labels the initial projections agree, and the coefficients of the linear equation agree. Uniqueness gives an even seed. Since the envelope is also even and $F_h$ is odd, the evaluation $g(a)\mathbf a(t,a)F_h(k_*\cdot a)$ is odd. Composing with the odd inverse flow preserves the required physical parity.

s5.radial-envelope.TorusEuler.radialEnvelope: The envelope is a function of the particle label, so along a trajectory of the parent it is constant. Each label derivative of the envelope costs $\ell_*^{-1}$; the weighted derivative $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$ cancels this cost. Hence its fixed-order weighted norms are bounded independently of the radius.

s5.envelope-plateau.TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_one: Every derivative of $g$ of positive order vanishes in the plateau. The central seed and covector are therefore unchanged by the spatial localization. In particular $g(0)=1$ in the computation of the rank-one central gradient (5.50). The divergence completion and all other corrections are accounted for separately in its error term.

s5.leading-profile.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.lea: For a profile with independent phase the divergence is $\widetilde{\mathbf d}\cdot A_1=(\mathbf d\cdot(g\mathbf a))F_h+g(\kappa\cdot\mathbf a)F_h'$. The last term is zero. Localization and the label dependence of the seed still leave the first term, so the leading field must be completed by a curl correction before it can be added to the divergence-free parent.
s5.leading-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.leading: At $x=0$ the term differentiating $g\mathbf a$ vanishes since $F_h(0)=0$; the term differentiating the phase is $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$ since $g(0)=F_h'(0)=1$. This matrix has norm $|\mathbf a||\kappa|$, and its square is zero by transversality. It is precisely the added shear that enters the central comparison for the next wave; (5.50) bounds the remaining gradients.

s5.switched-profile.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.gen: On the centered cell the wrapped leading profile is exactly $\widetilde\chi(t)g(a)\mathbf a(t,a)F_h(s)$, even for a nonintegral carrier $k_*$. This is the equality in `genericLeading_cell_eval`: localization keeps the wrapping from changing the formula there. Since $\widetilde\chi$ depends only on time, spatial differentiation commutes with switching; the time derivative instead produces the additional activation error.

s5.central-transverse-assumptions.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.exists_see: For a constant orthonormal basis $Q$ of $k_*^\perp$, set $A_\perp=FQ$. The identity $\kappa\cdot Fw=k_*\cdot w$ puts the moving planes into the same two coordinates. Writing $V=A_\perp v$ gives $v_t+2A_\perp^\dagger MA_\perp v=0$. The central propagator costs $\mathsf D^3\gamma(t)/\gamma(t')$, including the two coordinate changes. The generator varies by at most $\mathsf D^{-3}$ on the envelope. In Duhamel's formula the two powers cancel, as does the intermediate $\gamma$; Gronwall on an interval of length at most one costs only $e$.
s5.central-transverse-assumptions.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.CenterWave: The second inequality of (5.5) is needed even if the transverse inverse is already controlled. The localized coupling has positive sign, so the coefficient $c_{\mathbf a}=2\widetilde\chi g(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$ is nonnegative. The leading pressure tensor is $-c_{\mathbf a}F_h'\kappa\otimes\kappa$, and its positive part is bounded by $Chc_{\mathbf a}|\kappa|^2I$. The factor $h$ changes the scale $\mathsf D^3\lambda^{1/4}$ to $\mathsf D^3\lambda^{-1/4}$, which is small enough to sum in the pressure bound.

s5.near-center-size.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn: The comparison $|\mathbf a(t,a)-\mathbf a(t,0)|\le C\mathsf D^C|a||\mathbf a(t,0)|$ holds at the current time, rather than relative to the maximum seed length. Taking $2C\mathsf D^C\ell_*\le1/2$ gives $\tfrac12|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le|\mathbf a(t,a)|\le2|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. In particular the seed is small throughout the envelope when the central seed is small during activation.

s5.leading-velocity-size.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.wei: At a fixed $(t,a,s)$ the linked estimate bounds the switched velocity divided by $\gamma(t)$ by $\lambda^{-5/4}$, and the pressure divided by $\gamma(t)$ by $4\mathsf D^3\lambda^{-9/4}$. The velocity power comes from $|\mathbf a|\lesssim\gamma\lambda^{-3/4}$ and $|F_h|\lesssim h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. These are pointwise bounds; the all-order version in Lemma 5.3(iii) also uses the weighted derivative estimates on $g\mathbf a$ and $F_h$.

s5.parent-smallness.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trunc: The source of the first mean contains $-R_U\circ X$ and the phase average of the quadratic wave terms in (5.25). The identity $\partial_s(C_2\cdot\kappa)=-\mathbf d\cdot V_1$ gives, after integration by parts, $\langle H_2\rangle=\mathbf d\cdot\langle V_1\otimes V_1\rangle$. Thus the derivative falls on the stress at fixed phase: it costs only a parent power, not $\lambda/h$. With $V_1$ of size $\lambda^{-5/4}$, the mean source has scale $\lambda^{-5/2}$, explaining the required size of the inherited residual.
s5.parent-smallness.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Parent: If $r=\|R_U\|_{C_tL^\infty}>0$, (5.6) imposes the upper restriction $\lambda\le r^{-2/5}$ on the new frequency. The correction estimates impose a lower restriction. At step $j$ the preceding residual has already been made at most $\lambda_j^{-3}$, so the upper endpoint is at least $\lambda_j^{6/5}$. Thus the preceding step must be designed with the next frequency already in mind.

s5.envelope-radius.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.radius: One needs a radius that works at all derivative orders. If $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{pm+q}$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^p\le1$, then $\ell_*^m|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^q$; for $m\ge1$ it is even bounded by $C_m\ell_*\mathsf D^{p+q}$. This last factor of $\ell_*$ is used in Lemma D.3 to compensate the inverse bound each time a derivative falls on a coefficient. Increasing the expansion depth changes $C_m$, not the radius exponent.

s5.envelope-in-cell.TorusEuler.tsupport_radialEnvelope_subse: The closed support of $g$ has radius at most $2\ell_*\le1/4$ when $\mathsf D\ge2$. Thus the oscillatory field vanishes in a neighborhood of the faces of the centered unit cell. It can be repeated smoothly by cells even when $k_*$ is not a lattice vector; the phase-independent mean has its own periodic continuation.

r5-B-uniform-exponents.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6: There are two separate uniformity issues: the radius weights prevent a new parent power at each derivative, and the induction prevents a new parent power at each level. In (5.40) the source and $\lambda^{1/2}B_p$ are bounded by the level scale without a factor $\mathsf D^C$. The mean estimate (5.35) is stronger than this induction bound by a factor $\lambda^{-1/12}$ before parent powers. The same reserve in the worst transverse product pays for the inverse and coefficient costs, so they are not multiplied through all $P$ levels.
r5-B-uniform-exponents.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_1: If $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{C(m+1)}$, then the weighted derivative is at most $C_m\mathsf D^C(\ell_*\mathsf D^C)^m$. Taking $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-C}$ removes the $m$-dependent power of the parent without requiring the numbers $C_m$ to be bounded as $m$ increases.

r5-B-order-and-depth-constants.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6: At a given level $p$, the construction depends only on earlier levels, not on where the expansion will eventually be stopped. Thus a bound on that field may have constant $C_{n,p}$. Bounding the entire expansion and all products left over at its end introduces $C_{m,P}$ instead. Neither kind of constant changes the absolute exponent of $\mathsf D$.

r5-B-no-order-growth-assumption.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6: At step $j$, the order $q_{j+1}$ is selected using the bound $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\lambda_{j-1}$ in (7.8), before setting the depth using $K_{j+1}$. Even rapidly growing fixed-order constants can be accommodated by leaving $q_j$ unchanged for more steps. Each fixed derivative order is eventually reached because $q_j\to\infty$.

p5.1.derivative-weights.TorusEuler.hierarchyMixedDirection:
In the chain rule $
abla_x f^
atural=(F^{-T}
abla_a f+\kappa\partial_sf)^
atural$, the first term costs at most a parent power times $\ell_*^{-1}$ and the second at most $\mathsf D^2\lambda h^{-1}=\mathsf D^2\lambda^{3/2}$. The weighted norm records the derivatives before these factors are paid. In particular for a phase-independent mean or residual the second cost is absent.
p5.1.derivative-weights.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.fieldNorm: `fieldNorm` sums ordered words in the four scaled directions. In the paper each multi-index is counted once; for example the words $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ represent the same mixed derivative on a smooth profile. They give equivalent norms with constants depending only on order. The supremum is over time, labels and phase for each derivative; no time derivative occurs.

p5.1.phase-independent-norm.TorusEuler.hierarchyFiniteMixedWordNorm_: Every derivative word containing the phase direction vanishes on a phase-independent coefficient. The surviving words are exactly the label words, including the empty word. This is an exact identity for the library word norms; the paper's coordinate sums differ only by the fixed-order multiplicities.
p5.1.phase-independent-norm.TorusEuler.hierarchyFiniteWordNorm: The term of order zero is unchanged by scaling. For $m\ge1$, if $\ell_*\mathsf D^C\le1$, then $\ell_*^m\mathsf D^{C(m+1)}\le\ell_*\mathsf D^{2C}$. This spare small factor, absent at order zero, is useful in the differentiated inverse estimates when a derivative falls on a coefficient.
p5.1.phase-independent-norm.TorusEuler.hierarchyLabelDirection: The label directions are $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$. A word of length $m$ therefore costs $\ell_*^m$ times the corresponding ordinary derivative. This is applied to coefficients of the parent, which have no phase dependence, even when they multiply an oscillatory field whose phase derivatives are large.

p5.1.fixed-derivative-cost.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.weighted_: If $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{pm+q}$, multiplication by $\ell_*^m$ gives $C_m\mathsf D^q(\ell_*\mathsf D^p)^m$. With $\ell_*\mathsf D^p\le1$ all orders are bounded by the same power $\mathsf D^q$. In addition, for $m\ge1$ the same expression is at most $C_m\mathsf D^{p+q}\ell_*$, leaving a small factor for terms where derivatives hit a coefficient.

p5.1.coefficient-list.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_parentCoef: In (5.16), $\lambda\partial_s\mathsf p=(\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2)(\kappa/\lambda)\cdot(f-2MV)$. The two normalized coefficients of Proposition 5.1 therefore allow $\lambda\mathsf p$ to be estimated by the same norms as the force and transverse velocity, using the zero-mean phase primitive. The pressure is one power of $\lambda$ smaller than the velocity estimate; no derivative in the labels has been lost.
p5.1.coefficient-list.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_5: The projection depends on the direction of the wave vector. With $q=\kappa/\lambda$ it is $P_\kappa=|q|^{-2}q\otimes q$. Since $|q|\ge\mathsf D^{-2}$, differentiation of the scalar inverse introduces only powers of $\mathsf D$, and the product rule gives the same type of bounds for $P_\kappa$. No inverse power of the new physical width is involved.

p5.1.polynomial-coefficients.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_parentCoef: The linked coefficient estimate takes the common exponent $16m+16$. Thus $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-16}$ would remove the order-dependent power for this list alone. The proof of the full proposition enlarges the exponent, and the radius must also make the differentiated coefficients small relative to the mean and transverse inverse bounds. The value $16$ is a bound for this particular auxiliary estimate, not the final radius exponent.
p5.1.polynomial-coefficients.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound: In `ParentLabelJetBound` the exponent is $pm+q$: $p$ is the cost of one further derivative, $q$ the cost before any derivative is taken. Thus the coefficient bound has $q=C$ while the composed-field estimate has $q=0$ and a separate amplitude $A_f$. This distinction survives summation in (5.8).
p5.1.polynomial-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_1: The formal theorem first derives velocity jets from Bernstein, then flow jets from the differentiated flow equation, and finally the coframe, inverse length and projection by product and inverse rules. The assembled proof takes the common exponent $360$; the auxiliary coefficient estimate takes $16$. The existence of one exponent linear in order is the point needed to choose the radius before fixing the depth.
p5.1.polynomial-coefficients.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_parentComp: Each partition term for $D_a^m(f\circ X)$ contains exactly one derivative of $f$; its other factors are jets of $X$. Hence the amplitude $A_f$ occurs once, regardless of the number of flow factors. For the residual one can therefore keep $A_f=\|R_U\|_{C_tL^\infty}$ all the way through the weighted composition estimate.
p5.1.polynomial-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_5: The order-dependent constants are chosen from the assumed jet-bound constants before choosing $f$ or its amplitude. Thus (5.7) can be applied to both $\nabla U$ and $R_U$, using their own supremum norms as $A_f$. The assertion is for every finite order, with one absolute exponent, not a bound on the growth of $C_m$ with $m$.

p5.1.composition.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_parentComp: For a partition into $k$ blocks of total order $m$, the cost is $A_f\mathsf D^{k+5m-4k}=A_f\mathsf D^{5m-3k}$. Here $k\ge1$, unlike the forcing in the flow-jet recurrence where the one-block term is removed. The bound $C_m A_f\mathsf D^{6m}$ in Lean is a convenient enlargement. At order zero the composition has the original amplitude.
p5.1.composition.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_5: Apply (5.7) first with $f=\nabla U$, whose amplitude is at most $\mathsf D$, and later with $f=R_U$, whose amplitude is at most $\lambda^{-5/2}$. The derivative cost after transport is the same in both cases; their different sizes are preserved. This is why the residual does not require a separate composition calculus.
p5.1.composition.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.proposition_5_1_o: All derivatives in the composition statement are taken at fixed time. The chain rule applies to $a\mapsto f(t,X(t,a))$ after the flow jets have been bounded. In particular it does not require a time derivative of $f$ or a bound on its time oscillation. The common exponent in the conclusion is obtained by enlarging the composition exponent $6$.

p5.1.weighted-coefficients.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.weighted_: The lemma sums $\ell_*^j\sup_a\|D^jc(t,a)\|$ at each fixed time using $\ell_*\mathsf D^p\le1$. The paper instead sums the supremum over time of each coordinate derivative. To pass to that expression one may bound each summand by the uniform bound for its order and absorb the finite number of terms and coordinate components in $C_n$. The exponent of $\mathsf D$ is unchanged.
p5.1.weighted-coefficients.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_weightedCo: For $f\circ X$ the term of order zero is already bounded by $A_f$. Each further label derivative costs $\mathsf D^6$ in the linked estimate, canceled by $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-6}$. The sum is therefore $C_nA_f$, not $C_n\mathsf D^C A_f$; this is the useful form for the inherited residual.
p5.1.weighted-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_5: For a coefficient the order-zero bound can already cost a power of $\mathsf D$; for a composed field it is $C_0A_f$. The radius absorbs the additional derivative costs in both cases. The formal result bounds a fixed-time sum of spatial suprema of Fréchet derivatives. To obtain the paper’s sum of separate time suprema of coordinate derivatives, bound each summand uniformly and absorb the finite multiplicities in $C_n$.
p5.1.weighted-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.proposition_5_1_o: The constants in (5.8) may grow arbitrarily with order. Section 7 chooses the depth via a slowly increasing sequence $q_j$ so that $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$. With $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ and $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q_j+1)}$, the relevant cost satisfies $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\mathsf D^b\le\mu^{10b}\le\lambda^{1/32}$. This is how fixed-order estimates with an absolute exponent can be used at increasing depth.

p5.1.bernstein-input.TorusEuler.exists_parentVelocityJetBound: Apply Bernstein at order $k-1$ to $\nabla U$. This uses the available first-derivative bound rather than a possibly much larger bound on $U$, and gives $|U|_k\le C_k\mathsf D^k$ for $k\ge1$. The analytic helper permits a band $4\mathsf D$ instead of $2\mathsf D$; the factor of two is absorbed in $C_k$.
p5.1.bernstein-input.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S5a.exists_velocity: Since $\nabla U$ has band $2\mathsf D$, a derivative of it costs $C\mathsf D$ by (B.1). Thus $|U|_2\le C\mathsf D^2$ follows from the first bound of (5.1), without a bound on $U_t$. Repeating at order $k-1$ gives the factor $\mathsf D^k$ for the velocity derivative in a $k$-block term of the chain rule.

p5.1.variational-equation.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.labelJets_evolv: The one-block term of the chain rule is $(\nabla U\circ X)D_a^nX$. Moving it into the linear part leaves a forcing involving only derivatives of $X$ of orders strictly less than $n$. Since $X(0,a)=a$, the initial higher jet is zero for $n\ge2$. Its solution is consequently a time integral of the lower-jet forcing against the known first variation.
p5.1.variational-equation.TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_comp_sub_linea: At order two the forcing is $(D^2U\circ X)[D_aX,D_aX]$. At order three the chain rule adds the three terms with $D^2U$ applied to a first and a second jet and the term with $D^3U$ applied to three first jets. The formal partition sum deletes the one-block term, the one containing the unknown highest jet.

p5.1.faa-di-bruno.TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_comp_sub_linea: A partition into $k$ blocks describes which of the $n$ derivatives fall on each copy of $X$ in $U\circ X$. The block sizes $n_i$ sum to $n$. Removing the one-block partition leaves $k\ge2$ and hence $n_i<n$ for every block. Consequently every flow factor on the right of (5.9) has already been bounded in the induction on $n$.

p5.1.propagator-bound.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_multilinea: For $n\ge2$, $D_a^nX(0)=0$. Variation of constants therefore represents the higher jet by $\int_0^t F(t)F(\sigma)^{-1}N(\sigma)\,d\sigma$ with $F=D_aX$. The known bound on both $F$ and $F^{-1}$ gives the factor $\mathsf D^2$, and the time integral costs at most one. No exponential of the strain is introduced.

p5.1.flow-recurrence.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_iteratedFD: Each term in the recurrence has three costs: $\mathsf D^2$ for the propagator, $\mathsf D^k$ for the velocity jet and $\prod_i\upsilon_{n_i}$ for the flow jets. The number of partitions of a fixed order enters only $C_n$. This makes the exponent estimate a problem about the number and sizes of the blocks.

p5.1.flow-power.TorusEuler.exists_forward_flowJetBounds: The induction starts from $\upsilon_1\le C\mathsf D$. For the second jet the single quadratic forcing costs $\mathsf D^2\mathsf D^2=\mathsf D^4$ and the propagator adds $\mathsf D^2$, giving $\upsilon_2\le C\mathsf D^6$. At the next order the two-block term has cost $\mathsf D^{11}$ including the propagator, while the three-block term costs $\mathsf D^8$. Thus the two-block terms set the slope in $5n-4$.

p5.1.partition-power.TorusEuler.flowJet_partitionPower_le: The lower jets contribute $5\sum_i n_i-4k=5n-4k$ to the exponent. With the propagator and the velocity jet the exponent is $5n-4-3(k-2)$. Two blocks give equality in the desired power; more blocks only improve it. The estimate therefore closes at all orders with the same slope five.

p5.1.jacobian-power.TorusEuler.norm_iteratedFDeriv_labelJaco: A derivative of order $m$ of $F=D_aX$ is obtained from the flow jet of order $m+1$, with its last argument regarded as the vector on which the resulting linear map acts. The exponent becomes $5(m+1)-4=5m+1$. In particular the order-zero bound for $F$ agrees with (5.1).

p5.1.remaining-coefficients.TorusEuler.exists_parent_coefficientJetB: For $G=F^{-1}$, differentiation gives $\partial G=-G(\partial F)G$, with first derivative cost $\mathsf D^2\mathsf D^6=\mathsf D^8$. More generally each inverse derivative inserts a derivative of $F$ between inverse factors; the linked estimate gives $\mathsf D^{7m+1}$. Taking $q=G^Tk_*/\lambda$ gives $\mathsf D^{7m+2}$, and $|q|\ge\mathsf D^{-2}$ permits the same inverse rule on $|q|^2$. The resulting bounds for $|q|^{-2}$ and $P_\kappa$ have exponents $16m+4$ and $16m+8$.

p5.1.weighting-composed-field.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_weightedCo: For $f\circ X$ the $m$th summand in the scaled norm has size $C_mA_f(\ell_*\mathsf D^C)^m$. The factor in parentheses is at most one, including when $A_f$ is very small. The same radius therefore works for all residuals obeying the band bound; the size of the residual enters only as a multiplier of the final norm.

p5.1.residual-weighted.TorusEuler.exists_parentResidualWeighted: Bernstein on the $4\mathsf D$ band gives $|R_U|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^m\|R_U\|_{C_tL^\infty}$. The weighted composition estimate (5.8) cancels the derivative powers without enlarging the residual amplitude, giving (5.10). Thus even the extra label derivative of $R_U\circ X$ needed for (5.12) costs only an order-dependent constant times $\lambda^{-5/2}$. The mean estimate does not require $R_U$ to be localized in the envelope.

p5.2.mean-equation.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: Put $F=D_aX$ and let $\xi$ be the first variation of the parent trajectory under the added velocity. Then $\xi_t=M\xi+B$; writing $\xi=Fz$ and using $F_t=MF$ gives $z_t=F^{-1}B$. The endpoint conditions amount to $\int_0^T F^{-1}B\,dt=0$ at each label. They concern the first variation of the final particle position; they neither set $B(T)$ to zero nor prescribe the final position of the full perturbed flow.
p5.2.mean-equation.TorusEuler.trace_endpointPhysicalMean_eq: The label velocity is $v=F^{-1}B$, where $F=D_aX$. The Piola identity, using $\det F=1$, gives $(\operatorname{div}_x B^\natural)\circ X=\operatorname{div}_a v$. The linked theorem uses $\operatorname{div}_a v=0$ to prove the pulled-back divergence condition. Since $z(0)=0$ and $v=z_t$, the displacement is solenoidal as well. Ordinary label derivatives preserve these constraints, which is why the same inverse can be applied after differentiation.
p5.2.mean-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.MeanSolution: The endpoint inverse is applied to the displacement $z$ in the fixed label coordinates, with $v=z_t$ and $B=D_aXv$. The pressure enforces solenoidality; it is not determined up to a single constant for all times, but up to a spatial constant at each time. The mean equation in Lean does not fix that constant. In the expansion `IsExpansion` fixes it by requiring zero label-cell average of $\bar q_p$ at each time.

p5.2.mean-coordinate-readout.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.MeanSolution: There are two different changes of coordinates in this calculation. Velocity is pulled back by $F^{-1}$, so $v=F^{-1}B$; force is multiplied by $F^T$, so $g=F^T\bar f$. The latter makes the pressure a label gradient and the coefficient of $v_t$ the positive metric $K=F^TF$.
p5.2.mean-coordinate-readout.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.eq_5_14: To transform (5.11), put $B=Fv$ and multiply by $F^T$. Then $F^T\mathbf d\bar q=\nabla_a\bar q$ and $F^T(B_t+MB)=Kv_t+2F^TF_t v$. This gives (4.11) with $g=F^T\bar f$, whose time primitive is the datum in (4.9).

p5.2.initial-velocity-selected.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: For $U=0$ and a divergence-free force, the velocity satisfies $B(t)=B(0)+\int_0^t\bar f(\tau)\,d\tau$. The condition $\int_0^T B(t)\,dt=0$ gives $B(0)=-T^{-1}\int_0^T(T-\tau)\bar f(\tau)\,d\tau$. Even if the force is supported near the end of the interval, the initial correction is generally nonzero. The linked uniqueness result for an admissible parent gives equality of the mean velocities of any two endpoint solutions.

p5.2.source-derivative-loss.TorusEuler.paperAppendixD_holderComparis: For a derivative $w=\partial_a^\beta g$, the bounds $|w(a)-w(b)|\le2\|w\|_\infty$ and $|w(a)-w(b)|\le\|\nabla w\|_\infty|a-b|$ give a half-Hölder bound using one further derivative. With the radius weights this yields (D.2), with factor $4\ell_*^{-1/2}$ in Lean. No time derivative of the force is required.

p5.2.all-solutions.TorusEuler.paper_mean_columns: Subtracting two solutions with the same force gives a solenoidal displacement with zero endpoints and zero forcing. The coercive form in Section 4 bounds its time derivative, hence it must vanish. This determines the mean velocity uniquely; its pressure is determined only up to a function of time. The linked theorem obtains the bound for an arbitrary solution by identifying its velocity with the one furnished by the inverse.
p5.2.all-solutions.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_5: The phrase ‘every solution’ concerns pairs with the two displacement endpoints in (5.11). Without the terminal condition the homogeneous equation could have nonzero initial velocity even for $\bar f=0$, contradicting (5.12). It is this constraint that permits an estimate with only the force on the right, without an initial-data term.

p5.2.mean-estimate.TorusEuler.paper_mean_columns: The formal bound makes the order of choices explicit: fix a sufficiently large $s$ in $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$, and then vary $n$. Its parent factor is $\mathsf D^{b+2+2s}$ at every order. This permits an earlier mean to be differentiated again when forming any later source without changing the frequency separation required in Theorem 5.6.
p5.2.mean-estimate.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_5: The mean is bounded in the scaled label norm on $[0,T]$, without the factor $1/\gamma$. A late force can select a nonzero initial mean, so even a source proportional to the square of the seed at its time of application need not give a mean with the same time dependence. The extra label derivative on the source bounds its Hölder seminorm. The formal proposition allows any parent pressure satisfying the standing residual and coercivity hypotheses.
p5.2.mean-estimate.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_2: In forming $H_p$ and its mean we have all orders of the earlier profiles available. Thus estimating $B_p$ at order $n$ by $\bar f_p$ at order $n+1$ consumes an estimate already proved, rather than requiring another equation for $B_p$. Its only appearance in the same-level transverse source is $-(B_p\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$, which does not differentiate $B_p$. The formal statement admits the broader parent pressure class of §5.1.

p5.2.mean-coefficient-powers.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S5a.exists_KOmega_p: Put $F=D_aX$. The kinetic metric $K=F^TF$ and the skew coefficient $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$ involve only products of the already estimated parent coefficients. A derivative of order $m$ distributes among those factors with total order $m$. Thus (D.6) persists with a fixed linear exponent in $m$, before the weights $\ell_*^m$ are applied.

p5.2.inverse-constant-power.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S5a.exists_A_bound: The constant $A$ in (4.10) bounds the inverse of the two-endpoint equation. In its formula the inverse deformation and low-order norms of $M,K,\Omega$ are bounded by parent powers before choosing $\ell_*$. Choosing the radius afterward is important: the factor $\ell_*^{1/2}$ in (5.13) must offset an inverse norm which does not itself grow as the radius shrinks.

p5.2.radius-threshold.TorusEuler.exists_parentMeanWeightedCoef: The derivatives of positive order have a small factor in (D.7): $\ell_*^m|K|_m\lesssim_m\mathsf D^C\ell_*$, and likewise for $\Omega$. Passing to the half-Hölder norm costs $\ell_*^{-1/2}$ by (D.2), leaving the factor $\sqrt{\ell_*}$. The formal coefficient bound makes this explicit as a parent factor $\mathsf D^9\sqrt{\ell_*}$, times order-dependent constants.
p5.2.radius-threshold.TorusEuler.meanScalarRadius_absorbs_inve: In the explicit scalar bound, $A\le\mathsf D^a$ and the coefficient cost is $\mathsf D^9$. For $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$ the product $A\mathsf D^9\sqrt{\ell_*}$ is at most $\mathsf D^{a+9-s/2}$. Taking $s\ge2(a+9)$ makes it at most one. This one radius works at every positive derivative order.
p5.2.radius-threshold.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.eq_5_13: For a label derivative, the highest derivative of $v$ still has coefficients $K$ and $\Omega$. Only terms in which at least one derivative falls on a coefficient are moved to the datum. Thus (5.13) is a smallness condition on positive-order weighted coefficient derivatives; it does not require the metric $K$ or the skew term $\Omega$ to be small.
p5.2.radius-threshold.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_13: At first order the new term in the datum is $(\partial_aK)v$. Applying the inverse after weighting it by $\ell_*$ costs at most $C A\ell_*|K|_{1,1/2}\|v\|_{[0],1/2}$. By (5.13) this is bounded by an absolute multiple of the preceding order. At higher orders the inverse factor $A$ is similarly paired with the weight belonging to the derivatives that fall on $K$.
p5.2.radius-threshold.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.Text.eq_5_13_of: One can see the remaining radius factor directly: (D.7) at order $m$ and $m+1$ bounds the two terms on the right of (D.2) by $C_m\mathsf D^C\ell_*$. Multiplication by $\ell_*^{-1/2}$ leaves the half power of $\ell_*$. The final scalar inequality absorbs $A$ after its bound has been obtained.

p5.2.mean-lifting-coefficients.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S5a.Tower.main_towe: The equation being differentiated is $Kv-\int_0^t\Omega v+L=c+\nabla_a\phi$. Its new datum at first order is $\partial_aL+(\partial_aK)v-\int_0^t(\partial_a\Omega)v$. The integral has norm at most $T\le1$ in $C_tC^{1/2}$; applying the solenoidal projection changes only a fixed operator constant. Both coefficient commutators therefore fit the same lifting estimate.

p5.2.derivative-lifting.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD3_lifting: For each label derivative the differentiated displacement has the same two zero endpoints and remains solenoidal. The derivatives of $c$ are time-independent and the differentiated pressure term is again a label gradient. Thus the same endpoint inverse applies. Every commutator of order $n$ contains at least one derivative of a coefficient and at most $n-1$ derivatives of the unknown, as required for induction in (D.8).
p5.2.derivative-lifting.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.Text.eq_5_14_of: The integration $L(t)=-\int_0^t g(\tau)\,d\tau$ commutes with every label derivative. Hence $\|L\|_{[n],1/2}\le T\|g\|_{[n],1/2}$. The estimate for the label velocity inherits the same derivative order as the force, with no factor $T^{-1}$ and no derivative of $g$ in time.

p5.2.holder-estimate.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.eq_5_14: The input of the integrated inverse is $L=-\int_0^t g$, so the estimate (5.14) is for the same label Hölder order of $v$ and $g$. At this stage no derivative has been lost. The conversion (D.2) is made only afterward, when the right side is measured using suprema of derivatives; the left side can be reduced to that norm without an extra derivative.
p5.2.holder-estimate.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_14: The velocity $v=F^{-1}B$ in (5.14) has three label components and is solenoidal. This is the endpoint inverse on the whole slab, not the two-dimensional transverse inverse measured relative to the active seed. Its norm includes the Hölder seminorm at each derivative order through $n$. The Lean statement permits the broader parent pressure class under the residual and coercivity hypotheses.
p5.2.holder-estimate.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.Text.eq_5_14_of: Writing $u_n=\|v\|_{[n],1/2}$, the commutator estimate gives $u_n\le C_n(A\|L\|_{[n],1/2}+u_{n-1})$. Indeed (5.13) has already paid for the inverse acting on each differentiated coefficient. Induction from $u_0\le A\|L\|_{[0],1/2}$ therefore retains just one factor $A$; without (5.13) the naive recursion could lose a power of $A$ at each derivative.

p5.2.product-readout.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.proposition_5_2_o: The two changes of coordinates are $g=F^T\bar f$ on the input and $B=Fv$ on the output. Each uses the same-order Hölder product estimate, and (5.8), (D.2) bound the deformation factors. Neither change introduces an additional derivative of the unknown. The sole extra derivative of the source in (5.12) comes from replacing its Hölder norm by a supremum norm.

p5.2.fixed-power-readout.TorusEuler.paperAppendixD_holderComparis: The first inequality of (D.2) bounds the output supremum norm by its Hölder norm without loss. The second bounds the input Hölder norm by $4\ell_*^{-1/2}\|\bar f\|_{[n+1]}$. Thus the extra derivative is on the known force alone, and $\ell_*^{-1/2}$ is a fixed parent power.
p5.2.fixed-power-readout.TorusEuler.meanScalarBudget_le_power: In the Hölder readout, $F^T$ and $F$ each cost at most $\mathsf D^b\ell_*^{-1/2}$, and conversion of the source from supremum to Hölder costs $\ell_*^{-1/2}$. Their product with $A\le C\mathsf D^a$ is $C\mathsf D^{a+2b}\ell_*^{-3/2}$. The scalar lemma rounds this up to a fixed power $\mathsf D^{a+2b+2s}$ for $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$.
p5.2.fixed-power-readout.TorusEuler.paper_mean_columns: Fixing the radius $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$ gives the explicit exponent $b+2+2s$ in the formal mean estimate. It is unchanged when the source is differentiated to the next order. This is necessary when forming the next $H_p$, which may require arbitrarily high derivatives of earlier means.

e02.transverse.forward-zero.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.solve: Along $x=X(t,a)$ the phase $k_*\cdot a$ is constant under the parent flow. We solve an ODE in $t$ at each independent $(a,s)$, then restrict to $s=k_*\cdot a$. The zero initial value selects the transverse velocity; no terminal displacement condition is imposed.

e02.transverse.inactive-source.TorusEuler.exists_jointSmooth_oscillator: If the forcing has not started, the equation at a fixed label and phase is homogeneous with zero initial velocity. Hence the entire transverse velocity and the pressure slope vanish there; the zero-mean normalization gives zero pressure too. Later forcing cannot change these earlier values.

e02.transverse.weight.TorusEuler.paperHierarchyActiveVelocityN: Here $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$ on $[t_0,T]$. By (5.5), propagation from $t'$ to $t$ can cost a factor proportional to $\gamma(t)/\gamma(t')$. The weighted forcing norm controls the source relative to the seed at its time of application, not merely at the final time. No monotonicity of $\gamma$ is needed for the bound.
e02.transverse.weight.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.wNorm: For a derivative $\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^j V$, the factor $\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j$ compensates the two different spatial scales. Division by $\gamma(t)$ then compares its magnitude with the seed at that time. Only spatial derivatives are taken in this norm, so no derivative of $\gamma$ is involved.

e02.transverse.equation.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.exist: At fixed $(a,s)$ this is an ordinary differential equation with coefficients depending on the parent trajectory and not on the unknown profiles at other labels. Solving it preserves the simultaneous translation $(a,s)\mapsto(a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)$ of the data. On $s=k_*\cdot a$ this gives an ordinary periodic field in $a$, including when $k_*$ is nonintegral.
e02.transverse.equation.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trans: The forward initial condition selects the velocity. The pressure slope is then fixed by requiring the velocity to remain in the moving plane $\kappa^\perp$, and the zero phase mean fixes the pressure primitive at each $(t,a)$. The zero phase mean of $V$ follows from the centered force and zero initial data. The result records these identities together with the support and symmetry properties needed in the hierarchy.
e02.transverse.equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.TransverseSolution: Centering is necessary: averaging (5.15) gives $\langle f\rangle_s=\partial_t\langle V\rangle_s+M\langle V\rangle_s$, since the pressure derivative integrates to zero. If $\langle V\rangle_s=0$, the force must have zero mean too. The normalized velocity and pressure are specified here; existence comes from the projected ODE.

e02.transverse.pressure-slope.TorusEuler.norm_sq_mul_oscillatoryPressu: Use $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ in the derivative of $\kappa\cdot V=0$. Then $0=-\kappa\cdot MV+\kappa\cdot(f-MV)-|\kappa|^2\partial_s\mathsf p$. The two identical strain terms account for the factor two in (5.16). The nonzero wave vector makes division by $|\kappa|^2$ legitimate.

e02.transverse.projected-ode.TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator_a: Write $P_\kappa$ for projection onto the normal line. If the force is entirely parallel to $\kappa$ and the velocity starts from zero, it produces only pressure, with $V=0$. For a general transverse velocity, however, the normal component of $V_t$ must be $P_\kappa MV$ because $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. This accounts for the factor two in $-(I-2P_\kappa)MV$ rather than the instantaneous projection $-(I-P_\kappa)MV$.

e02.transverse.zero-start-pressure.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trans: If $r=|\kappa|^{-2}\kappa\cdot(f-2MV)$, then $\int_0^1r\,ds=0$ by centering of $f,V$. The unique normalized pressure is $\mathsf p(s)=\int_0^s r(u)\,du-\int_0^1\int_0^w r(u)\,du\,dw$. Periodicity follows from the zero integral of $r$; the second term fixes the constant. No evolution equation or separate initial pressure is needed.
e02.transverse.zero-start-pressure.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.solve: Velocity is found by integrating in time with zero launch value.
