The first follows from uniform convergence on the entire closed slab. The second requires a lower bound for the central first derivative, followed by an order-one estimate on the tail restricted to each activation interval. The latter estimate cannot be replaced by the global supremum bound.
e03-s8-bounded-velocity.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_2: The estimate $\|u(t)\|_\infty\le\|U_0\|_{C_tL^\infty}+2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j^{-1}$ is independent of $t<T_\infty$. The factor two counts the localized oscillation and the sum of the mean and truncation correction; bounding each $U_j$ instead by its parent bound $\lambda_j$ in (T2) would not give a finite limit bound.
e03-s8-bounded-velocity.TorusEuler.Paper.Proposition82Conclusion: The first field of the conclusion record gives a single real bound $M$ for the spatial essential supremum at every time $0\le t<T_\infty$. It does not merely bound each smooth slice by a constant depending on that time. The uniform limit on the closed slab gives precisely this stronger bound.

e03-s8-central-curl.TorusEuler.paper_section_8_of_inductiveE: On $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$ the preceding cutoff has already become one. The new curl, in contrast, is multiplied by a cutoff that varies during this interval. One must avoid subtracting its magnitude in the lower bound for the sum. Projection onto the instantaneous direction of $\kappa_j$ kills the new leading curl for every value of the cutoff, while the preceding curl has a positive component in that direction by the wave-vector comparison.
e03-s8-central-curl.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalVelocityCurl: The central particle remains at $0$ by oddness. The limit concerns the length of the vorticity vector there at all sufficiently late times, not a limit of its direction or a sequence of large values at selected crossings. The projection direction used below varies with the new wave.
e03-s8-central-curl.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_8: In (8.2) the retained curl is at least $c\mu^{1/8}$, where $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$. Dividing the right side of (8.2) by $\mu^{1/8}$ gives at least $c-C\mu^{-3/32}-C\mu^{-1/8}$, since $\lambda_{j-2}^9\le\mu^{1/32}$. This stays positive for all sufficiently large $j$. The order-one tail estimate then transfers the bound to the limiting curl with a vanishing additional error.
e03-s8-central-curl.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_2: The lower bound (8.2) is first obtained for $U_j$. On $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, all later $O_\ell$ vanish, so the difference of the curls of $u$ and $U_j$ is bounded by $C\sum_{\ell>j}\lambda_\ell^{-1}$. This tends to zero while the lower bound for $U_j$ tends to infinity.
e03-s8-central-curl.TorusEuler.Paper.Proposition82Conclusion: The record retains the quantitative estimate for the actual limiting velocity: for $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$ it gives $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\ge c_1\mu^{1/8}-C_1\mu^{1/32}-C_1$ throughout $[t_j,t_{j+1})$, with constants independent of sufficiently large $j$. This exported estimate, rather than just the qualitative limit, is used for the time integral.

e03-s8-compact-bound.TorusEuler.terminalVelocityBound_of_exte: The continuous extension on $[0,T_\infty]\times\mathbb T^3$ has finite supremum by compactness. Agreement on the half-open slab gives the same bound for the Euler velocity. This argument uses continuity of velocity only, so it gives no bound on its curl.
e03-s8-compact-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S678b.closedSlab_ve: The order-zero estimate gives $\|w-U_n\|_{C_tL^\infty}\le4\lambda_{n+1}^{-1}$ on the closed slab. In particular the supremum of $w$ is bounded by that of a single finite approximation plus a finite tail. Proposition 8.1 identifies $u$ with $w$ for all earlier times, so the bound holds independently of how close the time is to $T_\infty$.

e03-s8-rank-one.TorusEuler.coordinateCurl_rankOne: For the linear field $v(x)=\mathbf a(\kappa\cdot x)$, the gradient is $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$ and $\operatorname{curl}v=\nabla(\kappa\cdot x)\times\mathbf a=\kappa\times\mathbf a$. This fixes the sign in (8.1); the reverse cross product would give the opposite surviving component.

e03-s8-projection-cancel.TorusEuler.inner_normalize_cross3_left: At activation the new wave vector is $\lambda_jE_3$ in the preceding frame. At subsequent times put $n_j(t)=\kappa_j(t,0)/|\kappa_j(t,0)|$. Since $n_j$ is parallel to the actual wave vector, its scalar product with the new leading curl $\widetilde\chi_j\kappa_j\times\mathbf a_j$ is zero independently of the cutoff and amplitude. Using the initial direction instead would not give this identity.

r2-s8-geometry-before-projection.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The frame is the moving frame of the preceding pair, not the fixed frame at launch. Put $\Theta=r(S_j-t_j)$. In the scaled coordinates (2.3) the window bounds give $|\zeta_1|\le\Theta^2$, $|\zeta_2|\le\Theta$, $1/2\le\zeta_3\le3/2$. Since the physical components of $\kappa_j/\lambda_j$ are $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2/S,\zeta_3)$, its norm is at most $3\Theta^2$ for $S,\Theta\ge1$. Thus the cosine with the preceding curl direction $E_3(t)$ is at least $1/(6\Theta^2)$ throughout the window. The bound $\Theta\le CL_{j+1}^4$ gives (8.1).
r2-s8-geometry-before-projection.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71Conclusions: In item 2 of Theorem 7.1 the rate is $r\le C\mu^{1/8}L_j$, where $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$, and the reserved time is $S_j-t_j=2\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^3$. Their product is at most $CL_jL_{j+1}^3\le CL_{j+1}^4$. The wave-vector length bound is quadratic in this normalized time, giving the $L_{j+1}^8$ loss in the projection. The frequency power $\mu^{1/8}$ cancels when computing the normalized window.

e03-s8-retained-strength.TorusEuler.preceding_strength_retained_o: Since $\mathbf a\perp\kappa$, the pressure term of the amplitude equation makes no contribution to $\partial_t\log|\mathbf a|$. Adding the two logarithmic length equations gives $\partial_t\log\sigma=-B_{11}-B_{22}=B_{33}$ in the moving frame, by incompressibility. Over this short interval the total change in $\log\sigma_{j-1}$ is bounded by $\mu^{1/32}\mu^{-1/16}=\mu^{-1/32}\le1$. Exponentiating yields $\sigma_{j-1}(t)\ge e^{-1}\sigma_{j-1}(t_j)$, the fraction retained in the formal lemma.

e03-s8-curl-lower.TorusEuler.norm_curlOfDerivative_ge_of_t: For $n_j=\kappa_j/|\kappa_j|$, write $D=\nabla U_{j-2}+E_{c,j-1}+E_{c,j}$. After projection, the two rank-one terms contribute just the signed component of the preceding curl. The bound $|n_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}D|\le C|D|$ gives $|\operatorname{curl}U_j|\ge c\mu^{1/8}-C(\lambda_{j-2}^9+2\mu^{-1/4})$. The first inequality uses the signed component as a lower bound for the norm; it imposes no condition on the magnitude of the new leading curl.

r2-s8-curl-tail.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S678b.proposition82: Fix $j$ and use Proposition 8.1 on the prefix ending at $t_{j+1}<T_\infty$. For every $\ell>j$ the oscillation $O_\ell$ vanishes on that prefix, and $q_\ell\ge1$. Thus (7.4) gives $\|\nabla(u-U_j)\|_{C_tL^\infty}\le2\lambda_{j+1}^{-1}$ there. Taking the curl costs only the norm of a fixed linear map. In this way the derivative estimate is uniform on the moving activation interval without requiring derivative convergence up to $T_\infty$.

e03-s8-full-limit.TorusEuler.terminalCurl_tendsto_atTop_of: Let $b_j$ be the interval lower bound for $|\operatorname{curl}U_j|$ and $e_j$ the uniform bound for the curl of $u-U_j$ there. Then $b_j-e_j\to\infty$. Given a target $M$, choose $J$ so $b_j-e_j\ge M$ for every $j\ge J$. The half-open intervals $[t_j,t_{j+1})$ cover $[t_J,T_\infty)$; their shared endpoints introduce no gaps. This gives the full one-sided limit, not merely a sequence of times of large vorticity.

e03-s8-maximal-and-integrals.TorusEuler.paper_section_8_of_inductiveE: To prove maximality it suffices that the central curl diverges; a smooth extension would give a bounded curl on a compact interval. The integral assertion requires a further argument, since pointwise blow-up alone can be integrable. The paper invokes periodic BKM, while the formal proof uses the duration of the intervals on which the quantitative curl bound holds.
e03-s8-maximal-and-integrals.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalTime: The integrands are evaluated at smooth times $t<T_\infty$: they are the spatial $L^\infty$ norms of curl and of the velocity gradient. For each such slice continuity makes the essential supremum equal to the ordinary supremum. The formal conclusion integrates these nonnegative norms over the half-open time interval, using the extended nonnegative integral to express divergence.
e03-s8-maximal-and-integrals.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.corollary_8_3: For a nonnegative function, even a limit to infinity at a finite endpoint does not imply an infinite integral. Here the additional information is the time spent at each vorticity scale: for $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$ the lower bound is $c\mu^{1/8}$ on an interval of length at least $cL_j\mu^{-1/8}$. The product grows like $L_j$, so the formal proof can bound the full integral below by the integral on a single sufficiently late interval. The upper bounds on the durations used to prove finite accumulation cannot serve this purpose.
e03-s8-maximal-and-integrals.TorusEuler.Paper.corollary_8_3: The rate is frozen at launch. With $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$, the upper strength bound in (7.3), not the lower one, gives $r\le C\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}L_j$. The crossing's normalized delay is at least $2L_j^2$, so division by the upper rate leaves $\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}(t_{j+1}-t_j)\ge cL_j$. This is the lower time weight paired with the vorticity estimate.
e03-s8-maximal-and-integrals.TorusEuler.Paper.Corollary83Conclusions: Maximality refers to smooth Euler solutions, not to the existence of a continuous velocity trace: the trace at $T_\infty$ has already been constructed. The record rules out a smooth extension of this solution, and identifies the real lifespan of any other maximal solution with the same initial datum by uniqueness. It also records the two integrals separately as extended nonnegative integrals equal to infinity.

e03-s8-maximality-proof.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution.isMaximal_of_: Suppose a smooth extension exists beyond $T_\infty$. Its curl at the origin is continuous on the compact interval $[0,T_\infty]$ and hence bounded. On the earlier interval this curl agrees with that of $u$, which diverges by Proposition 8.2. Thus extension is impossible, independently of a continuation criterion.
e03-s8-maximality-proof.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.corollary_8_3: Existence on all earlier intervals was proved in Proposition 8.1; the blow-up of the central curl now excludes continuation through their supremum. This identifies the maximal time for the constructed solution. Uniqueness also identifies any other finite maximal lifespan from the same datum; the time-integral assertions use the separate quantitative bounds.

e03-s8-bkm-boundary.TorusEuler.theorem11_of_continuation_and: Both $(T-t)^{-1/2}$ and $(T-t)^{-1}$ tend to infinity, but only the second has a divergent time integral. An instantaneous curl blow-up leaves a time integral to justify. The continuation statement needed from BKM is that a smooth periodic solution on a finite interval $[0,T)$ with finite $\int_0^T\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_\infty\,dt$ has a smooth extension through $T$. The contrapositive applies once $T_*=T_\infty$ is known. The linked result assumes this continuation property; the checked corollary instead obtains the divergence from the activation estimates.
e03-s8-bkm-boundary.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.corollary_8_3: The paper uses BKM to infer divergence of the spatial supremum integral from maximality. The linked proof instead integrates the interval estimate from Proposition 8.2, using the lower bound on the crossing delay. That argument uses the vorticity at the origin itself; hence it gives the stronger central-particle integral as well (although the formal corollary records the spatial supremum integral).

e03-s8-gradient-integral.TorusEuler.gradientIntegral_eq_top_of_cu: For each smooth slice, $|\operatorname{curl}u(x)|\le C|\nabla u(x)|$, since curl is a fixed linear map on gradient matrices. The same inequality holds for their spatial suprema. Integrating shows that a finite gradient integral would give a finite curl integral, contrary to the preceding conclusion.

e03-s8-curl-gradient.TorusEuler.torusLInf_curl_le: For a gradient matrix $D$ with operator norm $|D|$, each difference $D_{ik}-D_{ki}$ has absolute value at most $2|D|$. Consequently $|\operatorname{curl}v|\le2\sqrt3|\nabla v|$. The formal inequality uses the operator norm of the linear curl map itself; either constant is independent of the time slice and survives taking the essential supremum.

e03-s8-off-origin.TorusEuler.paper_section_8_of_inductiveE: Spatial localization is enough for the velocity trace, but the pressure at a point away from the origin still depends on the flow near the origin. Proposition 8.4 uses local convergence of velocity derivatives for the nearby contribution and global order-zero convergence of the velocity tensor for the distant contribution. Neither requires a derivative estimate through the singular point.
e03-s8-off-origin.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalOffOrigin: The velocity traces on different compact sets are restrictions of the same globally continuous $w(T_\infty)$. The time-derivative traces agree on overlaps by uniqueness of their order-zero limits. Thus the conclusion gives well-defined spatial fields on the punctured torus for velocity and its first time derivative, but not a limit of every time derivative. The latter needs the extra estimates in the auxiliary note.
e03-s8-off-origin.TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits: In the periodic lift the punctured domain is $\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$. For each compact $K$ in this domain and fixed $m$, the definition supplies an open neighborhood of $K$ still avoiding the lattice and a $C^m$ field there. The ambient derivatives of the time slices of orders $0$ through $m$ converge uniformly on $K$ to the corresponding derivatives of that field. The neighborhood is needed to make sense of derivatives even when $K$ has empty interior.
e03-s8-off-origin.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_8: For velocity derivatives, the compact set eventually misses the entire late oscillatory support. For $\partial_tu$, it is not enough to discard that region: the nonlocal pressure still receives its contribution. The near part of the tensor $u\otimes u$ is controlled in a high spatial norm, and the far part only in $L^1$. The separation of the far source from the observation set permits all derivatives there to fall on the kernel rather than on the velocity.
e03-s8-off-origin.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_4: For the near tensor $\chi u\otimes u$, take spatial convergence through order $m+2$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}\chi$. Leibniz' rule and the extra derivative bound give convergence through order $m+1$ with half-Hölder seminorms on the torus; the product vanishes near the excluded point. Since $\mathbb P\operatorname{div}$ loses one spatial derivative in these norms, the near term converges through order $m$ on $K$. The cutoff is fixed in time, so its derivatives introduce no singular factor.
e03-s8-off-origin.TorusEuler.Paper.Proposition84Conclusion: The two limits also give a left time derivative of the terminal trace on every compact away from zero. Indeed, writing $g=\lim_{s\uparrow T_\infty}\partial_su(s)$ in $C^m(K)$, one has $(w(T_\infty)-u(t))/(T_\infty-t)=(T_\infty-t)^{-1}\int_t^{T_\infty}\partial_su(s)\,ds\to g$ in that norm. Proposition 8.4 itself asserts the two spatial traces; this calculation requires no higher time derivative.

r5-term-oscillation-support.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71Conclusions: The oscillation $O_j$ is the evaluated profile before Fourier truncation. The parent flow fixes zero and takes its label support of radius $2\ell_*$ into a ball of radius at most $2\mathsf D\ell_*\le2\mathsf D^{-2}\le\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$. Fourier truncation itself does not preserve spatial support; the nonlocal difference $v_{\Lambda_j}$ is included with the mean in the second bound of (7.4).

e03-s8-shrinking-support.TorusEuler.inductive_oscillations_eventu: Put $d=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T^3}(K,0)>0$. For late $j$, the ball of radius $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}<d/2$ misses the open $d/2$ neighborhood of $K$, uniformly in time. On that neighborhood the entire increment equals $U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j$. This is why one can apply (7.4) to its derivatives there even though the Fourier-truncated increment is not itself supported in the ball.
e03-s8-shrinking-support.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.proposition_8_4_o: If $d=\operatorname{dist}(K,0)>0$, first enlarge $K$ to a compact neighborhood avoiding the ball of radius $d/2$. For all sufficiently large $j$ the support of $O_j$ lies in that ball and $q_j\ge m$. The tail of the velocity sequence is then bounded by $2\lambda_{n+1}^{-1}$ in $C_tC^m(K)$ for large $n$, because every derivative of the late oscillations vanishes in a neighborhood of $K$. The time supremum includes $T_\infty$.

r2-s8-velocity-trace.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.proposition_8_4_o: Fix a large $n$ so the local tail beyond $U_n$ is small uniformly on the closed slab. Then $\|w(t)-w(T_\infty)\|_{C^m(K)}\le4\lambda_{n+1}^{-1}+\|U_n(t)-U_n(T_\infty)\|_{C^m(K)}$. The last term tends to zero since $U_n$ is smooth past $T_\infty$. Taking $n$ arbitrarily large proves the trace for $w$, hence for $u=w$ at earlier times. This uses no convergence of time derivatives of $U_j$.

e03-s8-cutoff.TorusEuler.exists_periodic_offOrigin_cut: Choose nested neighborhoods of $K$ whose closures miss the origin, and a periodic smooth cutoff equal to one on the smaller and supported in the larger. This ensures two positive separations: the support of $\chi$ from zero, where the velocity derivatives may diverge, and the support of $1-\chi$ from $K$, where the pressure kernel would otherwise be singular.

e03-s8-far-kernel.TorusEuler.exists_norm_iteratedFDeriv_pe: For $B=(1-\chi)A$, the local term $\operatorname{div}B$ vanishes near $K$. Writing the nonlocal part as $-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\partial_i\partial_k B_{ik}$, its component $\ell$ has kernel $-\partial_\ell\partial_i\partial_kG(x-y)$ for the periodic Green function $G$ of $\Delta$. An additional $d$ derivatives in $x$ cost derivatives of $G$ of order $d+3$, all bounded on the separated source and observation sets. The linked inequality estimates the difference of two far pressure gradients on a neighborhood of $K$ by the $L^1$ norm of their tensor difference; it requires no spatial derivatives of the sources.

r2-s8-time-pressure.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.proposition_8_4_o: Write $u_*=w(T_\infty)$. The uniform velocity bound gives $\|u(t)\otimes u(t)-u_*\otimes u_*\|_{L^1}\le(\|u(t)\|_\infty+\|u_*\|_\infty)\|u(t)-u_*\|_\infty$ on the unit torus. Multiplication by $1-\chi$ preserves this convergence. The separated-kernel bound then gives the far pressure limit in every fixed spatial order on $K$, even though $u_*$ need not have a bounded gradient near zero.

r2-s8-main-assembly.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_1_1_of: The construction supplies one smooth datum and one exact solution before $T_\infty$ by Proposition 8.1. Proposition 8.2 supplies bounded velocity and the divergent central curl; Corollary 8.3 identifies $T_\infty$ as its maximal time and proves the integral assertions. Proposition 8.4 gives the two local spatial traces at that time. No additional choice of a limiting solution is needed to combine the results.

e03-appa-time-norm.TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm: The time supremum is outside the spatial Hölder norm. In the intermediate space $C_a^{0,1/2}(L_t^2)$ the quotient between labels is instead $\|v(\cdot,a)-v(\cdot,b)\|_{L_t^2}/d(a,b)^{1/2}$. For $v(t,a)=h(t)w(a)$, the two norms are proportional to $\|h\|_\infty$ and $\|h\|_2$ respectively. Even with $\int_Ih=0$ the latter does not control $h(0)$, so the second inversion in §A.2 is needed to recover the initial velocity.

e03-r2-appa-dimensional-constants.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: The degree must be absolute, not chosen anew for each parent. In §5.3 the coefficient size $Q$ is at most a fixed power of the parent number $\mathsf D$, so a bound $CQ^p$ is at most $\mathsf D^{C'}$ for an absolute $C'$. This is the quantitative estimate needed before choosing the frequency of the next wave. An inverse bound exponential in $Q$ would not suffice for this power estimate.
e03-r2-appa-dimensional-constants.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_A_2: In the mixed application the spatial Fourier transform is still three-dimensional; a coefficient is now a whole path in $L^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$. The time projection has norm one and is independent of spatial frequency. The angular estimates and the kernel integrals below are therefore uniform for this infinite-dimensional coefficient space as well as for $\mathbb R^3$.

e03-r2-appa-symmetry.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: For the parent flow these symmetries follow from $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Skew-symmetry gives $\Omega w\cdot w=0$, but not $\Omega z_t\cdot z=0$. In the path problem the latter term represents the effect of the pulled-back vorticity on a displacement, and must be included in (A.2).

e03-appa-coefficient-regularity.TorusEuler.EndpointCoefficientC1Bound: The base-order proof uses a uniform spatial Lipschitz constant and continuity in time in $C_a^{0,1/2}$. `EndpointCoefficientC1Bound` records the latter continuity and the bounds $C_0,C_1$ for the coefficient and its first derivative on the periodic lift. In particular $\operatorname{Lip}K(t)\le2C_1$ and $\|K(t)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le C_0+2C_1$ on the torus.
e03-appa-coefficient-regularity.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: Freezing needs the estimate $\|B(a)-B(b)\|_{\mathcal L(H)}\le C d(a,b)$ for $B=K-J\Omega$; recovery at each time needs $t\mapsto\mathbb P K(t)$ continuous as a bounded operator on the solenoidal half-Hölder space. The numbered Lean statement uses these consequences of the printed $C_tC^{1,1/2}_a$ assumption, with uniform first derivative bounds and continuity in the weaker label norm.

e03-appa-primitive.TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive: Integration in $J$ keeps the label fixed. Thus $z=Jv$ gives $z(0)=0$ without a further integration constant, and its other trace is $z(1,a)=\int_0^1v(t,a)\,dt$. The space in which we solve for $v$ consists of paths with this integral zero; it does not require $v$ itself to vanish at either end.

e03-appa-ellipticity-and-energy.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: The second lower bound rules out a genuine obstruction. Take $K=I$, $\Omega=2\pi R$, where $R(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0)$, and the spatially constant velocity $v(t)=(-\sin 2\pi t,\cos 2\pi t,0)$. Then $v_t=\Omega v$ and $\int_0^1v=0$. Consequently $Kv-J(\Omega v)=v(0)$, so the homogeneous integrated problem with $L=0$ has a nonzero solution with both displacement traces zero. The first lower bound holds, but (A.2) fails. Skew-symmetry alone cannot exclude this closed displacement path.
e03-appa-ellipticity-and-energy.TorusEuler.EndpointSobolevEnergyBound: A displacement that starts and ends at zero has a velocity with zero time integral. Integrating any zero-mean velocity from the left endpoint gives a displacement that returns to zero. The correspondence $w=z_t$, $z=Jw$ identifies $H^1_0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ with the closed subspace $\{w\in L^2(I;\mathbb R^3):\int_Iw=0\}$. In these variables (A.2) is a lower bound on $\int_I(Kw\cdot w+\Omega w\cdot Jw)\,dt$. It can be applied to each label path separately, before imposing spatial incompressibility.
e03-appa-ellipticity-and-energy.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: To apply these inequalities to (4.9), write $Z(\tau)=T^{-1}z(T\tau)$. Then $Z_\tau=z_t(T\tau)$ and $Z$ has both traces zero. Changing variables in the label energy and dividing by $T$ gives precisely the form (A.2) with $K(T\tau)$ and $T\Omega(T\tau)$. By (4.6)–(4.7) one may take $\mu=[2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2]^{-1}$; (A.1) holds with $\kappa=D_-^{-2}$. There is no inverse power of the slab length in either constant.

e03-r2-appa-size-parameter.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: The reciprocals in $Q$ measure the costs of the two coercive inversions; the coefficient norms also control the spatial error of freezing. For the base bound Lean replaces $\|K\|_1+\|\Omega\|_1$ by $K_0+K_1+\Omega_0+\Omega_1$, the uniform bounds on the coefficients and their first label derivatives. The half-Hölder seminorms of those derivatives are not needed for (A.3).

e03-appa-forcing-continuity.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: Only $\mathbb P\mathcal QL$ determines the velocity. For example replacing $L$ by $L+\ell(a)$ leaves $v,z$ unchanged and changes $c$ by $\mathbb P\ell$ and $\nabla_a\phi$ by $(I-\mathbb P)\ell$. Adding a periodic gradient depending on both $t$ and $a$ is absorbed entirely into the gradient on the right. Thus there is no compatibility condition on $L$ beyond its stated regularity.
e03-appa-forcing-continuity.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: On the normalized interval the inclusion $C_tC_a^{0,1/2}\hookrightarrow C_a^{0,1/2}(L_t^2)$ has norm at most one: apply $\|h\|_{L_t^2}\le\sup_t|h(t)|$ to the values and to each difference of label paths. Continuity of $L(t)$ in the stronger norm is used when the right-hand side of (A.9) is formed.

e03-appa-a1-existence-uniqueness.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: For $K=I$ and $\Omega=0$, the projected equation gives $v(t)=c-\mathbb PL(t)$ and the terminal constraint gives $c=\int_0^1\mathbb PL(t)\,dt$. For instance $L=-tf$ with solenoidal, time-independent $f$ gives $v=(t-1/2)f$ and $z=\tfrac12(t^2-t)f$. Thus $v(0)=-f/2$ and $v(1)=f/2$, while $z$ vanishes at both ends. The endpoint condition selects the velocity rather than prescribing either of its endpoint values.
e03-appa-a1-existence-uniqueness.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: For another simple case take $K=k(t)I$, $k(t)>0$, and $\Omega=0$. Then $v=k(t)^{-1}(c-\mathbb PL(t))$, and $\int_0^1v\,dt=0$ gives $c=(\int_0^1k^{-1}\,dt)^{-1}\int_0^1 k^{-1}\mathbb PL\,dt$. In general $c$ cannot be obtained just by averaging $L$. Its dependence on the coefficients is accounted for by solving the projected equation before recovering the constant.
e03-appa-a1-existence-uniqueness.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_A_1: The solution class gives $z(t)=\int_0^t v(s)\,ds$ as an integral in the spatial Hölder space, with $v$ continuous up to both endpoints. In particular $v(0)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}z(h)/h$ in that norm. The initial correction is therefore well defined, unlike the value at zero of a mere $L_t^2$ representative.

e03-appa-a1-equation-and-traces.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: The condition $\operatorname{div}z=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}v=0$ by differentiating in time (in distributions in $a$). Conversely integration of a solenoidal $v$ preserves divergence freedom. Thus the two endpoint conditions and divergence condition can be imposed together as $\mathbb P\mathcal Qv=v$ before solving for the pressure.
e03-appa-a1-equation-and-traces.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution: Write $G=Kv-J(\Omega v)+L$. The two discarded components of $G$ have different roles: $(I-\mathbb P)G$ is a periodic gradient at each time, while $\mathbb PG$ is the same solenoidal field $c$ at every time. `PaperMeanIntegratedSolution` retains only the latter identity and the endpoint constraint. The gradient is recovered from the former component, after the solve.
e03-appa-a1-equation-and-traces.TorusEuler.paperMeanIntegratedMomentum: The quantity in `paperMeanIntegratedMomentum` is $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L$. Its solenoidal part is constant in time; its gradient part need not be. For a force source $L=-Jg$, the label pressure in the differential equation is $\mathsf q=-\phi_t$, not $\phi$ itself: differentiation removes the integration constant and gives $Kv_t+(K_t-\Omega)v+\nabla_a\mathsf q=g$.
e03-appa-a1-equation-and-traces.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: At $t=0$ the primitive vanishes, so $c=\mathbb P(K(0)v(0)+L(0))$. For the parent flow $X(0,a)=a$, $K(0)=I$ and the force source has $L(0)=0$; hence $c=v(0)=b(0)$, and $\nabla_a\phi(0)=0$. For the general source of Theorem A.1 the integration constant need not equal the initial velocity.
e03-appa-a1-equation-and-traces.TorusEuler.Paper.EndpointSystemSolution: `EndpointSystemSolution` includes the derivative relation, both zero traces and the equation at every time, with $z,v,c$ in the solenoidal space. The field $G=\nabla\phi$ is specified by a periodic potential at each time and is continuous in $C^{0,1/2}$. These are the conditions defining a solution; existence and uniqueness are the content of Theorem A.1.

e03-appa-a1-polynomial-estimate.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: The concrete proof can take $p=291$. The mixed inverse first gives a factor $Q^{145}$ in the path norm. Recovering $c$ and $J(\Omega v)$ costs at most one further factor $Q$ from the coefficients. The fixed-time inverse then costs another $Q^{145}$, giving $145+1+145=291$. These powers are sufficient bounds, not sharp ones.
e03-appa-a1-polynomial-estimate.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: For the higher-order mean estimates it is essential that (A.3) has no source derivative. For example the source for $\partial_i v$ is $\partial_iL+(\partial_i K)v-J((\partial_i\Omega)v)$. Multiplying its estimate by $\ell_*$, the commutator contribution has coefficient at most $CA\ell_*(|K|_{1,1/2}+|\Omega|_{1,1/2})\le C$, by (5.13). At order $m$ the same cancellation holds for every positive-order coefficient derivative with its factor $\ell_*^j$. The base inverse cost $A\le\mathsf D^C$ is thus not raised to a new power at each derivative order in (5.14).

e03-appa-a1-smooth-conclusion.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: The smooth-data clause gives regularity of the same solution selected by the endpoint conditions. First all label derivatives of $v$ are controlled as time paths; the instantaneous equation then gives them continuously in time, and its time derivatives give the remaining regularity. In §4.3 this permits differentiating the integrated momentum to recover the linearized Euler equation.
e03-appa-a1-smooth-conclusion.TorusEuler.exists_paperA1_smoothSolution: The assertion of `exists_paperA1_smoothSolution` is joint smoothness of the velocity in the projected solution, on the closed time slab. This is the field from which $z$ and $\nabla\phi$ are subsequently formed. The regularity of the latter fields is not a separate solvability problem.
e03-appa-a1-smooth-conclusion.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: For the parent flow $F_t=MF$, so $K_t-\Omega=2F^TMF=2F^TF_t$. With $L_t=-g$, differentiation of (4.9) gives (4.11) on taking $\mathsf q=-\phi_t$. Multiplication by $F^{-T}$ sends the label gradient to the physical pressure gradient along $X$, and the Piola identity transfers $\operatorname{div}_a v=0$ to $\operatorname{div}_x b=0$. Lean instead differentiates the projected equation and recovers the zero-mean pressure as a potential of the negative differentiated residual; it does not need to identify a particular $\phi_t$.

e03-appa-displacement-recovery.TorusEuler.paperA1_displacement_eq_primi: Integrating the velocity from zero imposes the initial trace identically. The remaining condition is $\int_0^1v(t,a)\,dt=0$ for each $a$, which is imposed on the domain of the inverse. Once $v$ is known, neither the displacement nor its initial trace introduces another unknown.

e03-appa-subtract-time-mean.TorusEuler.endpointSubtractMean: On an interval of length $T>0$, $\mathcal Qv=v-T^{-1}\int_0^Tv\,dt$, with the integral regarded as a path constant in time. Here $T=1$. Its fixed space consists of the velocities for which $Jv(1)=0$; its kernel consists of the time-independent paths. Thus the terminal constraint and the elimination of $c$ use the same projection.

e03-appa-remove-pressure-gradient.TorusEuler.paperMean_projection_C1_gradi: The gradient in the integrated equation is in the label variable $a$. A periodic gradient has Fourier coefficients parallel to $n$ at nonzero frequencies and has zero constant coefficient. Thus $\mathbb P$ kills it even though $\mathbb P$ retains spatially constant vector fields.

e03-appa-projections-commute.TorusEuler.endpointJointSpatialProjectio: Since $\mathbb P$ is independent of time it commutes with the time integral and hence with $\mathcal Q$. The product $\mathcal R$ is an orthogonal projection in the joint $L^2$ space. This gives $\langle\mathcal R Bv,v\rangle=\langle Bv,v\rangle$ for $v=\mathcal Rv$, without requiring either $K$ or $J\Omega$ to preserve the range.

e03-appa-compressed-equation.TorusEuler.endpointMixedPathCoefficient: At a fixed label $a$, $B(a)$ sends a path $w$ to $K(\cdot,a)w-J(\Omega(\cdot,a)w)$. The time dependence is retained in the coefficient even when $a$ is frozen. Neither term need have zero time mean when $w$ does; for example $\int_I k(t)w(t)\,dt$ need not vanish for a scalar coefficient $K=k(t)I$. It is the compressed operator $\mathcal R B$ on the fixed space that is inverted.

e03-appa-primitive-adjoint.TorusEuler.endpointPrimitiveLp_inner_eq_: In Lean the primitive identity before imposing the terminal condition is $\langle Ju,w\rangle+\langle u,Jw\rangle=J u(1)\cdot J w(1)$. It follows by integrating $(Ju\cdot Jw)'$ and uses only square-integrable paths. Taking $Jw(1)=0$ gives the adjoint formula in the paper, without assuming that $Ju(1)=0$; in this application $u=\Omega w$.

e03-appa-energy-identity.TorusEuler.endpointMixedPathCoefficient_: Since $(Jw)_t=w$, integration by parts gives $\int_I J(\Omega w)\cdot w=[J(\Omega w)\cdot Jw]_0^1-\int_I\Omega w\cdot Jw=-\int_I\Omega w\cdot Jw$. The boundary term vanishes because $Jw(0)=Jw(1)=0$, even though $J(\Omega w)(1)$ need not vanish. This recovers the plus sign of the second term in (A.2).
e03-appa-energy-identity.TorusEuler.EndpointSobolevEnergyBound: The hypothesis is imposed at a fixed label on every $L_t^2$ path of zero mean. There is no spatial divergence condition on an individual path at a label. This allows (A.2) to be used after freezing $a$ on each Fourier fiber, and also before freezing, by integrating the same inequality over labels.

r5-B-two-projected-inversions.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_A_2: The two applications of Lemma A.2 have different ranges. With $H=L^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ the projection is $\mathbb P\mathcal Q$ and the lower bound is (A.2); this solves for all times with the terminal constraint. With $H=\mathbb R^3$ the projection is $\mathbb P$ and the lower bound is (A.1); this solves for a solenoidal field at each time. The second inversion is made with the source recovered from the first, not with a fresh choice of endpoint data.

r5-B-frozen-fourier-coefficients.TorusEuler.complexifiedHalfHolderFourier: A constant operator $B_0$ passes through the Fourier integral in $a$, so $\widehat{\mathcal RB_0v}(n)=r(n)B_0\widehat v(n)$. If $B$ varies in labels, the product $Bv$ instead couples spatial Fourier modes. Freezing avoids this coupling and leaves the entire time dependence inside each coefficient in $H$.

e03-r2-appa-two-hilbert-spaces.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_A_2: With $H=\mathbb R^3$, the Hölder quotient measures the difference of two vectors. With $H=L^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ it measures the $L_t^2$ distance between two paths at distinct labels. In both cases the projection acts by a fixed Fourier symbol in $a$, which makes the same spatial kernel proof possible.
e03-r2-appa-two-hilbert-spaces.TorusEuler.endpointSubtractMean: The mean source in §5.5.1 is an average in the fast phase $s$, still depending on $t,a$. It determines a phase-independent field $B_p$ by the endpoint inverse. The projection $\mathcal Q$ here is a different operation, in physical time at fixed label: it imposes $\int_0^T(D_aX)^{-1}B_p\,dt=0$. The transverse correction instead solves a forward equation from zero initial data.

e03-r2-appa-coefficient-hypothesis.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_A_2: For the mixed coefficient, multiplication by $K(t,a)-K(t,b)$ has norm on $L_t^2$ at most $\sup_t|K(t,a)-K(t,b)|$. The primitive applied to $(\Omega(t,a)-\Omega(t,b))w$ costs at most one further factor $T$. Thus the uniform Lipschitz bounds of the time-dependent matrices give a spatial operator Lipschitz bound without differentiating a time path.

e03-appa-a2-coercivity.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder: The fixed-time application only assumes a lower bound on $w\cdot K(t,a)w$, which gives the same lower bound on $n^\perp$ for every spatial frequency. More generally, the symmetric part of a real nonsymmetric matrix is what enters (A.4). This is why the spatial version of Lemma A.2 does not need symmetry as a separate hypothesis.
e03-appa-a2-coercivity.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder: In the mixed problem all test paths in the range of the Fourier symbol have zero time mean, including the spatial zero mode. Thus the lower bound (A.4) need not hold on the constant-in-time paths. The term $I-r(n)$ in the extension below gives a positive quadratic form on precisely the directions that have been excluded.
e03-appa-a2-coercivity.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_A_2: The same $\mu$ works at every label. Freezing $B$ at any $a_0$ therefore preserves the lower bound on $r(n)H$, regardless of the direction $n$. For variable coefficients it also gives the integrated energy inequality for $v=\mathcal Rv$, since the projection can be removed when paired with a vector in its range.

e03-appa-a2-base-isomorphism.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder:
For a constant positive definite matrix $B$, a projected datum $\widehat f(n)\in n^\perp$ at $n\ne0$ requires $B\widehat v=\widehat f+\alpha n$. Imposing $n\cdot\widehat v=0$ gives

$\widehat v=B^{-1}\widehat f-B^{-1}n\frac{n\cdot B^{-1}\widehat f}{n\cdot B^{-1}n}$.

The denominator is positive and the second term enforces incompressibility. This is the inverse of the compressed operator on the Fourier mode, not the compression of $B^{-1}$. The variable-coefficient problem requires the estimate of Lemma A.2 because the spatial modes no longer separate.
e03-appa-a2-base-isomorphism.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder: On the mixed fixed space, the inverse takes a source with both projected constraints to a velocity with the same constraints. The source $-\mathbb P\mathcal QL$ already lies in that space for every admissible $L$. Hence there is no additional compatibility condition on the unprojected $L$; the two parts removed by projection are accounted for by $c$ and $\nabla\phi$.
e03-appa-a2-base-isomorphism.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_A_2: If $f$ is a general Hölder field, one solves $\mathcal RBv=\mathcal Rf$ with $v=\mathcal Rv$. Solving $\mathcal RBv=f$ requires $f$ to be in that range already. The formal conclusion uses a bounded linear equivalence on the fixed space of the projection, with a Lipschitz coefficient in both cases.
e03-appa-a2-base-isomorphism.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_A_2: By (A.5), $\mathcal RBv=0$ implies $v=0$. The range is also closed, since the estimate makes preimages of a Cauchy sequence of outputs Cauchy in the projected Hölder space. To prove that all projected data lie in the range, the paper starts with $B=I$, where this is true, and preserves surjectivity by continuation. `Paper.lemma_A_2` supplies the proved isomorphism in both the spatial and the path-valued cases.
e03-appa-a2-base-isomorphism.TorusEuler.Paper.FreezingConclusion: The equivalence in `FreezingConclusion` has forward map $e(v)=\mathcal R(Bv)$ on the fixed space. The definition also imposes the inverse estimate and preservation of every admissible higher Hölder class. These are the conclusions of the lemma, not hypotheses that one already has an inverse.

e03-appa-a2-base-bound.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder: With $B=K(t)$ and $\mu=D_-^{-2}$, the cost in (A.5) comes from the inverse deformation and the size and spatial variation of the metric $F^TF$. The concrete spatial theorem bounds the inverse by a degree-$145$ polynomial in these quantities. There is no derivative of the source in this estimate; the differentiated force in (4.11) is used for a different purpose, namely recovery of the physical equation.
e03-appa-a2-base-bound.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder: The same exponent $145$ works in the mixed and spatial cases. For the path coefficient $B=K-J\Omega$, integration on a slab of length $T$ has $L_t^2$ operator norm at most $T/\sqrt2$. Thus the coefficient size and its spatial Lipschitz bound are controlled by those of $K$ plus $T$ times those of $\Omega$. For $T\le1$ this introduces no new large parameter. The concrete mixed inverse is uniform over positive $T$ once the operator and coercivity bounds have been given.
e03-appa-a2-base-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_A_2: The bound depends on the reciprocal of the lower quadratic-form bound and the size and spatial variation of $B$. The Lipschitz version replaces $\|B\|_{C^1}$ by $\|B\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}B$. It is important that the source needs only the half-Hölder norm: no derivative of it is spent in (A.5).
e03-appa-a2-base-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.FreezingConclusion: The norm on the right of (A.5) is the norm of the projected output, not of $Bv$. Taking $v=e^{-1}f$ in the estimate defining `FreezingConclusion` gives a bound for $\|e^{-1}f\|$ in terms of $\|f\|$ for projected $f$. This matters when the equation contains an unknown gradient or time-independent field, since neither needs to be estimated before solving for $v$.

e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder_r: The higher-space inverse is a restriction of the base inverse, rather than a new choice of solution. If $f$ has higher regularity, a higher-space preimage solves the same equation in $C^{0,1/2}$, so injectivity identifies it with the base preimage. This is the reason the velocity obtained in §A.2 at each spatial order agrees with the first velocity path.
e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder_res: Higher label regularity here means derivatives of the path-valued field $a\mapsto v(\cdot,a)$ in $L_t^2$. The integral of each such derivative is zero since the time integral is a bounded linear map on $L_t^2$ and commutes with label differentiation. Higher regularity thus preserves the endpoint constraint, but still does not define a time trace of the velocity.
e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder_b: At order one the differentiated equation is $\mathbb P(B\partial_i v)=\partial_i f-\mathbb P((\partial_iB)v)$. A base inverse bound $M_0$ gives $\|\partial_i v\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le M_0\|\partial_i f\|_{C^{0,1/2}}+CM_0^2\|\partial_iB\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\|f\|_{C^{0,1/2}}$. Without a smallness bound on derivatives of $B$, repeated differentiation may give a new power of $M_0$ at each order. The stronger scaled conclusion of Proposition 5.2 uses (5.13) to avoid precisely this loss.
e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder_bou: For example, if $B=K-J\Omega$, then $(\partial_i B)v=(\partial_i K)v-J((\partial_i\Omega)v)$: differentiation in labels commutes with $J$. Thus the equation for each spatial derivative has a source in the same $L_t^2$-valued Hölder class. Higher spatial regularity is obtained without needing a time derivative of $v$.
e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder_b: The forward map requires a separate, simpler estimate: use the product rule in $C^{k,1/2}$ for $Bv$, then boundedness of the spatial Leray projection in that class. No coercivity is needed for this direction. The inverse bound, in contrast, uses the differentiated equations and the base inverse.
e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder_bou:
For a coordinate word $
u$, $\partial^
u(\mathbb P\mathcal Q(Bv))=\mathbb P\mathcal Q\partial^
u(Bv)$. The time projection is a contraction on each $L_t^2$ path and the spatial projection is bounded on the Hilbert-valued half-Hölder space. Applying the product rule gives a bound by the product of the higher norms of $B$ and $v$. This forward estimate uses no lower bound for the form of $B$.
e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_A_2: The higher-order conclusion can be read as $v\in C^{k,1/2}$ if and only if $\mathcal RBv\in C^{k,1/2}$, under the stated regularity of $B$. In the forward direction use the product rule. In the reverse direction use the higher inverse and uniqueness of the base solution. The higher constants are not required to be the base constant in (A.5).
e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.Paper.FreezingConclusion: In the higher-order clause of `FreezingConclusion` the map is the same equivalence $e$ as in (A.5), with $v$ of higher regularity exactly when $ev$ has higher regularity. Bounds for both $\|ev\|_{C^{k,1/2}}$ and $\|v\|_{C^{k,1/2}}$ give continuity in the higher norm. This is how the formal statement expresses an isomorphism in that norm.
e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.freezingConclu: `freezingConclusion_higher` assembles the higher-space estimates once a base equivalence and the higher-space preimages are known. If $ev$ has higher regularity, the preimage hypothesis gives a higher-regularity $w$ with $ew=ev$; injectivity gives $w=v$. This proves the reverse regularity implication in the conclusion. Existence of those preimages is supplied separately.

c8-holder-coercive-testing.TorusEuler.endpointSpatialWeakErrorEstim: Orthogonality gives $\langle\mathcal R(Bv),v\rangle=\langle Bv,\mathcal Rv\rangle=\langle Bv,v\rangle$. After integrating (A.4) over labels and applying Cauchy–Schwarz one obtains $\|v\|_{L_a^2(H)}\le\mu^{-1}\|f\|_{L_a^2(H)}$. The formal weak error estimate uses the harmless weaker bound with $\min(1,\mu)^{-1}$. This is the energy estimate that will close the Hölder estimate after interpolation.

e03-appa-leray-symbol.TorusEuler.angularLeray: For $n\ne0$, the condition $\operatorname{div}_a v=0$ reads $n\cdot\widehat v(n)=0$. Its projection is $P_n=I-n\otimes n/|n|^2$. In the mixed problem $r(n)=P_n\mathcal Q$; since $P_n$ is independent of time it commutes with the time average. The symbol is homogeneous of degree zero away from the origin.

e03-appa-zero-symbol.TorusEuler.angularLeray_zero: At $n=0$ the spatial divergence condition is automatic, so the spatial Leray symbol fixes constant vectors. In the path problem the full symbol is then $\mathcal Q$: it fixes spatially constant paths of zero time mean, not all spatially constant paths. This mode is handled directly rather than by the annular multiplier estimate.

e03-appa-frozen-symbol.TorusEuler.frozenSymbol: The extension is block diagonal for $H=r(n)H\oplus\ker r(n)$, with first block $r(n)B_0|_{r(n)H}$ and second block $I$. Thus $A_0(n)^{-1}$ preserves the range of $r(n)$, where it inverts the desired compressed operator. In general $A_0(n)^{-1}$ on that range is not $r(n)B_0^{-1}r(n)$: even for $B_0=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and projection onto the first coordinate these two scalar inverses are $1/2$ and $2/3$.

e03-appa-identity-on-complement.TorusEuler.frozenSymbol_apply_of_proj_eq: For $rw=0$ one has $rB_0rw=0$ and $(I-r)w=w$. This accounts for the identity on the orthogonal complement even if $B_0$ has no positivity there. Only the compressed coefficient on the range of $r$ enters the lower bound.

e03-appa-full-symbol-coercivity.TorusEuler.frozenSymbol_coercive: The cross terms between the two orthogonal blocks vanish. Hence $\operatorname{Re}\langle A_0w,w\rangle=\operatorname{Re}\langle B_0rw,rw\rangle+\|(I-r)w\|^2$. Coercivity of $B_0$ is needed only for $rw$. The identity block supplies the bound on the remaining directions, giving $\min(1,\mu)$ on the full fiber, including after complexification.

e03-appa-frozen-inverse-bound.TorusEuler.norm_complexFrozenInverseSymb:
Put $
u=\min(1,\mu)$. Cauchy–Schwarz and coercivity give $\|A_0w\|\ge
u\|w\|$, which gives injectivity and a closed range. A vector orthogonal to the range in the underlying real Hilbert space satisfies $\operatorname{Re}\langle A_0w,wangle=0$ and must be zero; thus the range is also dense. This proves invertibility with bound $
u^{-1}$ even without self-adjointness. Lean first constructs the real inverse and then complexifies it.

e03-appa-smooth-projection.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_angularLeray: On the rescaled annulus $1/2\le|\xi|\le2$, the entries $\delta_{ij}-\xi_i\xi_j/|\xi|^2$ have derivatives through order five bounded by absolute constants. Homogeneity gives the corresponding bounds on all other annuli. Multiplying by the fixed time projection adds no angular derivatives and no factor depending on the dimension of the path space.

e03-appa-inverse-derivative.TorusEuler.fderiv_frozenSymbol_inverse_a: Differentiating $A_0A_0^{-1}=I$ gives $D(A_0^{-1})[h]=-A_0^{-1}(DA_0[h])A_0^{-1}$. Here $DA_0[h]=(Dr[h])B_0r+rB_0(Dr[h])-Dr[h]$, since $B_0$ is fixed. Thus the first derivative is bounded by two factors of the inverse norm times a bound for the derivatives of $r$ and the size of $B_0$.

e03-appa-five-angular-derivatives.TorusEuler.complexFrozenSymbols_fiveJets: After $m$ differentiations of the inverse, each term contains $q+1$ inverse factors and $q$ differentiated factors of $A_0$, with $q\le m$. On the unit annulus each differentiated factor costs at most $C_m(1+\|B_0\|)$, each inverse at most $\min(1,\mu)^{-1}$. Thus at most $2m+1$ powers of $2+\mu^{-1}+\|B_0\|$ are needed. Taking $m\le5$ yields the degree $11$ used in Lean, also for $A_0^{-1}r$ since the derivatives of $r$ are uniformly bounded.

e03-appa-frozen-multiplier-bound.TorusEuler.exists_uniform_freezingHalfHo: Both symbols $A_0^{-1}$ and $A_0^{-1}r$ give order-zero operators with the same type of half-Hölder bound. The first acts on $f$ in (A.7); the second takes the unprojected coefficient errors as its inputs. The formal estimate takes $C_0\le C(2+\mu^{-1}+\|B_0\|)^{11}$, which controls the dependence on $B_0$ in the subsequent choice of the cutoff radius.

e03-appa-dyadic-kernel-decay.TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay: Five integrations by parts at unit scale give decay $|y|^{-5}$, whereas inserting one frequency factor for a kernel derivative costs only a bounded factor on the annulus. Rescaling to $2^j$ gives $2^{3j}$ from volume and $2^{dj}$ from $d$ derivatives. The choice five is enough both for the integrable half-Hölder moment of the kernel and for summing the differentiated kernels away from the diagonal, which is needed for the far term of (A.7).

e03-appa-dyadic-half-power.TorusEuler.norm_operatorLiftConvolution_: The cancellation of the annular symbol at frequency zero gives $\int G_j=0$. Thus $G_j*f(a)=\int G_j(y)(f(a-y)-f(a))\,dy$, so its supremum norm is bounded by $[f]_{1/2}\int\|G_j(y)\||y|^{1/2}dy\le CC_0 2^{-j/2}[f]_{1/2}$. The corresponding gradient bound is $CC_0 2^{j/2}[f]_{1/2}$. For a separation $d\le1$ choose $2^J\le d^{-1}<2^{J+1}$: the sum of the low-block differences is $O(d2^{J/2})$, and that of the high-block differences is $O(2^{-J/2})$. Both are $O(d^{1/2})$. Lean proves the cancellation and the summation separately; the series converges uniformly, not necessarily in the full half-Hölder norm.

e03-appa-zero-mode-bound.TorusEuler.norm_complexFrozenInverseSymb: The annular blocks do not see the zero Fourier coefficient. Its output is $A_0(0)^{-1}\widehat f(0)$, with norm at most $\min(1,\mu)^{-1}\|f\|_\infty$. For mixed paths $r(0)=\mathcal Q$, not the identity. Bounding this constant term is needed for the supremum part of (A.6), although it contributes nothing to the Hölder seminorm.

e03-appa-localization-cutoff.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff: In Lean the cutoff can be Lipschitz: $\chi(a)=\max(0,\min(1,2-d(a,a_0)/r))$. It equals one in the inner ball and vanishes outside the outer ball. This suffices because it is multiplied into the source, not differentiated through the projected equation; only its supremum and first difference estimates are used.

e03-r2-appa-cutoff-one.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff_eq_one: For $d(a,a_0)\le r$ the expression $2-d(a,a_0)/r$ is at least one, so the clipped cutoff equals one. Thus the far source $(1-\chi)(B_0-B)v$ vanishes on the entire radius-$r$ ball. This permits differentiation of its convolution at the center without encountering the singularity of the frozen inverse kernel.

e03-r2-appa-cutoff-support.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff_eq_zero: Where $\chi$ is nonzero, the coefficient is evaluated at distance at most $2r$ from the frozen label. Hence $\|\chi(B_0-B)\|_\infty\le2r\operatorname{Lip}B$. This estimate depends on the size of the region, not on smallness of $\operatorname{Lip}B$ itself.

e03-r2-appa-cutoff-range.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff_mem_Icc: The useful consequence of $0\le\chi\le1$ for the far term is $\|(1-\chi)(B_0-B)v\|_\infty\le2\|B\|_\infty\|v\|_\infty$. This is independent of $r$. All dependence on the small radius in the far estimate comes from approaching the singularity of the frozen kernel, rather than derivatives of the cutoff.

e03-appa-cutoff-gradient-variant.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff_lipschitz: The distance function is $1$-Lipschitz and clipping to $[0,1]$ does not increase differences. Hence $|\chi(a)-\chi(b)|\le d(a,b)/r$ even when the two labels lie on opposite sides of a transition radius. This is the bound used in the product difference for the localized coefficient.

e03-appa-localized-identity.TorusEuler.freezingHalfHolderMultipliers: For projected $v$ we have $A_0(D)v=\mathcal RB_0v$. Adding and subtracting $\mathcal RBv=f$ gives the displayed formula. It is essential to split $(B_0-B)v$ before applying $\mathcal R$: the far product then vanishes near $a_0$, whereas its Leray projection in general does not. The operator on either piece is the combined multiplier with symbol $A_0^{-1}r$.
e03-appa-localized-identity.TorusEuler.exists_freezing_split_sources: The freezing center is chosen separately for each increment. For a nearby pair $a,b$, take $a_0=a$; then both points lie inside the ball where the far source vanishes. The near multiplier term can be bounded globally in the Hölder norm, whereas the far term needs only a bound for its increment from $a$ to $b$. For distant pairs the supremum of $v$ already bounds the quotient. This is how a local freezing identity gives a global estimate.

e03-appa-localized-coefficient-bounds.TorusEuler.localizedCoefficient_holderHa: Let $E=\chi(B_0-B)$ and $L_B=\operatorname{Lip}B$. The two points in the difference $E(a)-E(b)$ may not both be in the support. If at least one is, expand the product difference so that the undifferenced coefficient in the cutoff increment is taken at that point. Then the factor $r^{-1}d(a,b)$ from the cutoff is multiplied by at most $2rL_B$, and the other term is at most $L_Bd(a,b)$. This proves $\operatorname{Lip}E\le CL_B$ globally.

e03-appa-localized-half-holder.TorusEuler.localizedCoefficient_holderHa: The useful inequality is $\min(r,d)\le\sqrt{rd}$. Applying it to the size and Lipschitz bounds for $E=\chi(B_0-B)$ gives $[E]_{1/2}\le C\sqrt r\operatorname{Lip}B$. Since also $\|E\|_\infty\le Cr\operatorname{Lip}B$, the full half-Hölder norm becomes small for small $r$. The Lipschitz norm itself need not become small.

e03-appa-far-source-vanishes.TorusEuler.exists_freezing_split_sources: It is $(1-\chi)(B_0-B)v$, before applying $\mathcal R$, that vanishes on the radius-$r$ ball. Thus the kernel to estimate off the diagonal is the combined multiplier $A_0(D)^{-1}\mathcal R$. Its source has supremum at most $2\|B\|_\infty\|v\|_\infty$. No Hölder seminorm of the far source is needed to estimate its contribution near $a_0$.

e03-appa-far-source-radius.TorusEuler.exists_uniform_freezingHalfHo: For a distance $\rho>0$ from the singularity, split the dyadic gradient sum at $2^j\rho\simeq1$. The low-frequency sum of $2^{4j}$ and the high-frequency sum of $2^{-j}\rho^{-5}$ are both $O(\rho^{-4})$. Integrating this bound against a source separated by $r/2$ costs $C C_0\int_{r/2}^1\rho^{-2}d\rho\le C C_0/r$, with a bounded periodization remainder. For a pair at distance $d\le r/2$ the resulting Hölder quotient costs $C C_0r^{-1/2}\|B\|_\infty\|v\|_\infty$. Lean uses $d\le r/4$; larger pairs in the Hölder seminorm of $v$ are controlled directly by $\|v\|_\infty$.

e03-appa-remaining-supremum.TorusEuler.halfHolder_norm_le_of_frozen_: Let $Q_0$ denote the coefficient size enlarged by an absolute constant, and $L_B=\operatorname{Lip}B$. In Lean the near term costs $8C_0L_B\sqrt r\|v\|_{C^{0,1/2}}$, so $r=(1+16C_0L_B)^{-2}$ allows absorption. Since $C_0=O(Q_0^{11})$ and $L_B\le Q_0$, we get $r^{-1/2}=O(Q_0^{12})$. The far gradient costs $O(Q_0^{11}r^{-1})=O(Q_0^{35})$; with the size of the source the lower-order coefficient is $O(Q_0^{36})$. The formal bound deliberately overestimates the far increment by dropping its factor $\sqrt{r/4}\le1$.

e03-appa-holder-l2-interpolation.TorusEuler.unitTorus_sup_le_holderHalf_a: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$ average $v$ over the ball of radius $\varepsilon^2$ about a label $a$. The difference from $v(a)$ is at most $\varepsilon[v]_{1/2}$, while the norm of the average is at most $|B(a,\varepsilon^2)|^{-1/2}\|v\|_{L_a^2(H)}\le C\varepsilon^{-3}\|v\|_{L_a^2(H)}$. The exponent three comes from the volume $\simeq(\varepsilon^2)^3$. The averaging works directly for Hilbert-valued fields, since both inequalities estimate the norm of an integral.

e03-appa-absorb-supremum.TorusEuler.freezing_torus_absorb_supremu: There are two absorptions. Localization has already removed a small multiple of the Hölder norm; the remaining unwanted term is $C_1\|v\|_\infty$. Averaging with $\varepsilon=(2C_1)^{-1}$ makes half of that contribution absorbable and leaves a multiple of $C_1^4\|v\|_2$. The energy bound removes $\|v\|_2$ at cost $\mu^{-1}$. In Lean the lower-order coefficient has degree $36$, giving the energy contribution of degree $4\cdot36+1=145$; the forcing term costs only degree $11$ before absorption.

e03-appa-coefficient-continuation.TorusEuler.freezingCoefficientLine: On the fixed space, $S_s=\mathcal RB_s=(1-s)I+sS_1$. One interpolates the coefficients, not the inverses. The operators along this segment have the same projection constraints, and their quadratic forms interpolate between the identity form and (A.4). Hence the estimates proved for $S_1$ apply uniformly along the segment.

e03-appa-uniform-coercivity.TorusEuler.freezingHaarEmbedding_line_co: For each $s\in[0,1]$ the quadratic lower bound is $1-s+s\mu\ge\min(1,\mu)$. Also $\operatorname{Lip}B_s\le\operatorname{Lip}B$ and $\|B_s\|_\infty\le1+\|B\|_\infty$. Thus the localization radius and the final inverse estimate can be chosen once, for the whole continuation. No inverse at an intermediate $s$ is assumed when establishing that a priori estimate.

e03-appa-coordinate-words.TorusEuler.exists_halfHolderWords_norm_l: The printed proof establishes a priori estimates on $C^{k,1/2}$ and then obtains existence in that space by continuation. In Lean the derivative fields are constructed using the base inverse. `exists_halfHolderWords_norm_le` estimates those fields recursively, but a separate difference-quotient argument identifies them with the derivatives of the base solution. This last step is essential: the commutator estimate alone would only bound derivatives if they already existed.
e03-appa-coordinate-words.TorusEuler.hasSpatialHolderWords_iff_spa: The empty word is $v$. In `HasSpatialHolderWords`, the field $w(i::l)$ is the $i$-th coordinate derivative of the field $w(l)$, for words $l$ of length less than $k$. Thus $w([j,i])$ represents $\partial_j\partial_i v$. These are relations between actual half-Hölder fields; their continuity allows the coordinate derivatives to be assembled into Fréchet derivatives of the periodic lift.

e03-appa-differentiated-compression.TorusEuler.endpointStrongSpatialLeray_al: Let $w$ solve $\mathbb P(Bw)=\partial_i f-\mathbb P((\partial_i B)v)$ by the base inverse. With $\Delta_h=(\tau_h-I)/h$, subtract its equation from the exact equation for $\Delta_hv$. The source of the difference is $(\Delta_h f-\partial_i f)-\mathbb P((\Delta_hB)\tau_hv-(\partial_iB)v)$. This tends to zero in $L_a^2$ and stays bounded in $C^{0,1/2}$. Coercivity gives convergence of $\Delta_hv-w$ in $L_a^2$, and interpolation with its uniform Hölder bound gives uniform convergence. Thus $w=\partial_i v$ without assuming existence of the derivative or translation continuity in the full Hölder norm.
e03-appa-differentiated-compression.TorusEuler.endpointStrongMixedLeray_allS: For the mixed inverse one uses the same differentiated equation, replacing $\mathbb P$ by $\mathbb P\mathcal Q$. Translations in $a$ preserve both constraints. The coefficient derivative acts on a whole $L_t^2$ path, and the difference-quotient error tends to zero in $L_a^2(L_t^2)$ with a uniform mixed Hölder bound. This identifies the derivative in $a$ without differentiating the velocity in time.

e03-appa-higher-bound-induction.TorusEuler.paperA2_wordNorm_le:
For a word $
u$, each product term in $[\partial^
u,B_s]v$ has at least one derivative on $B_s$. Its derivative of $v$ therefore has order less than $|
u|$. The term $B_s\partial^
u v$ is kept on the left, where the base estimate applies. Every positive-order coefficient derivative is $s$ times the corresponding derivative of $B$, so induction gives a higher bound uniform for $0\le s\le1$.
e03-appa-higher-bound-induction.TorusEuler.exists_spatialHolderHalfNorm_: In fixed dimension the Fréchet derivative of each order is determined by its coordinate components. Bounds for the half-Hölder norms of all derivative words through order $k$ therefore bound $\|v\|_{C^{k,1/2}}$ by a constant depending only on $k$ and dimension times the common word bound. The linked estimate performs this conversion once the fields are known to be actual derivatives.

e03-appa-neumann-continuation.TorusEuler.freezingContinuationLine_isUn: On the fixed space, $S_s=\mathcal RB_s$. Factor $S_{s+h}=S_s[I+hS_s^{-1}(S_1-I)]$. For $|h|M_k\|S_1-I\|<1/2$, the bracket has a Neumann-series inverse. Although this gives a preliminary bound $2M_k$ at the new point, the a priori estimate restores $M_k$. Thus one can use a fixed step size and reach $s=1$ in finitely many steps without a growing sequence of inverse constants.
e03-appa-neumann-continuation.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_A_2: `Proof.lemma_A_2` supplies both base isomorphisms with exponent $145$. It obtains the higher-space conclusion from the direct derivative construction and the higher forward and inverse norm bounds, rather than running the continuation again on each higher space. The higher preimage is identified with the base preimage by injectivity. Thus the numbered result proves the same higher-space isomorphism, while the method used to establish regularity differs from the printed proof.

e03-appa-mixed-solution.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder: The mixed solve uses $-\mathbb P\mathcal QL$ and returns $v$ in the range of $\mathbb P\mathcal Q$. Its displacement already has both endpoint traces in the sense of integration of the path. At this stage we have no value $v(0)$, nor a pointwise-in-time velocity equation. Those are obtained below from the constant of integration and the fixed-time inverse.
e03-appa-mixed-solution.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_A_1_of: For $B(a)=K(a)-J\Omega(a)$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|Jw\|_{L_t^2}^2\le\int_0^T t\|w\|_{L_t^2}^2dt=\tfrac12T^2\|w\|_{L_t^2}^2$. Thus $\|B(a)-B(b)\|\le\sup_t|K(t,a)-K(t,b)|+(T/\sqrt2)\sup_t|\Omega(t,a)-\Omega(t,b)|$. This explains how the spatial coefficient estimate needed for Lemma A.2 is obtained even though $B(a)$ is an operator on entire paths.
e03-appa-mixed-solution.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_A_2: The mixed inverse produces a unique zero-mean solenoidal velocity path. The equation says that $\mathbb P(Bv+L)$ has zero fluctuation in time, but its time-independent part remains unknown. Taking the time average determines it. This is the intermediate weak equation from which the fixed-time problem (A.9) follows.

e03-appa-mixed-norm-bound.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder: The mixed norm bounds the displacement already: $\sup_t\|Jv(t)\|_{C_a^{0,1/2}}\le\sqrt T\|v\|_{C_a^{0,1/2}(L_t^2)}$. Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the values and to the difference of the paths at two labels. On the normalized interval $T=1$ the factor is one. This still does not bound $v(0)$, the quantity needed for the initial mean correction.
e03-appa-mixed-norm-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_A_1_of: The factors of the slab length cancel in the passage to a uniform-in-time estimate. In the mixed norm, $\|v\|\le A_m\sqrt T\|L\|_0$. Taking a time average costs $T^{-1/2}$, so the contribution of $Bv$ to $c$ is at most $CQA_m\|L\|_0$. The primitive costs $\sqrt T$, giving a contribution at most $CTQA_m\|L\|_0$. Thus for $T\le1$ one has $\|g\|_0\le C(1+QA_m)\|L\|_0$, and the second inverse gives the degree $2p_A+1$ when both base inverse bounds have degree $p_A$.

e03-appa-recover-constant.TorusEuler.endpointProjectedWeak_eq_mean:
The projected momentum $\mathbb P(Bv+L)$ is constant in time. Changing the order of integration in its average gives

$c=\mathbb P\int_0^1(K(s)v(s)-(1-s)\Omega(s)v(s)+L(s))\,ds$.

The constraint $\int_Iv=0$ does not remove the first two terms with general coefficients. This formula recovers $c$ directly from the mixed solution without taking a time trace; only after the second inversion can we identify it with the initial velocity for the force source of §4.3.

e03-appa-instantaneous-equation.TorusEuler.endpointWeakInstant_of_subtra: The source $g(t)=c+\mathbb P(J(\Omega v)(t)-L(t))$ is known from the mixed solution. Evaluation of $v$ at a prescribed time is not bounded on $L_t^2$, but evaluation of its primitive is: $w\mapsto\int_0^t w(s)\,ds$ is a bounded functional on $L_t^2$ (componentwise). Thus $g(t)$ can be formed for every time before one has a continuous velocity.

e03-appa-time-holder-increment.TorusEuler.continuous_and_norm_sub_le_en: For $s<t$ the map $w\mapsto\int_s^t w$ has norm at most $\sqrt{t-s}$ on $L_t^2$. Apply this also to the difference of $(\Omega v)(\cdot,a)$ and $(\Omega v)(\cdot,b)$, then divide by $d(a,b)^{1/2}$. This gives continuity of the primitive in the full spatial Hölder norm, not merely separately at each label. The term $L(t)$ in $g(t)$ requires only the assumed continuity in that same norm.

e03-r2-appa-fixed-time-inverse.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_A_1_of: The domain of $S(t)$ is now the solenoidal Hölder space at one time. No time-average constraint is imposed when inverting $S(t)$, because the source $g(t)$ has already been constructed using the whole path and its constant $c$. The next step is to show that the velocities obtained at separate times are a representative of that very path, rather than solutions of unrelated instantaneous equations.
e03-r2-appa-fixed-time-inverse.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.exists_solenoi: The fixed space of the spatial Leray projection is the solenoidal half-Hölder space. The linked lemma identifies the compressed equivalence with an equivalence on that space with forward map $u\mapsto\mathbb P(K(t)u)$. Hence applying Lemma A.2 at each $t$ gives the inverse family used in (A.9), with a common bound from the uniform coefficient and ellipticity estimates.

e03-appa-inverse-time-continuity.TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointFixedInv: From $S(t)^{-1}-S(s)^{-1}=S(t)^{-1}(S(s)-S(t))S(s)^{-1}$ and the common inverse bound $A_s$ we get $\|S(t)^{-1}-S(s)^{-1}\|\le CA_s^2\|K(t)-K(s)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}$. The coefficient multiplication estimate is the reason the right-hand side controls the operator difference on the solenoidal Hölder space. No time derivative of $K$ is needed. Together with continuity of $g$, this proves continuity of the recovered velocity on the closed interval.

e03-appa-continuous-representative.TorusEuler.exists_endpointContinuousRepr: The formula $\widetilde v(t)=S(t)^{-1}g(t)$ gives a continuous field for all $t$, while the earlier equation holds for almost every $t$ in spatial $L^2$. In Lean the comparison uses a continuous embedding of the Hölder space into $L^2$ and compatibility of the two projected operators under that embedding. Weak injectivity then gives $\widetilde v=v$ almost everywhere, preserving the endpoint integral.

e03-appa-weak-elliptic-injectivity.TorusEuler.endpointProjectedHilbertOpera: For almost every time both velocities satisfy the same equation in $L_a^2$, but the original one is not yet known to lie in the Hölder space. Their difference $u$ is solenoidal. Testing its equation against $u$ gives $\kappa\|u\|_2^2\le\langle K(t)u,u\rangle=\langle\mathbb P(K(t)u),u\rangle=0$. This is why the identification uses weak elliptic injectivity rather than simply invoking uniqueness of the Hölder inverse.

e03-appa-recovered-endpoint-traces.TorusEuler.endpointRecoveredPrimitive_ha: Let $E:C_a^{0,1/2}\hookrightarrow L_a^2$ be the inclusion. Since $E\widetilde v=v$ almost everywhere, $E(\int_I\widetilde v)=\int_Iv=0$. The inclusion is injective because a continuous label field that is zero almost everywhere is zero everywhere. Hence the strong primitive of $\widetilde v$ vanishes at both endpoints; its derivative is $\widetilde v$ in the Hölder norm, including the within-interval derivatives at the endpoints.

e03-appa-recover-pressure.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e: Let $G=Kv-J(\Omega v)+L-c$. The projected equation gives $\mathbb PG=0$ at every time, so its spatial zero mode is zero and $\widehat G(n)$ is parallel to $n$ for $n\ne0$. The mean-zero potential is obtained by $\widehat\phi(n)=(n\cdot\widehat G(n))/(2\pi i|n|^2)$, $\widehat\phi(0)=0$. Since $\nabla_a\phi=G$, the gradient has the regularity of the already controlled residual; no further inverse estimate for the velocity is needed.
e03-appa-recover-pressure.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_A_1_of: After recovering the continuous representative, $G=Kv-J(\Omega v)+L-c$ is continuous in the label Hölder norm. Its projection is zero almost everywhere in time, so continuity gives $\mathbb PG=0$ also at $0,1$. This is why the reconstructed pressure gradient solves the equation throughout the closed interval.

e03-appa-uniqueness-through-recovery.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: Uniqueness can be read in the order of reconstruction. The projected inverse fixes $v$; $z(0)=0$ fixes its primitive; averaging the projected equation fixes $c$; subtracting $c$ from the momentum fixes $\nabla\phi$. The scalar $\phi$ itself is only determined modulo a function constant in space at each time, unless its spatial mean is fixed.
e03-appa-uniqueness-through-recovery.TorusEuler.paperA1_solution_of_unproject: A competing unprojected solution satisfies $z=Jv$ and $Jv(1)=0$. Applying $\mathbb P$ to its equation gives the projected momentum identity, so it defines a solution in the same projected class. The linked theorem makes this implication explicit; uniqueness of the projected velocity and of $c$ can then be used for the full system.
e03-appa-uniqueness-through-recovery.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_A_1_of: For the difference of two solutions with the same $L$, $\mathcal R B\delta v=0$ and $\mathcal R\delta v=\delta v$. The path inverse gives $\delta v=0$. Then $\delta z=J\delta v=0$, and projecting $\delta c+\nabla\delta\phi=0$ gives $\delta c=0$, followed by $\nabla\delta\phi=0$.

e03-appa-smooth-inverse.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointFixedInver: At each order $k$, the forward operator $S(t)$ is smooth in operator norm because multiplication by $K(t)$ is smooth in the corresponding coefficient norm. Lemma A.2 puts $S(t)$ in the open set of bounded isomorphisms on the fixed solenoidal space. The first derivative of its inverse is $-S(t)^{-1}S_t(t)S(t)^{-1}$; repeated differentiation gives all time derivatives in operator norm.
e03-appa-smooth-inverse.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_A_1_of: The printed proof uses the higher-order clause of Lemma A.2 and smoothness of inversion on each higher Hölder space. In `Proof.theorem_A_1_of` only the base clause of the assumed Lemma A.2 is used. The proof solves the differentiated equations for every spatial derivative word in the base space, applies the time recovery to each word and assembles joint smoothness. Uniqueness identifies this solution with the one constructed for the base estimate. No separate higher-space inverse hypothesis is needed in this part of the formal argument.

e03-appa-primitive-derivative-gain.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointPrimitive_: For a fixed spatial Hölder space, if $v$ has $n$ continuous time derivatives there, so does $\Omega v$. Since $(J(\Omega v))'=\Omega v$, the primitive belongs to $C^{n+1}$ in time with values in that space. No label derivative is spent in taking this primitive. The formal result uses derivatives within the closed interval.

e03-appa-all-time-derivatives.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointVelocity_a: After obtaining continuity of $v$ in $C_a^{k,1/2}$, differentiate (A.9) once to get $S(t)v_t=\mathbb P(\Omega v-L_t)-S_t v$. At order $m+1$, all terms on the right involve at most $m$ time derivatives of $v$: the derivative of the primitive is $\Omega v$, and the other terms arise by differentiating $S$ at least once. Inversion at the same spatial order gives the next time derivative without spending a label derivative. Doing this for each $k$ gives joint smoothness.
e03-appa-all-time-derivatives.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: Once $v$ is smooth, the primitive gives smooth $z$, and the formula for the time-independent projected average gives smooth $c(a)$. Subtracting $c$ in $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L$ gives the smooth gradient. This proves the smoothness of the fields asserted in Theorem A.1 without requiring a separate time regularity theorem for an arbitrarily normalized scalar potential.
e03-appa-all-time-derivatives.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.theorem_A_1_of: The smoothness conclusion is what permits recovering the physical forced equation from the integrated momentum. In the paper one differentiates (4.9); the numbered Lean proof differentiates the projected version and recovers the pressure from the residual gradient. The resulting velocity has the original endpoint constraint, since the smooth solution was identified with the base solution by uniqueness.

e03-r2-appb-cutoff-symbol.TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol: The cutoff need not be radial. For every odd input to remain odd it suffices that the multipliers at $\xi$ and $-\xi$ agree, since the corresponding Fourier coefficients of an odd field are negatives of one another. Lean assumes evenness on $\mathbb R^3$; the plateau, support and range conditions are unchanged.
The radius is unchanged under $\zeta\mapsto-\zeta$, so the radial symbol satisfies the evenness clause of `CutoffSymbol`. All the other hypotheses on $\psi$ are retained.

e03-appb-multiplier-definition.TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff: The cutoff leaves the modes $|\xi|\le\Lambda$ unchanged and removes those with $|\xi|>2\Lambda$. The intervening smooth transition gives an integrable rescaled kernel with uniform mass. Thus one can prescribe a Fourier band for the next parent without a norm bound that grows with the number of retained modes.
e03-appb-multiplier-definition.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_B_1: The Fourier coefficient of the finite sum at $\xi$ is $\psi(\xi/\Lambda)\widehat f(\xi)$, by orthogonality of the torus characters. The theorem permits every positive scale and even symbol of the stated class; the real-vector coefficient is read in the complexification.

e03-appb-commutation.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_commutes_: Write $S_\Lambda f(x)=\int K_\Lambda(y)f(x-y)\,dy$ on the periodic lift. Differentiating in $x$ gives the same integral with $D^m f$ in place of $f$. The linked identity works with the full derivative tensor of a complex Banach-valued field; the same kernel therefore controls all its components.
e03-appb-commutation.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_derivativ: For a field with $C^{m,1/2}$ periodic lift, differentiation under the kernel integral gives the convolution of $D^mf$. This theorem concerns spatial derivatives; the commutation of time derivatives uses the fact that the multiplier is fixed in time.
e03-appb-commutation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_realVectorFo: The Fourier coefficients vary in time, but the finite set of modes and their multipliers do not. Thus the time derivative passes through the finite sum. The formal identity includes derivatives within the closed time interval, so it also applies at its endpoints.
e03-appb-commutation.TorusEuler.fderiv_lift_realVectorFourier: On a periodic mode, both orders of the operations give the multiplier $2\pi i\xi_i\psi(\xi/\Lambda)$. The linked identity gives this commutation for one spatial coordinate of a continuously differentiable real velocity; higher orders follow on smooth fields.
e03-appb-commutation.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_B_1: Spatial derivatives can be passed through the kernel and time derivatives through the fixed multiplier. The theorem packages arbitrary complex Banach-valued spatial orders and first real spatial and time derivatives; iteration gives the higher real derivatives when the fields are smooth.
e03-appb-commutation.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_B_1: The commutations use the scalar multiplier and the time-independent scale, not radiality. The formal theorem allows even symbols and $\Lambda>0$; the real-field higher-order commutations follow by iterating its first-derivative identities.

e03-appb-parity-support.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_admis: Truncation preserves oddness and divergence freeness exactly, though it does not preserve spatial localization. The next parent is supported on $|\xi|\le2\Lambda$. Its residual is supported on $|\xi|\le4\Lambda$: two velocity frequencies add in the stress, and the projected divergence and time derivative do not enlarge the band.
e03-appb-parity-support.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_support_p: Pair the modes at $\xi$ and $-\xi$: their multipliers agree, so both even and odd symmetry are preserved. The support assertion comes from vanishing of the symbol. This theorem is for complex Banach-valued fields; the divergence assertion for real velocities is separate.
e03-appb-parity-support.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_parit: Reflection of a real velocity commutes with the cutoff, since its Fourier kernel is even. This gives preservation of either parity; the real band limit and divergence properties are established by the other conclusions of Lemma B.1.
e03-appb-parity-support.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_B_1: On each mode the divergence is proportional to $\xi\cdot\widehat f(\xi)$, so multiplying by a scalar preserves its vanishing. Evenness preserves reflection symmetry and the support of $\psi$ gives the band limit. The proof needs no radiality and works at every positive scale.

e03-appb-operator-bounds.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_LInfinity: The bound is independent of $\Lambda$ because it is an integral bound on the kernel rather than a sum of bounds on its individual Fourier coefficients: $\|S_\Lambda f\|_\infty\le\|K_\Lambda\|_1\|f\|_\infty=\|K\|_1\|f\|_\infty$. This also holds for measurable essentially bounded inputs.
e03-appb-operator-bounds.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_LInfi: The same kernel mass bound holds for an essentially bounded measurable real velocity. No spatial derivatives of the velocity are needed; the half-Hölder estimate uses the separate bound on spatial increments.
e03-appb-operator-bounds.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realBanachCutoff: The real-valued version integrates the input against the real part of the spectral kernel.
